en: The Sutra on the Origin of the World, Scroll One.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Dharmagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter One: Jambudvīpa. Chapter One: Jambudvīpa.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at the Kaliṅga Cave in the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, after having finished their meal, a great number of bhikṣus there all came out and gathered in the Kaliṅga Hall.
Once they were seated, each gave rise to this thought and deliberated together, saying:
"O elders, this is unprecedented!
In this world, how do the heavens, the earth, sentient beings, and the lands where we dwell revolve and combine?"
How do they disperse?
How, having dispersed, do they reunite again?
And how, having reunited, do they abide in stability?

At that time, the World-Honored One was alone in a quiet cave. With his divine ear, which was pure and surpassing that of humans, he heard that after the bhikṣus had finished their meal, they had all gathered in the Kāliṅga Hall and were engaging in such extraordinary conversation.
Having heard this, the World-Honored One emerged from meditative concentration at the hour of late afternoon. He rose from the Karīra Cave and proceeded to the hall.
Upon arriving at the hall, he sat upright and composed upon the seat prepared as usual before the great assembly of bhikṣus.
When the World-Honored One was seated, he knew [the situation] yet asked intentionally:
"Monks, what conversation were you discussing just now as you sat gathered together?"
Then, all the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha together, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!
After our meal, the entire assembly of bhikṣus gathered here at the Kāliṅga Hall and deliberated together, speaking these words:"
"Venerable elders, this is most wonderful and rare!
How does the world thus revolve and coalesce?
How does the world thus revolve and disperse?"
"How does the world disperse and then reassemble?
How does the world, having reassembled, remain stable?
"Venerable World-Honored One!"
"Just now we had these words, and for that reason we gathered to deliberate on this matter.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent,
O bhikṣus! You are able to practice with such faith in accordance with the Dharma.
"Sons of good family!
Because you have left the home life out of faith, it is inconceivable that you, being such as yourselves, can gather together and sit thus, engaging in discourse in accordance with the Dharma."

When you, bhikṣus, gather and sit together, you should cultivate these two kinds of Dharma-practice, each performing their respective tasks: either discussing the meaning of the Dharma or maintaining noble silence, without giving rise to indolence.
If you are able to do so, you should listen to this meaning as taught by the Tathāgata:
the world undergoes dissolution, the world undergoes formation; having undergone dissolution, it returns to formation; and having undergone formation, it remains stable.
When he had spoken these words, the bhikṣus together addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable World-Honored One!
Now is the time; Sugata, now is the occasion."
“If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, explains such a meaning for the sake of the bhikṣus, the bhikṣus, having heard what the World-Honored One has said, should uphold it accordingly.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: “You bhikṣus!...”
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it to you in due order.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha together, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
"We wish to hear it with joy.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!..."
Just as the sun and moon, in the course of their movement, illuminate the four continents, so too, within those worlds of the four continents, there are a thousand suns and moons, O bhikṣus!
This is what is called a "small thousandfold world system. O Bhikṣus!
Within a small thousandfold world system, there are a thousand moons, a thousand suns, a thousand Sumeru Kings of Mountains, and four thousand minor mountains.
four continents, four thousand great continents, four thousand small seas, four thousand great oceans,
four thousand lineages of nāgas, four thousand great lineages of nāgas, four thousand lineages of garuḍas, four thousand great lineages of garuḍas,
four thousand lineages of evil destinies, and four thousand great evil destinies.
The abodes of the lineage, four thousand minor kings, four thousand great kings, seven thousand varieties of great trees,
eight thousand varieties of great mountains, ten thousand varieties of great hells,
one thousand Yama kings, one thousand Jambudvīpas, one thousand Aparagoyānīs, one thousand Pūrvavidehas, and one thousand Uttarakurus.
Lakṣmī, one thousand gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, one thousand gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three,
one thousand gods of the Yāma Heaven, one thousand gods of the Tuṣita Heaven, one thousand gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, one thousand gods of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven,
one thousand gods of the Māra realm, and one thousand gods of the Brahma-world.
"O bhikṣus!
In that Brahma-world there is a Brahmā Lord whose power is most supreme and whom none can overcome; he presides over a realm of a thousand sovereign Brahmās and declares:
'I am the creator, the transformer, and the magician.'"
He says, "I am like my father.
By making such boastful and arrogant statements regarding various matters, he immediately gives rise to conceit.
The Tathāgata is not so.
Why is this? All worlds arise and manifest as this world according to their respective karmic forces.

O monks! Just as this small chiliocosm is like a *cūḍā*—the word *cūḍā* meaning "topknot" in the language of Sui—where foreigners bind a small amount of long hair on the crown of their heads into a topknot, so is it called a "thousandfold world-system."
"Monks! A thousand world-systems such as that of Cakravāḍa is called the second intermediate thousand-world system. Monks!"
Just as there is one second-order intermediate thousand-world system, so too are there as many first-order intermediate thousand-world systems;
this is called a trichiliocosm, monks!

This trichiliocosm, at one time contracts and merges; having contracted and merged, it then disperses again; having dispersed, it then contracts once more; and having contracted, it remains stable. Thus, when this world-system revolves and burns all around, it is called "ruination";
when it revolves and merges all around, it is called "accomplishment";
and when it revolves and remains stable all around, it is called "establishment."
This is the dwelling place of the sentient beings in the single Buddha-field called Abhayā. "O Bhikṣus!
This great earth is forty-eight hundred thousand yojanas in thickness, and its circumference is immeasurable."
"Monks! This great earth rests upon the waters; the waters rest upon the wind; and the wind depends upon space. Monks!"
The mass of water beneath this great earth is sixty thousand yojanas thick, with an immeasurable breadth.
Beneath that mass of water is a mass of wind, thirty-six thousand yojanas thick, with an immeasurable breadth.
"O bhikṣus!
The deepest part of that great ocean is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, and its breadth is immeasurable.
O bhikṣus!"
That King of Mountains, Sumeru, enters eighty-four thousand yojanas into the waters of the ocean, and likewise rises eighty-four thousand yojanas above the surface of the water.
O bhikṣus!
Sumeru, the King of Mountains, has a level and even base; its lower roots extend down and rest upon the great golden wheel. O bhikṣus!

This Sumeru, the King of Mountains, within the great ocean, is narrow at the bottom and broad at the top, gradually widening as it rises; it is straight and not crooked, possessing a firm and massive body that is most exquisite and sublime, wonderful and beautiful to behold, composed of four treasures, namely: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Various kinds of trees grow there, their foliage lush and verdant, emitting diverse fragrances that waft afar and pervade all the mountains.
It is the dwelling place of many holy sages and supreme, majestic, and wondrous devas.
"O Bhikṣus!

On the upper portion of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, there are peaks in the four directions. These peaks jut out from the sides with protruding corners, each seven hundred yojanas in height, exquisite and delightful, composed of the seven treasures—namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musāragalva, and aśmagarbha—and adorned with these, they curve down toward the great ocean."
"O Bhikṣus! Beneath Mount Sumeru there are three terraces, which are the dwellings of various deities.

The lowest terrace is sixty yojanas in length and breadth; it is surrounded on all sides by sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets of bells, and sevenfold rows of *tāla* trees, which are delightful and beautiful to behold. These trees are all composed of the seven treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate."

Each of those walls has four gates, and at each gate there are battlements, all fully adorned with multi-storied pavilions, balconies, defensive towers, watchtowers, palaces, halls, corridors, groves, gardens, and various ponds and marshes.

From the ponds emerge exquisite lotuses with various blended fragrances; there are trees of every kind, with diverse stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits, all perfectly complete, and they also emit various subtle and wonderful scents.
Furthermore, there are various birds, each producing exquisite sounds; their calls blend together in a manner that is harmonious, elegant, and crystal clear.

Within this area, which is divided into tiers and measures forty yojanas in length and breadth, all the adornments—such as the sevenfold walls, railings, networks of bells, and rows of *tāla* trees—are delightful and perfectly level.
It was perfectly symmetrical on all sides and adorned with the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.
The gates, pavilions, towers, terraces, palaces, gardens, ponds, fruit trees, and various birds were all fully present.
Its upper tier measured twenty yojanas in length and breadth; it featured sevenfold walls, and even the birds each produced wondrous sounds.
"O bhikṣus!
Among the lower ranks, there dwell yakṣas named Pāṇi;
among the middle ranks, there are yakṣas named Mālādhāra."
Within its upper tiers dwell various yakṣas named Constantly Drunk. "O bhikṣus!
Forty-two thousand yojanas from the midpoint of Mount Sumeru lie the palaces of the Four Great Heavenly Kings."
"O Bhikṣus!
Upon Mount Sumeru, there are the celestial palaces of the Thirty-three Gods, where Śakra dwells;
one double height above the Heaven of the Thirty-three, there dwell the celestial palaces of the Yāma gods."
Above the Yāma Heaven, at twice its distance, dwell the celestial palaces of the Tuṣita gods;
above the Tuṣita Heaven, at twice its distance, dwell the celestial palaces of the Nirmāṇarati gods;
above the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, at twice its distance, dwell the celestial palaces of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods.
Above the other Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, at double the distance, there dwell the Brahmakāyika devas in their celestial palaces;
between the other Paranirmita-vaśavartins above and the Brahmakāyikas below, there dwell the various palaces of Māra Pāpīyan;
and at double the height of the Brahmakāyikas, there is the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Twice the height of Ābhāsvara is the extent of Śubhakṛtsna;
twice the height of Śubhakṛtsna is the extent of Bṛhatphala;
and twice the height of Bṛhatphala is the extent of Avṛha.
Between the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala) and the Heaven of No Coarseness (Atapa), there are other celestial palaces situated therein called the Abode of Non-conceptual Beings (Asaṃjñisattva).
Above the Heaven of No Coarseness, twofold higher, is the Heaven of No Affliction (Atāpa);
above the Heaven of No Affliction, twofold higher, is the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudarśana).
Twice the height of the Sudarśana Heaven above is the Sudṛśa Heaven;
twice the height of the Sudṛśa Heaven above is the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, the palace of the various devas. O bhikṣus!

Above Akaniṣṭha, there are further devas known as the Heaven of the Sphere of Infinite Space, the Heaven of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the Heaven of the Sphere of Nothingness, and the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; all these are collectively termed the abodes of the devas.
"O bhikṣus! Such are the places and such are the realms where sentient beings dwell.
Such are these sentient beings, whether coming or going, being born or passing away, reaching the very limits of existence."
In this world, all classes of sentient beings are subject to birth, old age, and death; they abide within such paths of existence and do not transcend them.
For this reason, it is called the Sahā World, the fearless land.
In all other worlds as well, it is likewise so. "O Bhikṣus!
To the north of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, there is a continent named Uttarakuru; its land is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth, perfectly square on all four sides."
Moreover, the faces of those people resemble the shape of that land. Monks!
To the east of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, there is a continent named Pūrvavideha; its land is nine thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and it is as circular as the full moon.
The faces of the people there resemble the shape of the land itself. Monks!
To the west of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, there is a continent named Aparagoyānī; its ground is eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and its shape is like a half-moon.
The faces of those people resemble the shape of their land. Monks!

To the south of Sumeru, the king of mountains, there is a continent named Jambudvīpa; its ground is seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth, wide in the north and narrow in the south, shaped like the box of a carriage.
The human faces therein resemble the features of the terrain. "O Bhikṣus!
The northern face of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, is composed of celestial gold and illuminates that continent of Uttarakuru."
Its eastern face is composed of celestial silver and illuminates the continent of Pūrvavideha;
its western face is composed of celestial crystal and illuminates the continent of Aparagoyānī;
its southern face is composed of celestial blue lapis lazuli and illuminates this continent of Jambudvīpa.

“O Bhikṣus! On the continent of Uttarakuru, there is a great tree named Āmra. Its trunk is seven yojanas in circumference and breadth, it extends twenty-one yojanas deep into the earth, rises one hundred yojanas high, and its branches and foliage spread out and cover fifty yojanas.”
"O Bhikṣus!

On the continent of Pūrvavideha, there is a great tree named Kadamba. Its trunk is seven yojanas in width and breadth, it extends twenty-one yojanas deep into the earth, it rises to a height of one hundred yojanas, and its branches and leaves spread out and cover fifty yojanas."
"O Bhikṣus!
On the continent of Aparagoyānī, there is a great tree named Tiṇḍuka; its trunk is seven yojanas in circumference, and its branches and leaves extend to cover fifty yojanas."
Beneath that tree there is a stone ox, one yojana in height; for this reason, it is called the continent of Godānīya.
O bhikṣus!
In this Jambudvīpa, there is a great tree named Jambu; its trunk is seven yojanas in circumference and width, and its branches and leaves extend to cover fifty yojanas.
Beneath that tree, there was a mass of Jambūnada gold twenty yojanas high; because this gold originated from beneath the Jambū tree, it is therefore called Jambūnada.
"Jambūnada gold" is named for this reason. "O Bhikṣus!
In the abode of the nāgas and garuḍas, there is a great tree called Kūṭaśālmali, whose trunk is seven yojanas in height and breadth, and whose branches and leaves extend to cover fifty yojanas."
"O bhikṣus!
In the realm of the asuras, there is a great tree named Sujātāpāṭala; its trunk is seven yojanas in length and breadth, and its branches and leaves extend to cover fifty yojanas."
"O Bhikṣus!

Among the Trāyastriṃśa devas, there is a great tree named Pārijātaka-kovidāra. Its trunk is seven yojanas in circumference and breadth; it extends twenty-one yojanas into the earth and rises one hundred yojanas high, with its branches and leaves covering fifty yojanas."
“O Bhikṣus!

Beneath Mount Sumeru, there is another mountain named Khadiraka, forty-two thousand yojanas in height and likewise in width at the top; it is delightful and upright, composed of the seven treasures, namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musāragalva, and agate.”
"O bhikṣus!
Between Mount Sumeru and Mount Khadiraka, the distance is eighty-four thousand yojanas, and its circumference is immeasurable."
The waters are completely covered with *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, and *saugandhika* lotuses. Monks!

Next, outside of Khadiraka, there is a mountain named Īṣādhara, twenty-one thousand yojanas high and as many wide at the top; it is exquisite and delightful, composed of the seven precious substances such as agate and so forth.
Between those two mountains, Khadiraka and Īṣādhara, the width is forty-two thousand yojanas, and its circumference is immeasurable.
Blue lotuses (utpala), red lotuses (padma), white lotuses (kumuda), pink lotuses (puṇḍarīka), and saugandhika flowers completely cover the waters.

Next, outside of Īṣādhara, there is a mountain named Yugandhara, twelve thousand yojanas in height and likewise in width at its summit; it is delightful and exquisite, composed of the seven treasures such as agate and so forth.
Between the two mountains, Īṣādhara and Yugandhara, the expanse is twenty-one thousand yojanas wide and its circumference is immeasurable.
Blue lotuses (utpala), red lotuses (padma), white lotuses (kumuda), yellow lotuses (puṇḍarīka), and saugandhika flowers completely cover the waters.

Next, outside Gandhāra, there is a mountain named Sudarśana, six thousand yojanas high and as many wide at the summit; it is delightful and exquisite, composed even of the seven treasures such as agate.
The region of Kāñcanamālā lies between Mount Sudarśana and Mount Yugandhara; it is twelve thousand yojanas wide and its circumference is immeasurable.
It is completely covered with waters filled with *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, and *saugandhika* lotuses.

Next, outside of Sudarśana, there is a mountain named Aśvakarṇa (Horse-Ear), three thousand yojanas high and as wide at the top; it is delightful and beautiful, composed of the seven precious substances such as agate and so forth.
Between the mountains of Sudarśana and Aśvakarṇa, the width is six thousand yojanas and the circumference is immeasurable.
The waters are completely covered with *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, and *saugandhika* lotuses.

Next, outside the Horse-Head [Mountain], there is a mountain named Nimindhara, one thousand two hundred yojanas in height and likewise in width at the summit; it is delightful and exquisite, composed even of the seven treasures such as agate.
Between the two mountains, Aśvakarṇa and Nimindhara, the expanse is two thousand four hundred yojanas wide and its circumference is immeasurable.
It is completely covered with waters filled with *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, and *saugandhika* lotuses.

Next, outside of Nimindhara, there is a mountain named Vinataka, six hundred yojanas in height and the same in width at its summit; it is exquisite and delightful, composed even of the seven treasures such as agate.
Between the two mountains, Nimiṃdhara and Vinataka, the width is one thousand two hundred yojanas, and its circumference is immeasurable.
Various kinds of flowers, up to and including the saugandhika, completely cover all the waters.

Next, outside of Vinataka, there is a mountain named Cakravāḍa (Sui: "wheel"), three hundred yojanas high and as wide at the top; it is exquisite and delightful, composed of the seven treasures such as agate and so forth.
Between those two mountains, Vinataka and Cakravāḍa, the width is six hundred yojanas and the circumference is immeasurable.
Four kinds of variegated flowers and saugandhika lilies completely cover all the waters.
"Not far from Mount Cakravāḍa, there is a vacant space where green grass spreads everywhere and there is a great ocean.

To the north of that great ocean stands a king of trees called the Jambu tree; its trunk has a circumference of seven yojanas, its roots extend twenty-one yojanas into the earth, it is one hundred yojanas high, and its branches and leaves hang down and cover fifty yojanas on all four sides. In the vacant space surrounding it, green grass spreads everywhere."
Next there are groves of āmra trees, jambu trees, tāla trees, and nāda trees, each fifty yojanas in length and breadth, with open spaces between them where various green grasses grow.

Next there are a male grove named Tree Forest and a female grove named Tree Forest, as well as the Śāṇḍana Forest and the Cāndana Forest; each is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, and their surrounding empty spaces are covered with lush green grass.
Next there were groves of harītakī fruit trees, bhallātaka fruit trees, āmalaka fruit trees, and āmrātaka fruit trees, each measuring fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Next there are the Kakkola groves, the Bilva fruit groves, the Panasa fruit groves, and the pomegranate fruit groves, each measuring fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Next are the Kāśa groves, Naḍa groves, Ikṣu groves, Sūkṣma-veṇu groves, and Mahā-veṇu groves, each fifty yojanas in width.
Next are the Śarī groves, Veṇu groves, Kara groves, Mahākara groves, and Kaśamanda groves, each fifty yojanas in width.

Next there are groves of atimuktaka flowers, campaka flowers, pāṭala flowers, and rose flowers, each fifty yojanas in width; the empty spaces along their borders are entirely covered with green grass.
Furthermore, there are various ponds completely covered with *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers.
There are also various ponds filled with venomous snakes, each fifty *yojanas* in width; the empty spaces between them are entirely covered with lush green grass.

"Next there is a sea named Ucchanaka, twelve yojanas in breadth. Its waters are clear and cool, its taste is exceedingly sweet, and it is light, soft, and limpid. It is surrounded on all sides by sevenfold layers of brickwork, sevenfold alternating patterns, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold networks of bells; outside these are seven rows of *tāla* trees. It is exquisitely beautiful and adorned with the seven treasures, being composed of sapphire and the other six precious gems."

Extending throughout the four directions, there are various stairways and pathways, lovely and well-proportioned, composed likewise of the seven treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.
Furthermore, there were *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers.
Those flowers that were the color of fire immediately manifested the form of fire;
those that were golden immediately manifested the form of gold.
Those that were blue manifested as blue forms;
those that were red manifested as red forms;
those that were white manifested as white forms.
It has the color of *bāhudā* and manifests the form of *bāhudā*.
Its flowers are like chariot wheels, and their stalks are like chariot axles.
From the roots of these flowers flows a sap, white in color like milk and sweet in taste like honey.
“Monks! Within the ocean of Ucchanaka, there are paths for the wheel-turning sage kings (cakravartin rājas) to travel, twelve yojanas wide above. Monks!”
When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world within Jambudvīpa, those various sea routes naturally emerge and become level with the surface of the water.
"O bhikṣus!
Beyond the ocean of Ucchanaka, there is a mountain named Ucchankala.
O bhikṣus!"
That Mount Ucchankhala is delightful, upright, subtle, and beautiful to behold.

All kinds of trees, leaves, flowers, fruits, and fragrances, as well as various exotic grasses and diverse birds and beasts—whatever things exist in the world—are all present upon that Mount Ucchankhala without exception.
"O bhikṣus!
This Mount Ucchaṅgala is thus delightful, upright, and beautiful to behold; you should maintain this well."
“Monks! Beyond Ucchangala there is a mountain named Suvarṇakukṣi. Monks!”
Within Mount Suvarṇakakṣa, there are eighty thousand caves.
Within those caves dwell eighty thousand nāga-elephants, all of whom are white like the kumuda flower;
they support themselves on seven limbs touching the ground, possess supernatural powers, and travel through the air.
Their crests are red in color, like the indragopaka insect;
they all possess six tusks, which are slender and sharp, inlaid with gold of various colors.

“Monks! Beyond Mount Suvarṇakakṣa there is a mountain called Himavat. It is five hundred yojanas high, and its breadth and thickness are likewise; that mountain is exquisite, composed of four precious substances: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.”
At the four corners of that mountain, four golden peaks protrude, each twenty yojanas high.
Within them, there are further peaks composed of various jewels, rising one hundred yojanas high.
In the center of that mountain peak is Lake Anavatapta, where the Dragon King Anavatapta dwells.

The lake is fifty yojanas in length and breadth; its waters are cool, sweet, light, and delicious, pure and free from turbidity. It is encircled on all sides by sevenfold tiers of brickwork, sevenfold pavements of stone slabs, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold networks of bells—all of which are delightful and beautiful, composed of the seven treasures including agate.
Furthermore, there were various flowers—*utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka*—of diverse colors: blue, yellow, red, and white; these flowers were as large as chariot wheels.
Furthermore, there are lotus roots as large as chariot axles, their sap white as milk and their flavor like honey.
"O Bhikṣus! Within the Lake Anavatapta, there is the palace of the Nāga King Anavatapta; its hall has five pillars and is exquisite and delightful."
The Naga King Anavatapta, together with his retinue, sports therein, enjoying the five celestial desires and possessing perfect happiness.
O Bhikṣus!
To the east of Lake Anavatapta is the Ganges River, which issues from the elephant’s mouth; together with five hundred tributary rivers, it flows into the eastern ocean.
To the south of Lake Anavatapta is the Sindhu River, which issues from the bull’s mouth; together with five hundred tributary rivers, it flows into the southern ocean.
To the west of Lake Anavatapta is the Vakṣu River, which issues from the horse’s mouth; together with five hundred tributary rivers, it flows into the western ocean.
To the north of Lake Anavatapta is the Sītā River, which issues from the Lion’s Mouth and flows into the Northern Sea together with five hundred tributary rivers. "O bhikṣus!
For what reason is this dragon named Anavatapta?
Monks! There are three reasons.
What are these three? Monks! Within Jambudvīpa there dwell various nāgas;

with the exception of the Nāga King Anavatapta, when all the other nāgas experience pleasure, hot sand immediately falls upon their bodies. Those nāgas all lose their celestial forms and colors, manifesting instead the form and color of snakes; thus those nāgas undergo such suffering at that time.
The Nāga King Anavatapta does not experience such things; this is called the first causal condition. Monks!

Within Jambudvīpa, with the exception of the Nāga King Anavatapta, when all other nāgas sport and enjoy themselves, a hot wind arises and blows upon their bodies, whereby they immediately lose their celestial forms and manifest the shape and color of snakes; such is their suffering.
For the Nāga King Anavatapta, such a thing does not occur; this is called the second causal condition. Monks!

Whenever the various nāgas within Jambudvīpa are sporting and enjoying themselves, the Golden-Winged Bird King flies into their palaces. Upon seeing the Golden-Winged Bird King, they are struck with terror; because of that terror, they immediately lose their celestial forms and manifest the shape of snakes, fully experiencing that suffering.
The Naga King Anavatapta is not like that; if a Garuda were to give rise to such a thought as, "I now wish to enter the palace of the Naga King Anavatapta," [it would be impossible].
"At that time, because his merit was inferior, that garuḍa immediately suffered for himself and was unable to enter the palace of the Nāga King Anavatapta.
O Bhikṣus!"
This is the third causal condition; for this reason, it is called Anavatapta. "O Bhikṣus!
Not far from the southern side of the Snowy Mountains, there is a city named Vaiśālī."
To the north of Vaiśālī are the Seven Black Mountains; to the north of the Seven Black Mountains lies the Fragrant Mountain (Gandhamādana).
Within that Fragrant Mountain, there are immeasurable kinnaras who constantly produce the sounds of song, dance, and music.
That mountain abounds with various kinds of trees, each tree emitting various fragrant incenses, and it is the dwelling place of deities of great majesty and virtue.
O bhikṣus!
Within that Fragrant Mountain, there are two jewel caves:
the first is named Variegated (Citraprabha) and the second is named Well-Variegated (Sucitraprabha).

They are exquisite and delightful, composed of the seven treasures including agate; each is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, soft and smooth, such that touching them is like touching a kāñcanatiktaka garment.
"O Bhikṣus!

Within those two caves, the Variegated and the Well-Variegated, there dwells a gandharva king named Anupama, together with five hundred kinnarī maidens. There they reside, fully enjoying the five objects of desire, sporting and playing as they walk, stand, sit, and lie down."

“Monks! To the north of the two caves, Variegated and Well-Variegated, there is a great king of sāla trees named Supratiṣṭhita. That king of sāla trees, Supratiṣṭhita, is surrounded on all sides by eight thousand sāla groves.”
At that time, beneath the Śāla grove where he dwelt, there lived a nāga-elephant who was also named Suvilīta.
His color was pure white, like a kumuda flower;
his seven limbs touched the ground as he moved through the air.
The crown of his skull is elevated like the indragopaka insect;
his head is crimson in color;
he is endowed with six tusks that are slender and sharp, and upon these tusks are specks of golden sand.

Furthermore, there were eight thousand other dragon-elephants as his retinue; they were all white in color like the kumuda flower, with seven limbs touching the ground, and their tusks were entirely adorned with gold.

Directly to the north of that Forest of the Well-Established Śāla Tree King, there is a lake born from the Great Naga Elephant King Suvyavasthita, named Mandākinī, which is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, being perfectly equal in all dimensions.

The water is cool, refreshing, sweet, and pure, free from all turbidity or impurity; even the lotus roots are as large as chariot axles, and when broken, they exude a sap white as milk and as sweet as honey.
"O bhikṣus!
Surrounding that Mandākinī pool, there are eight thousand other pools that encircle it, each one exactly like the Mandākinī pool."
Those eight thousand ponds were likewise so. "O Bhikṣus!

Whenever the mind of the Nāga-elephant king Supratiṣṭhita desired to enter the Mandākinī pond for sport and pleasure, he would then immediately call to mind his retinue of eight thousand nāga-elephants."
At that time, those eight thousand dragon-elephants also gave rise to this thought:
"Our noble king, the Dragon-Elephant King Sthira, is thinking of us.
We should now go to the presence of King Sthira."
When the various dragon-elephants had arrived, they stood with their heads bowed before the Great Dragon-Elephant King, Sunāman.
At that time, the Great Dragon-Elephant King, Sunāman, immediately proceeded toward the Mandākinī Pond.
At that time, those eight thousand nāga-elephants surrounded him from front and back.
King Supratiṣṭhita proceeded with steady grace;
among the host of nāga-elephants, some held white parasols to shade him, while others held white maṇi-jewel whisks in their trunks to fan him.
Before him were various musical deities, singing, dancing, and performing as they led the way.

When the Great Nāga Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita arrived, he entered that Mandākinī pool, diving in and out in joyful sport, bathing and playing, following his heart’s desire and moving about in the enjoyment of pleasure.
Among them were dragon-elephants washing their trunks;
some dragon-elephants were rubbing their tusks;
and some dragon-elephants were scratching their ears.
Some dragon-elephants poured water over his head;
some dragon-elephants sprinkled water upon his back;
and some dragon-elephants rubbed his flanks.
Some dragon-elephants washed their thighs;
some dragon-elephants washed their feet;
some dragon-elephants bathed their tails.
Some nāga-elephants, having pulled up lotus roots with their trunks and washed them clean, placed them into the mouths of the well-established nāga-elephants;

others, having plucked blue lotuses (*utpala*), red lotuses (*padma*), night-blooming water lilies (*kumuda*), and white esculent lilies (*puṇḍarīka*) with their trunks, fastened them upon the heads of the well-established nāga-elephant kings.

At that time, the Great Nāga Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita, within that Mandākinī pool, bathed and sported at will according to his heart’s desire; having enjoyed himself with unrestrained joy and received great pleasure, he ate the lotus roots offered by the other nāga elephants and adorned his head with various flowers such as the *utpala*.
Having completed their adornments, they emerged from that pond and stood upon the bank.

At that time, those eight thousand nāga-elephants each dispersed into their respective eight thousand ponds, bathing at will and sporting with ease. Having enjoyed these pleasures, they all ate the lotus roots within the ponds; having eaten, they then adorned themselves with various flowers such as the *utpala* upon their heads.
Having been adorned with flowers, they all gathered together and assembled at the side of the Great Dragon-Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita, surrounding him on all four sides.

At that time, the Great Dragon-Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita, accompanied by those eight thousand dragon-elephants as his vanguard and retinue, intended to return to the forest of the Sala-tree king named Supratiṣṭhita.

As he proceeded on his journey, the various dragon-elephants either held aloft white parasols or grasped white *maṇi* whisks; furthermore, various deities played all manner of music as they led the way before him.
"At that time, the Great Naga Elephant King, Susthitamati, arrived at the foot of the king of trees in the Susthita Sāla Forest and remained there, rising and reclining as he pleased.
Then, those eight thousand naga elephants also each went to the feet of their respective eight thousand sāla trees in the forest, moving, standing, reclining, and rising with ease and comfort."
At that time, in that forest there were sāla trees; some had trunks with a circumference of six fathoms;
some sāla trees had trunks with a circumference of seven or eight fathoms, or nine or ten;
some sāla trees had trunks with a circumference of twelve fathoms; and that king of sāla trees, Sthira, had a trunk with a circumference of sixteen fathoms.
In that forest of eight thousand śāla trees, whatever withered and yellowed leaves fell were immediately blown away by a wind, so as not to defile the grove.
"Monks! Whenever those eight thousand nāga-elephants voided excrement or urine, yakṣas would sweep it up and cast it away."

When a Wheel-Turning King appears in Jambudvīpa, among those eight thousand dragon-elephants, there is the smallest dragon-elephant who comes before the Wheel-Turning King every morning to provide service and attend upon him; for this reason, he is named the Well-Tamed Elephant King.

Furthermore, on the morning of the fifteenth day, the Great King of Naga-Elephants, Supratiṣṭhita, would go to the presence of Śakra, Lord of the Devas; standing before the deity, he would attend to him and carry out his commands.
"O monks! That Great King of Elephants, Supratiṣṭhita, possesses such supernormal powers and such majestic virtue.
Although he was born among the animals as one of the dragon species, he nevertheless wields such great power and spiritual majesty."
"You all should maintain this in mind and uphold it thus.
**Chapter Two: On Uttarakuru-dvīpa** *Qishi jing*, Chapter on Uttarakuru-dvīpa, Part One. "O Bhikṣus! [Listen as I explain]..."
In that continent of Uttarakuru, there are immeasurable mountains.
Among those various mountains are all kinds of trees;
these trees are lush and verdant, emitting all manner of fragrances.
Its fragrance wafts everywhere, pervading that entire place.

Various kinds of grass grow there, all of a deep blue-green color, curling to the right like peacock feathers; their scent is like that of the pāriyātraka flower, and they are as soft to the touch as kāñcanatanti cloth. They are four finger-widths in length; when one places a foot upon them, they bend down, and when the foot is lifted, they spring back up.

There are various kinds of trees, from which emerge diverse stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits; they are perfumed with various fragrances, and various birds each sing their own songs, harmonious, elegant, and exquisite.
Those various mountains have diverse rivers that branch out in all directions; they flow smoothly downward, gradually and peacefully, without waves and not with great speed.
Their banks are not deep, being level and shallow, easy to cross;
the water is pure, covered with various flowers, and flows in a wide expanse of half a yojana, filling the entire course.

On both banks of those rivers, there are various groves of trees that reflect upon the water; diverse fragrant flowers and green grasses are spread everywhere, abounding with many kinds of fruits, while flocks of birds all sing.

Furthermore, on both banks of those rivers, there are many exquisite boats of various pleasing colors, all fashioned from the seven treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.

“Monks! That continent of Uttarakuru has level and even ground, free from thorns, pits, ravines, or dense forests. It is also devoid of privies, filth, impurities, as well as gravel, stones, and rubble; it consists entirely of gold and silver.”
It is neither cold nor hot, and the seasons are harmonious.

Furthermore, the ground is perpetually moist and lush, covered everywhere with green grass; the various groves of trees always have flourishing foliage, and their flowers and fruits are fully ripened.
"O Bhikṣus!

In the continent of Uttarakuru, there are forest groves called 'Abiding' (Pratiṣṭhita). The trees therein are all six krośas in height; their leaves are densely layered so that raindrops do not leak through, and they join one another in succession like the thatching of a house. Those people dwell beneath these trees."

Furthermore, the various fragrant trees are also six krośas in height; some are five krośas, or four, three, two, or one krośa; even the smallest are half a krośa in height, all of them possessing various kinds of leaves, flowers, and fruits.
From those various trees, diverse fragrances emerge according to one's wishes.

There are also kalpavṛkṣa trees, six krośas in height, and others ranging down to five, four, three, two, or one krośa; the smallest of these are half a krośa in height, all of which possess various leaves, flowers, and fruits.
From the side of those fruits, various kinds of mixed garments naturally emerge and hang among the trees.

Furthermore, there are various kinds of *kaṇṭhaka* (necklace) trees; these trees are also six *krośas* high, down to five, four, three, two, or one *krośa*, with the smallest being half a *krośa*. All of them possess various leaves, flowers, and fruits.
From those various fruits, diverse kinds of necklaces emerge according to one’s mind and hang suspended.

Furthermore, there are various garland-trees; these trees are also six *krośas* high, or even five, four, three, two, or one *krośa*, with the smallest being half a *krośa*, all likewise possessing various leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Those various fruits emerge from the trees according to their minds, taking the form of diverse garlands and hanging thereon.

Furthermore, as for the trees of musical instruments, those trees are also six *krośas* high; others are five, four, three, two, or one *krośa*, with the smallest being half a *krośa*. They likewise possess various leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Those fruits, according to their respective minds, emerge in various vessel-like shapes and hang from the trees.

Furthermore, there are various kinds of diverse fruit trees; these trees are also six *krośas* high, or even five, four, three, two, or one *krośa*, with the smallest being half a *krośa*, all of which possess various leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Those various fruits, produced in manifold varieties according to their respective minds, are found upon the trees.

Next, there are musical trees; these trees are likewise six *krośas* in height, or even five, four, three, two, or one *krośa*, with the smallest being half a *krośa*. They also possess various leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Those various fruits, manifesting as forms of manifold music according to their minds, hang among the trees.
Furthermore, upon that ground there is naturally grown non-glutinous rice, pure and white, not encased in husks or chaff.

If they wish to cook, at that time there spontaneously appear various vessels made of *dhundhula* fruit to serve as cauldrons and pans; there are fire-pearls (*agni-maṇi*) which, without requiring fuel, naturally emit flames.
When the various tasks they wished to perform were fully accomplished and all had finished their meals, the jewel-flames naturally subsided and no longer blazed forth.

"O Bhikṣus! Around the four sides of the continent of Uttarakuru, there are four lakes. These lakes are named Anavatapta; each is fifty yojanas in length and breadth. Their waters are cool, sweet, light, soft, fragrant, pure, and free from turbidity. They are surrounded on all sides by seven tiers of brickwork, seven tiers of wooden planks, and seven tiers of railings. There are also seven tiers of bell-nets, and further, seven rows of *tāla* trees encircling them. These are of various delightful colors, all composed of the seven treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate."
The pond is square, with stairways on each side, made of various delightful colors up to the seven precious gems, including agate.
There are various flowers, such as the utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka, in blue, yellow, red, white, and pale green hues.
The flowers are round and broad, as large as chariot wheels; their fragrance is dense and pervasive, most subtle and supreme.
There are lotus roots as thick as chariot axles; when broken, they exude a sap the color of milk, which is sweet and delicious to eat, with a flavor as sweet as honey.

"O Bhikṣus! On the four sides of that Lake Anavatapta, there are further four great rivers which flow downward in accordance with the terrain; they flow straight, without waves, neither too fast nor too slow;
their banks are not high, being level, shallow, and easy to enter."
The waters do not rush wildly, but are covered everywhere with various flowers over an extent of one yojana.
On both banks of those rivers, there are further various groves of trees, intermingled and casting their reflections across one another.

Furthermore, various kinds of exquisite fragrances were diffused; various grasses grew, green and soft, curling to the right in elegant spirals. To speak briefly, they reached a height of four finger-widths, sinking down as one’s feet stepped upon them and returning to levelness when the step was lifted. There were also various birds and other creatures, producing all manner of sounds.

On both banks of that river, there are various boats of diverse and delightful colors, even composed of precious substances such as musāragalva and musāragalva-like carnelian; when touched, they are as soft as kācalindika cloth.

“O Bhikṣus! On that continent of Uttarakuru, at the constant midnight, from among those four lakes of Anavatapta, great dense clouds arise, completely covering the continent of Uttarakuru as well as its mountains and seas. Once they have spread everywhere, they then rain down water of eight meritorious qualities for the duration of milking a cow; the falling rain is four finger-widths deep and does not flow sideways.”
At that very moment, it sank into the earth.
Returning to that same midnight, the rain ceased and the clouds dispersed; the vast expanse of the sky above became entirely clear and pure.

From the ocean there arises a wind that blows cool and refreshing, soft, sweet, and temperate; its touch is blissful, moistening the continent of Uttarakuru, making it everywhere lush and glossy, fertile and richly nourished.
It is like a skilled garland-maker or a garland-maker’s apprentice who, having finished making a garland, sprinkles it lightly with water; once sprinkled, that garland becomes lustrous and brilliant.
"So it is, so it is, monks! That continent of Uttarakuru is always lush, moist, and fertile.
Just as if someone were to smear it with oil and ghee, the moisture and fertility of that land are likewise."
"O Bhikṣus!

On that continent of Uttarakuru, there is furthermore a lake named Sudarśana. This lake is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth; its waters are cool, refreshing, soft, pure, and free from turbidity. It is paved with bricks of the seven precious gems, and so forth, until it is described as having a flavor as sweet as honey."

“Monks! To the east of that Lake Bhadra there is a grove, also named Bhadra. This grove is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth, surrounded on all sides by sevenfold railings, sevenfold networks of bells, and sevenfold rows of tāla trees. It is of various delightful colors, composed of the seven treasures, including even musāragalva and aśmagarbha.”

On each side, there are various gates, and those gates are all provided with defensive towers; they are of many pleasing colors, composed of the seven precious gems, including even musaragalva and agate.

"O Bhikṣus! That Subhavyūha Garden is level, upright, and majestic; it is free from thorns, hills, mounds, pits, and hollows, and likewise devoid of privies, gravel, potsherds, rubble, and various impurities. It abounds in gold and silver; it is neither cold nor hot, with temperate seasons and harmonious climates. There are always flowing springs that overflow on all four sides."
The tree leaves flourish and spread, flowers and fruits are brought to fruition, and various fragrances waft through the air.
Diverse birds constantly utter wondrous sounds, their calls harmonious and elegant.
Furthermore, there are various grasses that are green and curl to the right, soft, supple, and smooth like peacock feathers, and they are constantly fragrant.
Those *bālisika* flowers, when touched, feel like *kācalindika* cloth; when stepped upon by the feet, they sink and rise according to the movement of the feet.
Furthermore, there are various trees, which possess many kinds of roots, trunks, leaves, flowers, and fruits, each emitting various fragrances that permeate everywhere. "O Bhikṣus!"
In that Garden of Good Manifestation, there are also trees called "Abiding.

These trees rise to a height of six krośas; their leaves are so dense that rain cannot penetrate them, and the foliage is joined together like a thatched roof over a house. Many of those people dwell and lodge beneath them.

There were various fragrant trees, various kalpavṛkṣa trees, various garland trees, as well as various wreath trees, various vessel trees, and various fruit trees; furthermore, there was naturally pure, matured rice in the form of cooked meals.
"O monks! That Caitraratha Grove is without self, without owner, and without a guardian.
When those people of Uttarakuru enter the Caitraratha Grove, having entered, they sport, experience various pleasures, and act according to their desires."

Or, having entered through the eastern gate, or the southern, western, or northern gates, they sport, bathe, enjoy themselves, and proceed; they go wherever they desire to go, departing as soon as they wish.

“Monks! To the south of that Lake Bhadra, for the sake of the people of Uttarakuru, there is a grove named Samantabhadra. This grove is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth, and it is surrounded on all sides by seven tiers of railings.”
"O Bhikṣus!
That Samantabhadra Garden has no guardian.

Only when the people of Uttarakuru wish to enter the Samantabhadra Garden to bathe, sport, and enjoy themselves, do they enter through the eastern, southern, western, or northern gates; having bathed, sported, and enjoyed themselves, they depart wherever they desire."

“Monks! To the west of that Lake Sudarśana, for the sake of the people of Uttarakuru, there is a grove named Supuṣpita. This grove is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth, surrounded on all sides by seven tiers of railings, and so forth, as previously described; it is no different from the Sudarśana grove, and likewise, there is no one who guards it.”

Only the people of Uttarakuru, wishing to enter the Saṃkusumita Garden to bathe, sport, and enjoy themselves, enter through the eastern gate, the southern, western, or northern gates; having bathed, sported, and enjoyed themselves, they depart for wherever they wish to go.
“Monks! To the north of that Lake Sudarśana is a grove named Nandana, exactly one hundred yojanas in length and breadth, and so forth, even unto having no guardians.”

When those people of Uttarakuru wish to enter the Nandana Grove to bathe, play, and enjoy themselves, they enter through the eastern gate, the southern, western, or northern gates; having bathed, played, and enjoyed themselves, they depart for wherever they wish to go, as was briefly described previously regarding the Sudarśana Grove and others.

“Monks! To the east of the Subhadda Pond, bordering the Subhadda Garden, there is a great river named Easy Access (Sukhāvatī), which flows gradually downstream without waves and without rapid current; its waters are covered with various flowers and it is two and a half yojanas wide.”
"O Bhikṣus!

On both banks of that River Easy-to-Enter (Sukhāvatī), there are various trees providing shade, various fragrances wafting about, and various grasses growing; to speak briefly, even down to the point that those who touch it find it as soft as kācalindika cloth: when the foot treads upon it, it sinks down four finger-breadths, and when the foot is lifted, it rises back up four finger-breadths."
There are various kinds of trees, fully endowed with diverse leaves, flowers, and fruits, and perfumed by various fragrances; there are various birds, each singing its own song.

On both banks of the river Easy-Entry (Sukhāvatī), there are many exquisite boats, pleasing to the eye with their variegated colors, fashioned from the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate—and beautifully adorned and embellished.

"O Bhikṣus! To the south of Lake Sudarśana, for the sake of the people of Uttarakuru, there is a great river named Sītā. It flows gradually downstream; a brief description of it is like that of the river Praveśanī."
All the various things found here are no different from those [in the previous realm], even the boats, which are composed of diverse colors and are as soft as kācalindika cloth.
"O Bhikṣus!
To the west of that Lake Sudarśana, for the sake of the people of Uttarakuru, there is a great river named Rathakāra; [and so on,] to be described briefly, flowing gradually downward."
"O Bhikṣus!

To the north of that Lake Sudarśana, for the people of Uttarakuru, there is a great river named Oghavatī which flows downstream. To speak briefly, it continues until its two banks are provided with boats adorned with the seven treasures, as soft as kācilindika cloth."
In this interval, there is an uddāna-gāthā:
Subhūti, Samantabhadra, and others, Sukusuma, Nanda,
and Sukhita, Supraveśa, Subhūti, Tathāgata, Ratha, Īśvara, and Sindhu.

“O Bhikṣus! When those people of Uttarakuru wish to enter the rivers—such as the Easy-to-Enter, the Well-Bodied, the Car-like, and the Lord-of-Majesty—to bathe, play, and enjoy themselves, they all go to both banks of those rivers; each removes their garments and places them on the bank.
Desiring to enter the water, they sit upon boats and row toward the middle of the river, bathing their bodies and enjoying themselves in play.”
Whichever among them was the first to emerge took the upper garment and put it on as they pleased; having done so, they departed at will, no longer seeking out their own designated original garments.
Why is this? Because those people of Uttarakuru have no sense of "I" or "mine," and they possess no protectors.

Furthermore, when they approach the fragrant trees and arrive at them, the trees bend their branches down for their sake; for those people, the fragrant trees immediately emit various exquisite perfumes, allowing them to grasp them with their hands.
At that time, those people took various kinds of incense from that tree and anointed their bodies; they then each proceeded toward the *kalpavṛkṣa* tree.
Upon arriving, the tree likewise, as before, caused its branches to bend downward and produce various garments, reaching down so that the hands of all those people could grasp them.
Those people take various exquisite garments from that tree; having taken them, they put them on. Having put them on, they turn toward the trees of necklaces (*hāra*).

Upon reaching those trees, for the sake of those people, the branches of the necklace-trees also bend downward. For their sake, those necklace-trees produce various necklaces, just as the previous tree did, which can be grasped by the hand.
Those people take various kinds of necklaces from that tree, fasten them upon their bodies, and proceed toward the Garland Tree (*māla-vṛkṣa*).
Having reached the Garland Tree, for their sake, the branches of that Garland Tree also bend down of their own accord.
Then, from that Garland Tree, various garlands emerge, reaching the hands of those people so they may grasp them.
Having taken the various garlands from that tree and fastened them upon their heads, they proceed toward the Vessel Tree.

Having reached the vessel-tree, the branches of that tree also bend downward so that they reach the grasp of his hand; he takes whatever vessel he desires and, holding it, proceeds toward the fruit-tree.

Having reached the fruit trees, for their sake the branches of the trees bent down; for their sake, those fruit trees produced various kinds of fruits within reach of their hands. Those people, beneath those trees, took whatever fruits they desired according to their wishes.
Having taken them, some eat the fruits, while others squeeze out the juice and drink it.
Having finished eating and drinking, they proceed toward the grove of musical trees.
Having reached that grove, for their sake, the branches of that Grove of Music also bent downward, producing various musical instruments within reach of their hands.

Among those trees, those people each took whatever musical instruments they required and held them; these were exquisite in form and harmonious in sound. They played when they wished to play, danced when they wished to dance, and sang when they wished to sing.
Having thus experienced various pleasures to their full extent, they each follow their respective destinations; when they wish to depart, they depart. (From the *Qishi yinben jing*, Scroll One.

This scripture is titled the *Qishi jing* in the Song Canon, translated by Jñānagupta together with Dharmagupta; it was promoted as the preceding scripture and included in the Cheng box. However, in the Dan Canon, it is titled the *Qishi yinben jing* and attributed solely to Dharmagupta; it was relegated to the position of a subsequent scripture.

Now, having consulted the *Kaiyuan lu*, the edition from the Danzang (the "Cinnabar" collection) is deemed authoritative; therefore, the title has been augmented with the two characters "Yinben" (Based on the Original). Furthermore, the translation by Śīlajñāna has been excluded and relegated to a later scripture, as it was intended for inclusion in a separate case.
The Sutra on the Causes and Origins of the World, Scroll Two,
translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Dharmagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on Uttarakuru, Part Two.

“O bhikṣus! Those people of Uttarakuru have hair that is blue-black in color and hangs down eight finger-widths long; they are of one color, one form, and one appearance, with no distinct colors by which their differences could be known.”
"O bhikṣus!

The people of Uttarakuru do not go about entirely naked, nor do they go about half-naked; they have no sense of 'this' or 'that. Their teeth are all even and closely set, neither sparse nor missing; they are beautiful, clean, and white, like conch shells—luminous, pure, and pleasing."
"O Bhikṣus!
When the people of Uttarakuru are hungry or thirsty and require food or drink, they simply take it—the naturally grown non-glutinous rice, which is pure, white, and free of husks or chaff."
Having taken them, he placed them inside a vessel for holding fruit; once they were set therein, he immediately placed a fire-gem at the bottom.
By the power of the merit of sentient beings, that fire-gem spontaneously emitted flames. Once the food was cooked, the flames immediately subsided.

When those people who wish to eat rice sit upon their seats, at that time, for all those who come from the east, west, south, and north desiring food, meals are provided; yet the rice is never exhausted, remaining perpetually full until those who have offered the food rise from their seats.

They eat that naturally ripened rice, free from husks and chaff, pure, fragrant, and delicious, requiring no broth or sauce; it is endowed with all flavors, white as a cluster of flowers, and its color is like the celestial *sudhā* nectar.

When those people eat this food, their bodies become full and free from deficiency; they neither age nor undergo change, remaining serene and unmoving. Furthermore, that food benefits them such that they possess physical strength, well-being, and perfect eloquence.

“Monks! If any among the people of Uttarakuru should give rise to a mind of defiled attachment toward a woman and have a desire for her, that man will look upon her, and that woman will immediately follow him until they reach the foot of a tree.”

If those women are that man’s mother, or perhaps his maternal aunt, or his sister, and so forth, then for their sake the branches of those trees do not bend downward; their leaves immediately wither and fall off, no longer shading one another, and neither flowers nor couches appear.

However, if they are not his mother, nor his aunt, nor his sister, then those trees immediately bend down to cover them; their branches and leaves become lush and verdant, each branch casting shade over the others, and many flowers bloom in brilliant splendor. Furthermore, for that man, hundreds of thousands of kinds of couches, seats, and bedding are produced. They enter that place together, enjoying themselves in pleasure and indulging in whatever they desire.
“Monks! Those people of Uttarakuru remain in the womb for seven days; on the eighth day, the woman gives birth.”
Once the birth was completed, whether it was a boy or a girl, they would immediately place that child sitting in the middle of a crossroads and depart.

At that time, people coming from the east, west, south, and north would, for the sake of nourishing those boys and girls, each insert their fingers into the mouths of those children; from the tips of their fingers, excellent sweet milk would emerge, which they would give to the boys and girls, and having drunk it, they would survive.
After seven days in this manner, those men and women again attain that same kind of physical stature, becoming indistinguishable from the other people there.
If they are men, they then follow along with their male companions, traveling together.
If they are women, they follow their female companions and depart together. "O Bhikṣus!
Those people of Uttarakuru have a fixed lifespan and do not die prematurely; when their life comes to an end, they are immediately reborn in a higher realm."
Furthermore, therein, for what causes and conditions do those people of Uttarakuru obtain a fixed lifespan, and after their lives have ended, all go upward?

"Monks! There is a person in the world who is habitually engaged in killing, stealing the property of others, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech, as well as covetousness, malice, and wrong views.
Because of these causes and conditions, when his body breaks up at the end of life, he shall fall into the evil realms within the hells."

Furthermore, there is another person who has never killed living beings, has not stolen the property of others, and has not committed sexual misconduct; nor has he spoken falsely, used divisive speech, engaged in frivolous chatter, or uttered harsh words; he is without covetousness or malice, and is free from wrong views.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, when his body breaks up at the end of life, he proceeds toward the good realms and is reborn among humans or devas.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions are beings born in the lower realms?
It is due to killing, wrong views, and so forth.
Those born in the higher realms do so because of non-killing, right views, and so forth.
Furthermore, there is another person who thinks:
"I should now practice the ten wholesome actions.
By reason of this cause and condition, when the body perishes, they shall be reborn among the Uttarakurus.
Having been born there, he dwells for a thousand years, neither increasing nor decreasing.

Having made such virtuous vows, he practices the ten wholesome courses of action; when his body perishes, he will be reborn among the Uttarakurus. There, his lifespan will remain for a full thousand years, neither increasing nor decreasing.
"Monks! For this reason, the people of Uttarakuru attain a fixed lifespan. Monks!"
For what reason and by what causes are they reborn above? Monks,
when the people of Jambudvīpa have received the ten wholesome courses of action from others, upon the dissolution of the body, they shall be reborn among the Uttarakurus.

As for those people of Uttarakuru, if they have previously been endowed with the ten wholesome courses of action and have practiced them in accordance with the Dharma, then upon the dissolution of the body, they shall all be reborn in the higher realms among the various devas.
"Monks! By this cause and by this condition, those people of Uttarakuru go to a superior destination above. Monks!"

When the lifespan of those people of Uttarakuru comes to an end, there is no one who feels grief or weeps for them; having merely adorned them, they are cast away in the middle of a great crossroads and depart, leaving them behind.
“O Bhikṣus! Among the people of Uttarakuru, there is such a custom:
when the lifespan of those beings has come to an end, at that very moment a bird flies there; this bird is named Uccāgāma, which in the language of Sui means ‘High-farer.’”
At that time, a bird named Ucchaṅgamā flew swiftly from a great mountain valley, immediately seized his hair in its beak, and cast the corpse onto another continent.
Why is this? Because the karma of the people of Uttarakuru is pure and their intentions are joyful, the wind does not cause their foul and stinking odors to be blown abroad.
"O Bhikṣus!
Whenever those people of Uttarakuru wish to relieve themselves, for their sake the earth cracks open; once they have finished, it closes back up again."
Why is this? Because those people of Uttarakuru desire purity and take delight in their intentions.
Furthermore, what is the reason for calling that continent Uttarakuru?
"O Bhikṣus!

Among the four continents, the continent of Uttarakuru is the most superior, the most exquisite, and the most excellent compared to the other three continents; therefore, it is called the continent of Uttarakuru—Uttarakuru being translated in the Sui language as 'Supreme Action' (shàngzuò)."
Chapter Three: The Cakravartin Kings. *Sūtra on the Arising of the World*, Chapter Three: The Cakravartin Kings. “Monks!

When a Cakravartin king appears in the world within Jambudvīpa, this Jambudvīpa naturally becomes fully endowed with the seven treasures. Furthermore, that Cakravartin king possesses four kinds of supernormal powers and virtues.”

What are the seven treasures? First, the golden wheel treasure; second, the white elephant treasure; third, the dark-blue horse treasure; fourth, the divine jewel treasure; fifth, the jade woman treasure; sixth, the treasurer treasure; and seventh, the military commander treasure. These are the seven treasures.
"Monks! How does a Wheel-Turning Sage King possess the perfection of the wheel-treasure? Monks!"

When that Wheel-Turning King emerges from Jambudvīpa and is consecrated with water as a Cakravartin, on the Puṣya day—the fifteenth day of the month when the moon is full—he washes his hair and puts on unwashed white cotton garments. With his hair hanging downward, adorned with mani-jewels and various necklaces, he stands atop a pavilion surrounded by his kinsmen and ministers before and behind him.

At that time, there spontaneously appeared before the king a divine golden wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*), complete with a thousand spokes, hubs, and rims, its various characteristics fully perfected; it arrived of its own accord, not fashioned by any craftsman, and was seven cubits in diameter.
At that time, the consecrated Kṣatriya wheel-turning monarch had this thought:
"In the past, I have heard it said:

'If there is a consecrated Kṣatriya king, on the fifteenth day of the month when the full moon is perfectly round, having bathed his head and wearing unwashed white cotton garments and various necklaces and ornaments, while standing upon a pavilion surrounded by his kinsmen and ministers before and behind him..."

At that time, before the king, there spontaneously appeared the divine precious wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*), with its thousand spokes, hub, and rim, all its characteristics complete. It arrived of its own accord, not fashioned by any craftsman; it was entirely golden, with a diameter of seven cubits.
"When such an auspicious omen appears, one then achieves the merit of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin).
I must certainly be such a Wheel-Turning King now.

At that time, the consecrated Kṣatriya Wheel-Turning King, wishing to test that divine Wheel-Treasure, immediately ordered the fourfold divisions of his military forces to be fully prepared—namely, the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry.

Having fully equipped his body with the fourfold power of the divisions, he immediately proceeded toward the celestial golden wheel. Upon arrival, he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground before the golden wheel, and with his right hand grasped that precious celestial wheel, speaking these words:
"O precious celestial wheel, if I am indeed a Wheel-Turning King, may all lands not yet subdued be brought under my subjugation."
"Then that divine wheel-treasure turned at once, for the purpose of subduing those who had not yet been subdued.

Monks, at that time, having seen that divine wheel-treasure turn, the consecrated Kṣatriya king, the Wheel-turning Monarch, immediately prepared his carriage and set out toward the eastern direction; the divine wheel-treasure, along with the fourfold army consisting of elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry, all followed him simultaneously."
"O Bhikṣus!

Ahead of that Wheel-Treasure, there further proceed the bodies of four great devas. To whatever other region the divine Wheel-Treasure arrives and halts, the Cakravartin King, along with his fourfold forces—the elephant corps, the cavalry, and the infantry—all halt and take up residence therein."

"At that time, all the kings of the eastern regions each took golden vessels filled with silver grain, or silver vessels filled with golden grain. Having prepared these, they all proceeded to where the Wheel-Turning King was; having arrived, they addressed the Wheel-Turning King, saying:
'Welcome, Great King!'"
"This is a realm of the devas; the people of the eastern quarter are prosperous, abundant, peaceful, and happy, free from fear and dread. It is populous and exceedingly delightful."
We pray only that Great Heaven will deign to show compassion and accept us, having pity on us minor kings.
Today, we serve the Heavenly King with single-minded devotion, without any duplicity.
Then the Wheel-Turning King addressed the various kings, saying:

"If you are sincere in heart and can act thus, each of you shall govern and transform your respective realms according to the Dharma, ensuring that no part of your kingdoms acts contrary to the Dharma."
Why is this? If you cause any unrighteous or evil conduct to manifest within my kingdom, I shall punish you.

I now instruct you: you must abstain from taking life and teach others not to kill; do not take what is not given; refrain from sexual misconduct, false speech, and so forth, up to and including wrong views—none of these should be committed.

If you and your followers abstain from taking life, teach others not to kill, do not take what is not given, refrain from sexual misconduct, and maintain truthful speech and right view, then I shall know that you kings have brought your kingdoms under subjugation.

"At that time, the kings of the various nations in the eastern direction, having heard such an edict from the Wheel-Turning King, simultaneously and together undertook the practice of the ten wholesome courses of action. Having undertaken them, they followed and observed them, each ruling and transforming their respective territories according to the Dharma."
By the power of his sovereign authority, wherever this Wheel-Turning King goes, the wheel-treasure follows him.
At that time, having thus subdued the kingdoms of the east, the divine golden wheel-treasure of that holy king reached the eastern shore and circled it completely.
Proceeding in succession, he traveled to the south, the west, and even the north, guiding his way according to the ancient path of the wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).

As the wheel-turning king and his fourfold army marched one after another, before the celestial wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*), there further appeared the bodies of the four great devas who walked ahead.
At that time, wherever the precious wheel came to rest, the Wheel-turning King and his fourfold army would halt there for the night.

Then, all the kings of the various kingdoms in the northern direction each brought vessels of natural gold filled with silver grain and vessels of natural silver filled with gold grain; they all came together to where the Wheel-turning King was, and having arrived, they knelt down with their right knees on the ground and spoke these words:
"Welcome, O Great King! Welcome!"
"Excellent, O Deva!
Because we are protected by you, the Heavenly King, our people in the north are flourishing; the land is abundant and peaceful, free from all fears, and most delightful."
"The heavens have entrusted us with the task of governing and transforming;
we shall comply accordingly. The Wheel-Turning King then issued this command:
"If you are able to do so, each of you shall govern and transform your own respective domains, strictly adhering to my instructions and not acting contrary to the Dharma."
Why is this? So that there shall be no persons who act contrary to the Dharma or commit evil deeds within my realm.
Furthermore, you must not take life yourselves, nor teach others to do so; do not take what is not given; abandon sexual misconduct, false speech, and even wrong views; you must sever these entirely.
If you abstain from taking life, and so forth, up to practicing right view—if you are able to do such things, I shall know that your lands have been well-subdued.
Those kings all addressed the Wheel-Turning King together, saying:
"As the Heavenly Lord has commanded, we shall respectfully carry it out.
At that time, the various kings of the northern regions, having heard such an edict from the Wheel-Turning King, each complied with it and undertook the ten wholesome courses of action.
Having received [the teachings], they practiced them all in accordance with the Dharma, governing and transforming others according to the Vinaya.
By virtue of the sovereign power of that Wheel-Turning King, wherever he traveled, the divine wheel-treasure followed him.
This celestial golden wheel proceeds in this successive manner:
having subdued the northern region and crossed to the north shore of the ocean, it traverses all the lands surrounding its perimeter, and having completed the circuit, it returns.

At that time, within Jambudvīpa, he selected the most supreme, majestic, and exquisitely refined site; there, the divine wheel-treasure (cakraratna) was positioned above it, extending east and west for seven yojanas and spanning twelve yojanas from south to north.
Having thus crossed over, at that time the various devas descended during the night and spontaneously constructed a palace for that Cakravartin King, which was completed in an instant.
Once it was accomplished, it was of exquisite color and dignified appearance, fashioned from four precious substances—namely, celestial gold, silver, crystal, and beryl.

At that time, that divine wheel-treasure of pure gold hovered in the air above the inner gate of the noble king’s palace, remaining suspended with great stability, like a wheel fixed upon its axle, neither shaking nor moving.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King will experience great joy and boundless exultation, thinking to himself:
"I have now truly received the celestial wheel-treasure!"
"O bhikṣus! That wheel-turning king possesses such a form, and the divine golden wheel-treasure is spontaneously and fully present. O bhikṣus!"
Furthermore, what kind of white elephant-treasure (*hastiratna*) should a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) possess? Monks!
When this wheel-turning monarch sits in his palace pavilion during the first watch of the day, the elephant-treasure shall appear before him.

The elephant’s exquisite color was pure white, like a *kubjaka* flower; its seven limbs touched the ground, and it possessed great supernatural power, soaring through the void. Its head was red in color, like the *indrāyudhaka* insect; the elephant had six tusks, all of which were slender and sharp. These tusks were subtle and wondrous, adorned with various colors like golden grains. This elephant was named Upoṣadha, which in the Sui language means "Observing the Fast."
Having seen the elephant-treasure, the Wheel-Turning Sage King thought to himself:
"Now that this elephant has appeared, when it is tamed, will it be capable of performing all tasks and serve as a noble mount?"

At that time, this elephant-treasure was tamed within a single day, becoming fit for all manner of tasks as if it had been trained for countless hundreds of thousands of years; it was dignified, virtuous, compliant, and well-tempered.
In this very way, that elephant-treasure, within a single day, underwent all forms of training and became capable of performing all tasks; it was just so.

At that time, the Wheel-Turning King, wishing to test the elephant-treasure, mounted it at the break of dawn when the sun first rose, and traveled in circuitous succession across all the coastal shores until he reached the very limits of the earth;
having completed his circuit, he returned once more to the site of his original palace.
The Wheel-Turning King then partook of some light food.
For this reason, at that time, the king felt great joy and exultation within his heart, thinking: "For my sake, such a precious elephant has appeared."
"Monks! That wheel-turning king possesses such a white elephant-treasure, naturally complete. Monks!"
What is the possession of the horse-treasure by that Wheel-turning Sage King? Monks!
When it is the first part of the day, while the Wheel-turning King is seated upon his palace, the dark-blue horse-treasure appears before the king.

His body was blue and his form was lustrous; the color of his coat was pleasing and glossy, and his head was black with a flowing mane. Possessing supernatural powers, he could fly through the void; the horse's name was Bharalaha, which in the Sui language means "Long-haired."
When the Wheel-Turning King saw this horse, he thought to himself:
"Now that this horse has appeared, if it is tamed, will it be capable of enduring all tasks and able to serve me as a noble mount?"

At that time, within a single day, that horse-treasure was tamed according to the occasion and became capable of performing all tasks, as excellent, noble, and well-trained as if it had been disciplined for countless years.
When that horse had been tamed in such a manner, within a single day it was capable of enduring all those tasks.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King, wishing to test the Horse-Jewel, mounted it at the break of dawn when the sun first rose, and after traversing the entire earth, returned to his own palace.
That Wheel-Turning King, even as he partook of food,
felt such joy through these causes and conditions that he leaped for immeasurable delight, thinking:
"I have now produced the treasure of the dark-blue horse."
"Monks! This wheel-turning king is thus fully endowed with such a horse-treasure. Monks!"
Regarding this Wheel-Turning King, what is meant by his being "endowed with the jewel-treasure"? Monks!
That Wheel-Turning King possesses a maṇi-jewel, the color of lapis lazuli, exquisite and octagonal, not fashioned by a craftsman but born spontaneously, pure and brilliantly radiant.
When the wheel-turning monarch saw this jewel, he thought to himself:
"This maṇi gem is endowed with all auspicious marks; it should be suspended within the palace so that its radiance may be made manifest."

At that time, the Wheel-turning King, wishing to test that maṇi jewel, arrayed his fourfold army—namely, the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry. Having fully prepared these four forces, it was at midnight, amidst heavy clouds and darkness, when a flash of lightning appeared and a light rain fell from the sky.

At that time, the Wheel-Turning King took that precious jewel and suspended it atop a banner; he then departed from the park and garden, intending to travel about and observe, in order to test the virtue of the jewel.
"O Bhikṣus!
