That mani-jewel, situated atop the banner, radiates light that pervades everywhere, universally illuminating the four directions as well as the bodies of the fourfold army, making them all clearly visible, just as the sun shines upon the world."
At that time, all the brahmins and householders dwelling in that land awoke and began their various activities, saying:
"It is already dawn; has the sun risen?"
For this reason, the wheel-turning king experienced great joy and immeasurable exultation, thinking to himself: "Has this treasure been born for me?"
"Monks! That wheel-turning king is endowed with such a jewel of form. Monks!"
What is meant by the possession of the Woman-Jewel by a Wheel-Turning King? Monks!

This Wheel-Turning King gives birth to a Woman-Jewel who is neither too short nor too tall, neither too stout nor too slender, neither too fair nor too dark; she is upright and beautiful, most lovely and delightful, supreme and exquisite, with her physical appearance fully perfected.
When it is hot, the body of the Woman Jewel is cool; when it is cold, her body is warm.
From her body issues the fragrance of sandalwood, and the breath from her mouth is always like the scent of the blue utpala lotus.
As a wheel-turning monarch, she went to bed late and rose early, diligently serving him with reverence; in all her actions, she never failed to accord with the King's wishes;
such was her state of mind that she did not even give rise to an evil thought, much less in deed or speech.
For this reason, the Wheel-Turning Sage King experienced great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight, thinking within his heart:
"Has this maiden-jewel already been born for me!"
"Monks! That wheel-turning king was thus fully endowed with such a female treasure (strī-ratna). Monks!"
What is meant by the Wheel-turning Sage King possessing the treasure of the Minister of the Treasury, endowed with majestic power?
Monks! That Wheel-turning King gives birth to the treasure of the Minister of the Treasury, who is immensely wealthy and possesses abundant riches, having performed many meritorious deeds.

By virtue of karmic retribution, he is born with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), which penetrates the earth. Whether there is a guardian of the treasury or no guardian of the treasury, all are clearly seen by that eye. Even across water or land, whether far or near, whatever exists therein—all those who serve as guardians of the treasury—provide protection for him in accordance with the Dharma.

If there is no owner, he shall immediately take the gold and silver therein; for whatever resources a Wheel-Turning King requires for his affairs of wealth and treasure, they shall be prepared and provided at the proper time.
At that time, the treasurer immediately went to where the Wheel-turning King was; having arrived, he addressed the Wheel-turning King, saying:
"O Great Holy Heavenly King!
Should Your Majesty require any wealth or treasures for use, may Your Majesty not worry; I am able to provide everything Your Majesty requires."
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King, wishing to test the Treasurer, went to the water’s edge, boarded a boat, sat upon it, and remained in the middle of the current, addressing the Treasurer:
"O my Treasurer, I require wealth and treasures; you must prepare them quickly! You must prepare them quickly!"
The treasurer replied, "I only pray that Your Majesty will wait a brief moment; once this ship reaches the shore, I shall gather wealth from there for Your Majesty's use."
The king said to his treasurer:
"I do not wish to retrieve the wealth from the shore; simply prepare it for me right here.
Thereupon, the treasurer addressed the king, saying:
“As Your Majesty commands, I dare not disobey.

Then, having heard the king’s command, the treasurer bared his right arm, knelt with his right knee upon the deck of the ship, and plunged his hands into the seawater; his fingers moved like crabs as he scooped up vast quantities of gold and silver, filling the jars and placing them upon the deck. He presented these to the Wheel-Turning King and addressed him, saying:
“This is celestial gold and silver; may Your Majesty use these treasures to provide for your royal needs and financial affairs.”
Then the Wheel-Turning King said to the treasurer:
"I have no need for wealth; I was merely testing you.
When the treasurer heard these words from the king, he withdrew the gold and silver and placed it back within the water.
For this reason, the Wheel-Turning King experienced great joy and boundless exultation, thinking, "I have now produced the Jewel of the Steward.
O Bhikṣus!
That wheel-turning king is fully endowed with such treasures as these.
"Monks, what are the majestic characteristics that constitute the fulfillment of the wheel-turning sage-king’s treasure of the military minister?
"O Bhikṣus!

By the power of his merit, this Wheel-Turning King naturally produces the treasure of a military commander, who is possessed of skillful wisdom, many stratagems, a profound understanding of military affairs, and complete divine intelligence."
That wheel-turning king, should he require military forces, is able to provide them at will.
That is to say, if he desires the troops to march when his person moves, they all march together; if he desires them to disperse, they disperse; if he desires them to halt, they are able to halt.
Then, the Jewel of the Military Commander immediately went to where the Wheel-Turning King was; having arrived, he addressed the Wheel-Turning King, saying:

"If Your Majesty requires the military forces to be trained, may Your Majesty not worry; I shall train the military forces for Your Majesty so that they become as compliant and disciplined as you desire."

At that time, the Wheel-Turning King, wishing to test that Jewel of the Military Commander, immediately commanded the preparation of the fourfold army corps—namely, the elephant corps, the horse corps, the chariot corps, and the infantry corps—all of which were likewise fully equipped.
Having strictly commanded that the fourfold army be fully prepared, the king then addressed the general named Ratna:

"O General, you must skillfully prepare my military forces for me, instructing them to act in accordance with my will—to advance well, retreat well, assemble well, and disperse well—acting in conformity with the law and without transgression."
Having heard these instructions from the Wheel-Turning King, the commander of the army addressed the Great King, saying:
"In accordance with Your Majesty's command, I dare not disobey."

Once the bodies of those four types of troops were fully equipped, they followed the King’s instructions: they could run when told to run, disperse when told to disperse, and were capable of performing every task he might wish to establish.
For this reason, that Wheel-Turning King experienced great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight, thinking: "I have now produced the Jewel of the General of the Army.
O Bhikṣus!
That wheel-turning king possesses such a commander-in-chief of the army, endowed with majestic power. Monks!
Only when such seven treasures appear does one receive the name of a Wheel-Turning Holy King.
“Monks! What are those four kinds of sovereign supernormal powers with which that Wheel-Turning Sage King is fully endowed? Monks!”

That wheel-turning monarch lives for a long time and endures for many years; throughout the entire world, during this present age and time, there is no one born who can abide in such peace and security for as long as that wheel-turning monarch, living a long life and enduring for many years.
This is called the first supernatural power possessed by a Wheel-Turning Sage King: the perfection of his lifespan.
"Furthermore, monks, the body received by that Wheel-Turning King is free from illness and has few afflictions, and he is endowed with all the primary marks."

Furthermore, his abdomen was neither too large nor too small; cold, heat, chill, and warmth were regulated according to the seasons; his movements were light and agile; his food and drink were digested; and he dwelt in peace, security, and happiness.
At this time, during this kalpa, there is no other person born in the world who can be so free from illness and devoid of all afflictions and maladies as that noble king.
This is called the second supernatural power of the body possessed by a Wheel-Turning Sage King.

Furthermore, monks, that Wheel-Turning King possesses a retributive form that is pleasing and upright; he is always a joy for all the world to behold, being most excellent and most wonderful, with a pure physical body fully adorned.

At this time, at this very moment, there is no one born among human beings who can attain such beauty and loveliness as to be desired and gazed upon by the world, like that Universal Monarch (cakravartin) who is endowed with all the physical marks.
This is called the third physical excellence of the Wheel-Turning Sage King, the perfection of supernormal powers.

Furthermore, monks, by reason of the karmic retribution of that Wheel-Turning King, he possesses great merit and virtue; that is to say, his various assets are abundant, and he is endowed with all manner of rare and precious jewels of the world.

At that time, during that kalpa, there was no one born among human beings who possessed such wealth, such riches, such a multitude of garments and ornaments, and such an abundance of precious objects as to equal that Universal Monarch (cakravartin).
This is called the fourth fruit of retribution and the perfection of supernormal powers of a Wheel-Turning Sage King. O Bhikṣus!
If one possesses these four kinds of supernormal powers in their entirety, only then may one be named a Wheel-Turning Sage King.

"O Bhikṣus! Furthermore, that merit-endowed Wheel-turning Sage King is loved and revered by all his subjects, who always rejoice in him with hearts full of joy, just as children love and respect their father;
likewise, all the subjects receive the compassionate regard of the Wheel-turning King, who constantly cherishes them with thoughts of kindness, just as a father loves his son."

“Monks! That Wheel-turning King, seated upon the Vaijayanta—translated in the Sui language as ‘the most excellent and superior chariot’—desired to go out on an excursion to view the gardens and various auspicious lands.”
At that time, when the people beheld the Universal Monarch, they were all filled with great joy and spoke together to the charioteer, saying:
"O skillful charioteer, we pray you hold the reins and proceed slowly and steadily; do not go too fast."
"Why is this? If you proceed at a steady pace and allow the chariot to travel with ample space, we shall have the opportunity to behold the Wheel-Turning Sage King for a long time.
When the Wheel-Turning King heard these words, he likewise spoke thus to his charioteer:
"O skillful charioteer, proceed slowly and steadily; be careful not to go too fast. Why is this?
If you remain composed and drive the chariot with care, it will allow me to observe those people thoroughly for a long time."

"O Bhikṣus! When those people have seen the Wheel-Turning King, each brings forth their own precious treasures. Some offer these precious treasures before the Wheel-Turning Sage-King, and having presented them, they say:
'I now offer this to Your Majesty; this object belongs to Your Majesty. We pray that Your Majesty accept it and use it as you see fit; for this object is intended solely for Your Majesty's use.'"

"O Bhikṣus! When that Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, this Jambudvīpa is pure and level, free from thorns, dense forests, mounds, ruins, pits, and hollows, as well as other places of filth, latrines, impurities, and foul odors, and objects such as gravel, potsherds, sand, and saline soil. It is naturally replete with the seven treasures of gold and silver; it is neither cold nor hot, and the seasons are perfectly harmonized."
Furthermore, monks!

When a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, this Jambudvīpa is naturally established with eighty thousand cities, all of which are joyful, free from all fears, and most delightful; grain is abundant, villages are numerous, and the population is flourishing.
Furthermore, monks!

When a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, in this Jambudvīpa—within the villages, towns, and cities where he rules—the houses stand so close together that their eaves touch, and a rooster can fly from one to the next; the happiness of the people is inconceivable.
Furthermore, monks!

When a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, in this Jambudvīpa, at midnight, great clouds arise from Lake Anavatapta, spreading across Jambudvīpa, its mountains, and its seas. They immediately pour down rain for as long as it takes to milk a cow; that water possesses the eight meritorious qualities. The depth of the water is four finger-breadths, and it does not flow sideways; rather, it sinks into the earth where it falls, disappearing entirely without a trace.

Toward the latter part of the night, the clouds completely clear away, and a cool breeze rises once more from the ocean. It blows upon that moisture and touches all the people, who all experience peace and happiness. Furthermore, that sweet rain moistens Jambudvīpa, making it everywhere lush and vibrant.

It is just as when a skilled worldly garland-maker or a disciple of a garland-maker has finished making a garland and sprinkles water upon it to make it glossy and radiant, so that the colors of the flowers shine with fresh brilliance; it is exactly like this.
"Furthermore, when a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, the lands of this Jambudvīpa are perpetually fertile and lush.
They are just like a person who has smeared the ground with ghee and oil; they are likewise succulent, rich, and nourishing."
"O bhikṣus!
That wheel-turning king, having appeared in the world and passed through immeasurable ages of time, although he experienced all the sensations of human contact,"

For example, when a person of delicate, soft, and weak constitution eats fine food and engages in physical activity, they experience a slight sensation of fatigue for a short time, which is then digested in a moment.
In this very way, as that wheel-turning monarch dwells in the world for a long time, his perception of the touch of birth and death is likewise.
"O bhikṣus!
When that wheel-turning king reaches the end of his life and has relinquished his body and life-force, he is reborn in the heavens, dwelling together with the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
"Furthermore, monks!

When that Wheel-turning King is about to pass away, various fragrant flowers—such as the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka*—will rain down from the sky above as an offering to the Wheel-turning King. Moreover, celestial powdered aloeswood, *tagara*, sandalwood, and celestial *māndārava* flowers will also rain down. Furthermore, celestial musical instruments of exquisite sound will resonate spontaneously without being struck, and there will also be the sounds of celestial songs and hymns of praise, for the sake of making merit and providing benefit for the body of that Wheel-turning King."
“Monks, [listen.]”

At that time, the Jewel of the Woman, the Jewel of the Treasurer, the Jewel of the General, and the others took the body of the Wheel-turning King and washed it with various kinds of fragrant water. Having washed it with the fragrant liquid, they first wrapped it in *karpāsa* cloth, and thereafter wrapped it in unwashed fine cotton cloth. Next, they further wrapped it in five hundred pieces of exquisite, fine cotton cloth, layering them one after another in this manner. Then, they took a golden coffin and filled it with ghee; they placed the body of the Wheel-turning King inside the coffin. Once he was settled within the coffin, they took a silver outer casing and placed the golden coffin inside it. Having placed it within the silver casing, they fastened it with nails. Furthermore, they gathered all kinds of fragrant wood and constructed a great pyre, and then performed the cremation.

Once the cremation was completed, a stūpa for the Wheel-Turning King—called a *sustūpa* (translated in the Sui language as "Precious Tower")—was constructed at the crossroads of the four suburbs. It was one *yojana* in height and half a *yojana* in width, adorned with various colors and composed of the four precious substances: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The four courtyards of this stūpa were fifty *yojanas* in circumference and breadth, featuring seven layers of walls and seven layers of railings; the details are as described above, even down to the various birds, each singing its own song.

At that time, the Jewel-Woman, along with the Jewel of the Treasury and the Jewel of the Military, having completed the construction of the stūpa for the Wheel-Turning King, subsequently prepared exquisite offerings. That is to say, to all who came seeking—whether they required food, drink, vehicles, clothing, wealth, or jewels—they gave them everything, providing for each until they were fully satisfied.

“Monks! After that wheel-turning king has passed away, when seven days have elapsed, his precious golden wheel, the precious elephant, the precious horse, and the precious mani-jewel will all spontaneously vanish and disappear; the precious queen, the treasurer, and the general, as well as all others, will likewise pass away.”
Those four cities made of the seven precious substances each changed, becoming cities of clods of earth, and the people therein likewise gradually diminished in number. Monks!

All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; thus they undergo transformation and change, lacking any state of permanence. They are subject to destruction and dispersal, devoid of autonomy, and are of a nature to perish. Existing but for a fleeting moment, they do not abide for long.
"O bhikṣus!
You must abandon all conditioned formations; you must distance yourselves from them, you must grow weary of them, and you should swiftly seek the path to liberation."
Chapter Four: The Hells, Part One. *The Sūtra on the Origin of the World*. "O Bhikṣus!

Beyond the four great continents, the eighty thousand small islands, and all other great mountains including Sumeru, the king of mountains, there is another mountain named Cakravāḍa (formerly translated as 'Iron Encircling Mountains'). It is six million eight hundred thousand yojanas in height, and its length and breadth are likewise six million eight hundred thousand yojanas. It is dense and solid, composed of vajra, and is difficult to destroy."
"O Bhikṣus!
Beyond this Cakravāḍa mountain, there is another great Cakravāḍa mountain, equal in height and breadth to the former.
Between these two mountains, there is a profound darkness, devoid of any light."
The sun and moon possess such great majesty, power, and virtue, yet they cannot illuminate that place so that light may be seen there. Monks!
Between those two mountains lie the eight great hells.
What are these eight?
They are the Saṃjīva Great Hell, the Kālasūtra Great Hell, the Saṃghāta Great Hell, the Raurava Great Hell, the Mahāraurava Hell, the Tapana Great Hell, the Pratāpana Hell, and the Avīci Great Hell.
“Monks! Each of those eight great hells is further surrounded by sixteen minor hells as its retinue; these sixteen hells are all five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.”
What are these sixteen? They are:

the Black Cloud Sand Hell, the Excrement and Filth Mire Hell, the Five Forks Hell, the Hunger Hell, the Thirst Hell, the Pus and Blood Hell, the Single Copper Cauldron Hell, the Many Copper Cauldrons Hell, the Layered Mill Hell, the Measuring-Granary Hell, the Chicken Hell, the Ash River Hell, the Sawing-Board Hell, the Knife-Sheath Hell, the Fox and Wolf Hell, and the Cold Ice Hell.
“Monks! For what reason and by what cause is it called the Sañjīva Great Hell? Monks!”

Among those sentient beings in the Saṃjīva Great Hell—those who have been born, those who exist, those who have appeared, and those who abide—their fingers naturally develop iron claws that are slender, long, sharp, and entirely jagged like the edges of blades.

Once those sentient beings have seen one another, their minds become turbid and disturbed. With their minds thus disturbed, each uses their own iron claws to tear at their own bodies; they may rip their bodies apart, tearing again and again, or tearing them wide open, ripping again and again, or ripping them wide open; they may cut their bodies, cutting again and again, or cutting them wide open.
"O bhikṣus! At that time, those beings will know thus:
'I have been wounded; I am now dead.'"

However, at that time, due to the retribution of karma, a cold wind arises again and blows upon his body; in an instant, he is restored to life once more, and his body—skin, flesh, sinews, bones, blood, and all—is revived again.
Once they have regained their lives, by the power of their karma, they rise up and move here and there, each saying to the others:
"O you beings, did you wish to live? Now that you are alive, is it better?"
"O Bhikṣus! Within this interval, because there is a slight degree of discernment, it is therefore called 'Reviving.

However, within that realm, there are further distinct karmic retributions involving extreme suffering and hardship, as well as great and heavy afflictions, agonizing pains that are difficult to endure."

And therein, as long as life has not yet ended, and until those evil and unwholesome karmas have been exhausted, extinguished, eliminated, transformed, partially manifested, or fully manifested—whether they were produced and created in a previous life, or performed while in a human or non-human body.
"Furthermore, monks!

Within that Saṃjīva Great Hell, those beings who are born, who exist, who appear, and who remain there, have their fingers become iron knives and half-iron knives—extremely long, slender, and sharp. As they grasp one another, their minds become agitated; they tear, rend, split, cut, and hack each other until they die. Then, a cold wind blows upon them, and in an instant they are restored to life."
"O bhikṣus!
Such a small portion, speaking briefly, is called 'living.
O bhikṣus!"

Furthermore, due to other distinct karmic actions, they undergo extreme suffering and affliction therein; because their suffering is not yet finished, they seek death but cannot attain it. This continues until those evil and unwholesome karmas—whether performed or created by them in a previous human existence or in a non-human existence—are exhausted, extinguished, eliminated, and abandoned. Only then do they fully experience all such consequences in their proper sequence.

Furthermore, when those sentient beings in the Saṃjīva Great Reviving Hell have exhausted their retribution for suffering after an immeasurable time, they emerge from the Saṃjīva Great Reviving Hell. Having emerged, they run about again, seeking other dwellings, places of refuge, and places of sanctuary.
Having formed this thought, due to their karmic offenses, they immediately enter the Black Sand Small Hell, which is five hundred *yojanas* in extent.

Once they have entered it, a great black cloud arises in the sky above and rains down sand-like particles; these are fiercely blazing and extremely hot. They fall upon the bodies of the sentient beings in that hell, burning the skin as they fall on the skin, burning the flesh as they fall on the flesh, reaching the sinews to burn the sinews, reaching the bones to burn the bones, and reaching the marrow to scorch the marrow. Emitting smoke and flames, they burn through with intense heat, causing the beings to undergo extreme suffering.

Because the suffering they undergo has not yet been fully exhausted, they cannot seek death; this continues until their evil and unwholesome karma is finished—until it is extinguished, eliminated, transformed, altered, departed from, or lost. Whatever was done by humans or non-humans in the past, they must experience the consequences in succession for an immeasurable length of time.

“Monks! Those sentient beings, having traversed an immeasurable and vast expanse of time, emerge from the Black Sand Hell. Having emerged, they run about, seeking a house, seeking a dwelling, seeking rescue, seeking shelter, and seeking a place of refuge.”
Having formed this thought, they enter again into the minor hell of Hot Excrement and Mud, which is five hundred yojanas in extent.

Once they have entered, from the throat downward, they are born into the midst of boiling excrement and mud with scorching flames. Having entered, the flames move and burn their hands and feet; their ears, noses, bodies, and limbs are all simultaneously scorched until those evil and unwholesome karmas are exhausted, extinguished, eliminated, and transformed—until they are neither abandoned nor lost—due to the heavy karma committed in the past by humans or non-humans.

Furthermore, monks! Within that minor hell of Excrement and Mud, there are iron insects called Needle-Mouths. Dwelling within that hell, they bore into the bodies of sentient beings everywhere, piercing them through and through. First they bore through the skin; having pierced the skin, they next bore through the flesh; having pierced the flesh, they next bore through the tendons; having pierced the tendons, they then break the bones. Once they have broken the bones, they dwell within the marrow and consume the fat and marrow of those sentient beings, causing them to undergo intense and agonizing suffering.

Until their lifespan has come to an end, and as long as those evil and unwholesome karmas have not been exhausted and have not yet been extinguished, they shall experience them in full succession in this manner.

“O bhikṣus! Those sentient beings in those hells, after a long time, a vast duration, and a great distance, emerge from the Minor Hell of Excrement and Mud. Having emerged, they run about, seeking a chamber, seeking a house, seeking protection, seeking an island, and seeking a place of refuge; they then enter the Minor Hell of the Five Forks, which is also five hundred yojanas in extent.”

Once they have entered the Five-Forked Hell, the hell-wardens seize those sentient beings who are undergoing punishment there and throw them upon the ground of glowing, heated iron, from which flames burst forth intensely.

At that time, the sinners lie supine within it; having thus lain down, two iron nails, blazing with fierce flames, are driven into the soles of their two feet; furthermore, two iron nails are driven into the palms of their two hands, their flames likewise fierce; and finally, one iron nail is driven into the navel center, its flame also fiercely blazing.

The hell-wardens then strike them with five-pronged forks, causing them to undergo extreme and severe suffering until their lifespan in that place has not yet ended and their evil karma has not been exhausted—whether created in a previous life or committed while in human or non-human bodies—they experience it in that hell in this successive manner.

"O bhikṣus! Those sentient beings, after a long and vast period of time, emerge from the Five-Forked Minor Hell; they run about seeking rescue, seeking a dwelling, seeking an island, seeking refuge, seeking shelter, and seeking protection, and arrive at the Hungry One Minor Hell, which is five hundred yojanas in extent."
Having entered that place, the wardens of hell saw those sentient beings approaching from afar and immediately went forward to ask them:
"What do you wish to come here for now?"
They all answered together:
"Venerable sir!
We are hungry."

Then the wardens of hell immediately seize those sentient beings from the hells, throw them down upon the blazing, hot iron ground, and force them to lie on their backs. They then pry open their mouths with iron tongs and hurl glowing iron balls into their mouths.

At that time, the lips and mouths of those sentient beings in hell are set ablaze; having burned the lips, they burn the tongue; having burned the tongue, they burn the palate; having burned the palate, they burn the throat; having burned the throat, they burn the heart; having burned the heart, they burn the chest; having burned the chest, they burn the intestines; having burned the intestines, they burn the stomach; and having passed through the stomach, they pass through the small intestine and exit downward, while the testicles remain red.

Thus, those sentient beings in the hells undergo extreme and severe suffering during that time; because their lives have not yet ended, it is said in brief that they experience, in succession, all manner of such things as were previously committed by humans or non-humans, within those hells.

“Monks! Those beings, after a long and vast period of immeasurable time, emerge from that minor hell of hunger and run on in haste—as briefly described before—seeking a place of refuge, and arrive at the minor hell of parching thirst, five hundred yojanas away.
Having entered that place, the guardians of hell see those sentient beings of the hells approaching from afar and ask them:
"What do you seek now?"
They replied, "O worthy one!
We are now extremely thirsty."

Then the wardens of hell immediately seized those beings from the hells and threw them down upon the ground of glowing, blazing red-hot iron. They laid them supine amidst fierce flames and, taking iron tongs, forced their mouths open and poured molten, crimson copper into their mouths.

At that time, the sentient beings in that hell find their lips and mouths immediately scorched and rotted; once the lips and mouths have rotted, they burn the tongue; having burned the tongue, they burn the palate; having burned the palate, they burn the throat; having burned the throat, they burn the heart; having burned the heart, they burn the chest; having burned the chest, they burn the intestines; and having burned the intestines, they burn the stomach, piercing straight through the small intestine and exiting downward.
Those sentient beings each undergo severe suffering, extreme pain, and various kinds of misery therein.

Until their life-span has ended, and unless they have exhausted those evil and unwholesome karmas—as briefly described before—even for deeds committed during human or non-human existences, they must experience them in full succession in this manner.
*Sūtra on the Causes and Origins of the World*, Scroll Two.
*Sūtra on the Causes and Origins of the World*, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Dharmagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
In the "Chapter on Hells":
"Furthermore, monks!

Those sentient beings in those hells, after a period of immeasurable time and a long journey, emerge from that small hell of parching thirst measuring five hundred *yojanas*. Having emerged, they run away—in brief, until they reach the point where—seeking a place of refuge and protection, they immediately go toward the pus-and-blood hell measuring five hundred *yojanas*."
Having entered that place, pus and blood immediately arise for them, boiling hot from the throat downward.
Those sentient beings in that hell, once they have entered, run back and forth, crisscrossing from east to west.
As they were thus running about, their hands and feet were burned, or their ears and noses; once their ears and noses were burned, all their limbs and joints were set ablaze.
When all their limbs and joints have been set ablaze, those sinners undergo suffering there that is severe, harsh, and inconceivable.

Since their life has not yet ended and their evil, unwholesome karma has not yet been fully exhausted— this being the result of what was created and brought forth during their human existence— furthermore, monks!
In the Pus-and-Blood Hell there are various worms called Most Fierce and Victorious Dwellers; these worms inflict great harm upon the sentient beings in that hell.

Or, within the body, one first cuts through the skin; having cut the skin, one next cuts the flesh; having cut the flesh, one cuts the tendons; having cut the tendons, one breaks the bones; and having broken the bones, one extracts the marrow and eats it.

Those sentient beings undergo severe suffering therein; until their lives have come to an end, they must fully experience all the evil and unwholesome karma that has been brought forth by their human bodies.

Furthermore, monks! Whenever the sentient beings in that Pus-and-Blood Hell become hungry or thirsty, they scoop up the boiling pus and blood with both hands and place it in their mouths. Once placed in their mouths, it immediately burns their lips; having burned the lips, it burns the palate; having burned the palate, it burns the throat; having burned the throat, it burns the chest; having burned the chest, it burns the heart; having burned the heart, it burns the intestines; having burned the intestines, it burns the stomach; and having burned the stomach, it passes straight through the small intestine and exits downward.

Those sentient beings, in that hell, undergo various forms of severe and heavy suffering until their lives have not yet ended and until their evil and unwholesome karma—accumulated while in human form—has been fully exhausted; they experience it all in this sequential manner, in its entirety.
"Furthermore, monks!

Those sentient beings in those hells, after traversing an immeasurable period of time along the long path, emerge from the Small Hell of Pus and Blood, which is five hundred yojanas in extent. Having emerged, they run on, seeking a place of refuge and protection, until they reach the Small Hell of the Copper Cauldron, which is five hundred yojanas in extent."

Having entered that place, the hell-wardens seize those various sentient beings of the hells and cast them into cauldrons with their heads downward and their feet upward. Because they are scorched and boiled there by the fires of hell, if the boiling liquid surges upward, they are cooked and ripened;
if it surges downward, they are likewise cooked and ripened;
and if it remains in the middle, they are again cooked and ripened.
Whether they are interlaced or crossed, they all become thoroughly cooked;
whether they are covered by froth or not, they all become thoroughly cooked;
whether they are seen or unseen, everything becomes thoroughly cooked.

For example, suppose in the world one were to cook small beans, large beans, mung beans, or the like; having placed them inside a cauldron and filled it with water, one lights a fire beneath it. Thus they boil and bubble, the broth and beans blending together: if they rise upward, they are being cooked and are becoming done;
if they sink downward, they are likewise being cooked and are becoming done;
and if they remain in the middle, they too are being cooked and are becoming done.
If they are intertwined, they are likewise thoroughly cooked;
if covered by froth, they are likewise thoroughly cooked;
whether seen or unseen, they are cooked at all times.

"O monks! In this way, and so it is, within that small hell of the single copper cauldron, there are wardens who seize those sentient beings of that hell, turn them upside down with their feet above and heads below, and hurl them from afar into the copper cauldron. There they are tormented by the fires of hell, which boil with intense heat."

At that time, the various sinners are driven upward by the boiling [liquid]; as soon as they are boiled, they are cooked through. To speak briefly, this continues until—whether they see it or not—they are likewise boiled and cooked through.

Therein they undergo intense suffering, even for those deeds committed while in human or non-human forms; in this manner, they experience [the results] in that hell in their entirety and in successive order.

"O bhikṣus! Those sentient beings within that hell, having traversed immeasurable time along the long path, emerge from the Small Hell of One Copper Cauldron, which is five hundred yojanas in extent. Having emerged, they run about, seeking a place of refuge and protection, and head toward the Small Hell of Many Copper Cauldrons, which is also five hundred yojanas in extent."
Having entered that place, the wardens seize those sentient beings from the hells, holding them with their feet upward and heads downward, and hurl them into copper cauldrons.
In that hell, the fierce fires are so oppressive that if the boiling water surges upward, they are cooked and ripened instantly;
if it surges downward, they are likewise cooked and ripened instantly;
and if they remain in between, they are also cooked and ripened instantly.
Whether positioned horizontally or inverted, whether visible or invisible, they are all thoroughly boiled and cooked.

It is like various beans and the like being boiled in a cauldron; driven by the heat of the fire, they surge and bubble upward, being both boiled and cooked. To speak briefly, this applies even to those that are visible or invisible—all are entirely boiled and cooked.
"O Bhikṣus!

In this very way, in the small hell called the Copper Cauldron, measuring five hundred yojanas, the beings there are seized by the wardens of hell, who take their two legs, turn them upward, and seize their heads downward, casting them into the copper cauldrons. Therein, they are tormented by the fires of hell; if they boil upward, they are cooked crosswise and thoroughly. Briefly stated, whether seen or unseen, they are all boiled and all cooked."
"Furthermore, monks!

In that minor hell of five hundred yojanas called Many Copper Cauldrons, the sentient beings are seized by the hell-wardens with iron crab-claws and moved from one cauldron to another. As they are being carried from one cauldron to another, their pus, blood, skin, and flesh are completely dispersed and exhausted, leaving nothing but skeletons."

Within that state, they undergo even the most severe and agonizing suffering until their life comes to an end; indeed, as long as those unwholesome karmas are not exhausted, they must experience the full consequences of every action they committed while in a human body.

"O monks! Those sentient beings within that hell, having traversed for immeasurable time through the long path, emerge from the Small Hell of Many Copper Cauldrons, which is five hundred yojanas in extent. Having emerged, they run on, seeking a place of refuge and protection, until they arrive at the Small Hell of Grinding Stones, which is five hundred yojanas in extent."

Having entered that place, the wardens of hell immediately seize the various sentient beings who are undergoing punishment, throw them face-up onto iron grinding stones that are ablaze with a single, intense, and piercing flame; once they are lying supine upon them, the wardens take other stones and press down upon them.
Having pressed them, their color changes; then they grind them further;
having ground them, they grind them yet again until they are reduced to fine powder.
Having ground it into a fine powder, he grinds it again and again; finally, the fine powder is set aside in a separate place.

Having ground it, he rubs it further; having rubbed it, he rubs it yet more; having ground it, he grinds it once more. When he reaches the stage of the final fine powder, blood flows from one side of his limbs while on the other side there still remains the residue of bone powder.

Within that place, they undergo the most severe suffering; until their life there has come to an end and those unwholesome karmas have been exhausted—namely, those produced during their time as human beings—they must experience them all in full, in this successive order.

"O bhikṣus! Those sentient beings in those hells, after passing through immeasurable time upon the long path, emerge from the small hell of the Grinding Mill, which is five hundred yojanas in extent."
Having emerged, they run about, seeking a dwelling, seeking a place of refuge and shelter, and arrive at the minor hell of the *kudava* measure, five hundred yojanas in extent.
Having entered that place, the wardens of hell seize those beings from the hells and, using iron measures glowing with intense flames and utterly ferocious, compel them to measure out fire.

When they measure out the fire, it burns their hands and feet, burns their ears and noses, and burns their major and minor limbs; having thus burned their limbs, they undergo extreme torment and experience the most agonizing suffering therein.

As long as their lifespan has not ended, and until those evil and unwholesome karmas are exhausted—not extinguished, not vanished, not departed, and not lost—they must experience, in their proper sequence and in full measure, all that was previously created, whether performed by the person in this life or brought from the past.

“Monks! Those sentient beings in those hells, after passing through an immeasurable period of time on that long and distant path, emerge from that small hell of five hundred yojanas in circumference.”

Having emerged, they run about, seeking a dwelling, seeking shelter, seeking rescue, seeking an island, and seeking a place of refuge; they then proceed toward the minor hell of Five Hundred Yojanas, known as Chicken.
Having entered that place, they dwell there amidst a mass of chickens filling it up to their knees; it is ablaze with flames, intensely and uniformly hot.

As those beings move within it, burning with heat at every step, they run hither and thither, looking in the four directions for a place of refuge, but finding none. The great fire blazes fiercely, burning their hands and feet, burning their ears and noses; having burned their ears and noses, it burns all their limbs and joints, so that both large and small parts are simultaneously set ablaze.
Therein they undergo extreme and severe suffering, even unto the most agonizing and heavy torments.
While their lives have not yet ended therein, and while those unwholesome and evil karmas—those committed by persons in human form—have not yet been exhausted, they remain there.
In that sequence, they experience everything in full. "O bhikṣus!
After passing through immeasurable time and a long, distant path within those hells, the sentient beings there finally emerge from that Chicken Small Hell."
Having emerged, they run straight ahead in flight until they reach a place where they might seek refuge; there they enter the Ash River Minor Hell, which is also five hundred yojanas in extent.
"O Bhikṣus!
Once the sinners have entered, that River of Ash flows with great rapidity; its waves surge high, its roar is most thunderous, and the boiling ash-water overflows, filling the banks to the brim."
Within the lower reaches of that River of Ashes, there are iron spikes as sharp as if they had been whetted.
On both its banks, there are further distinct groves of razors;
within these razor-groves on both riverbanks, there are also dogs, purple-black in color, filthy and terrifying.
Furthermore, on both banks, there are separate guardians of the hell;
moreover, on both banks grow śālmali trees, which have thorns that are slender, long, and sharp, their points as if ground smooth.
At that time, the various sentient beings in hell enter that river, desiring to cross to the other shore.
As they are crossing, they are swept away and submerged by great waves; sinking downward, they are then pierced through their bodies by iron spikes within that river.
Once pierced, they remain there, experiencing extreme and severe suffering, enduring great and heavy agony.
Having floated out, they cross from the River of Boiling Ashes to the other shore.

Having reached the other shore, they immediately enter that Forest of Razors again; the forest is vast and wide, and they wander through it for a long time, braving the sharp blades. Moving everywhere within it, they enter and re-enter, undergoing extreme suffering: sometimes their hands are cut off, sometimes their feet, or both their hands and feet; their ears are cut off, their noses, or both their ears and noses; their limbs are cut off, their joints, or both their limbs and joints.

Therein, they undergo severe suffering, even unto extreme suffering; until their life-span ends and until their evil and unwholesome karma—whether committed in a previous human existence or elsewhere—is entirely exhausted, they must experience it all therein.
Furthermore, when the various hell-wardens on both banks of that River of Ashes see those sentient beings who have come there to undergo punishment, they ask them:
"What do you desire to obtain from your bodies now?"
Those sentient beings replied in unison, "We are extremely hungry.

Then, the wardens of hell seized those beings and threw them onto the ground. Amidst blazing flames and intense, piercing heat, they laid the beings flat on their backs. Using iron tongs, they forced open their mouths and placed glowing iron balls inside. Instantly, these burned the lips and mouths of the hell-beings until they were scorched and shattered; in brief, the balls passed down through the throat and reached the small intestine, passing straight through without obstruction.
Within that place, they undergo severe and agonizing suffering; they undergo extremely heavy suffering.
As long as their life has not yet ended, and until those unwholesome karmas—as well as those committed in their previous human lives—are completely exhausted, they must experience them all in full.
"Furthermore, monks!

Moreover, on both banks of that River of Boiling Ashes, there are dogs with bodies that are blackish-purple, filthy and greasy, and terrifying. They devour the bodies of those sentient beings in hell, biting off and eating piece by piece the flesh from their limbs and joints."
The dogs may make sounds, growling and barking.
Within that place, they undergo severe and piercing suffering, even up to the most extreme and heavy suffering.
Without their lives coming to an end, and until those unwholesome karmas—as well as those performed in former human existences—are exhausted, they must experience them all in full.

"O monks! When those sentient beings in that hell are tormented by the surging, intensely hot River of Ashes, they are further driven by the sharp iron spikes and the forest of razors, terrified by the wardens, and flee from the blackish-purple, filthy dogs; thus, due to these various urgent perils."
At that time, the various sentient beings in that hell immediately ran up that śamala tree.
As they climbed the tree, its branches and twigs were composed entirely of iron thorns; these thorns were sharp and piercing, with their points all facing downward, slender and long as if polished.
When they wish to descend, those iron thorns turn their heads upward, becoming slender, long, and sharp.

As those sentient beings of that hell climb that śālmali tree, there appear birds called "iron-beaks. Once these birds arrive, they peck at the heads of the hell-beings; having broken open the heads, they suck out and devour the brains.
Therein, they undergo extreme and severe suffering, agonizing pain that is utterly unbearable.

They then fall back again into the River of Boiling Ashes; there, they are once more tossed about by great waves, sinking to the bottom of the river, and having reached that place, they are further pierced and lacerated by iron spikes.
Once their bodies have been pierced, they are unable to move further; they remain right there, suffering therein with extreme and most cruel intensity.

Unable to endure it, they again rise up and run away, crossing over the River of Ashes; having crossed, they return once more to this shore. They enter the Forest of Dense Razors again and again; as they enter, their hands are cut, their feet are cut, or both hands and feet are cut, even unto the severing of all their limbs and joints, wherein they undergo the most extreme and severe suffering.
"Until their life-span is exhausted—briefly stated, even including all that has been brought forth from past actions committed as humans or non-humans—they must experience these in successive order.
Furthermore, monks!"
All the hell-wardens on this shore of the River of Boiling Ashes, upon seeing the sentient beings who have come there to undergo punishment in hell, immediately call out to them from afar, saying:
"O you all, for what purpose have you come so far?"
"What do you desire? Those beings each replied,
"We are parched with thirst."
Then, the wardens seize those sentient beings and throw them down upon the ground of glowing, blazing red-hot iron, forcing them to lie on their backs.
Once they are lying on their backs, flames erupt violently; the wardens then pry open their mouths with iron tongs and pour molten, glowing copper into their mouths.

At that time, those sentient beings in the hell, having drunk the molten copper, had their lips and mouths burned all the way down through their small intestines, which then passed straight out below.

Within those [hells], they undergo extreme and severe suffering until their life-span has not yet dispersed, not yet ceased, and not yet exhausted; therein they experience in full all the unwholesome karma that originated from their human bodies.
"Furthermore, monks!

Those sentient beings in those hells, having undergone the retribution for their offenses and passed through immeasurable time upon the long and distant path, there arises a wind; this great wind is named 'Harmonizing' (Saṃvartanīya), which blows those sentient beings in the hells toward the shore."

In this sequence, having emerged from the Kukkula-nadī (Boiling Ash River) hell, they run forth, seeking a place of refuge and protection, until they arrive at the Pañcaśata-yojana Phalaka-cchedana (Five Hundred Yojanas of Chopped Boards) minor hell.

Having entered that place, the wardens of hell seize those beings from the hells and throw them down upon the ground of glowing, blazing hot iron. Once they have been made to lie prostrate on the ground, they take iron axes—blazing with fierce flames and emitting intense, brilliant radiance—and for the sake of those beings in hell, they hack off their hands, hack off their feet, and hack off both their hands and feet; they hack off their ears, hack off their noses, and hack off both their ears and noses; they hack off their limbs, hack off their joints, and hack off both their limbs and joints.
Therein, they undergo even the most severe suffering.
As long as their life has not yet ended, and until their evil and unwholesome karma—accumulated through human existence—is fully exhausted, they must endure all such experiences in succession.
"Furthermore, monks!
Those sentient beings in those hells, after a vast and immeasurable period of time, emerge from that Small Chopping Board Hell."

Having emerged, they run on until they seek a house, seek shelter, seek an island, seek a place of refuge, and seek a place of protection, heading toward the Small Hell of the Sword-Leaf Forest, which is five hundred yojanas in extent.
Having entered therein, because they lack the fruit of any wholesome karma, a wind suddenly arises and blows them down from the air onto the forest of iron-bladed leaves.

For those sentient beings in that hell, that forest of iron blades chops their hands, chops their feet, and also chops both hands and feet; it chops their ears, chops their noses, and also chops both ears and noses; it chops their limbs, chops their joints, and also chops both limbs and joints. Within that place, they undergo extremely severe and agonizing suffering.
Since their lives have not yet ended, the brief explanation is as above; even those karmic results produced by human beings that come to them are all fully experienced therein.
"Furthermore, O bhikṣus!

In that minor hell of the Forest of Sword-Leaves, because there is no fruit of virtuous karma, iron-beaked crows suddenly appear; they fly toward the two shoulders of the sentient beings in that hell.
Having established its feet, it then pecks out both eyes of that offender with its iron beak and departs.
At that time, the person undergoes extremely severe, agonizing, and heavy suffering.

Since their life-span has not yet ended, the brief account is as described above; even those karmic results produced by human beings that have come forth, they must experience all of them in this sequential order.
"Furthermore, O Bhikṣus!"
Those beings within that hell, after an immeasurable period of time and a long journey, emerge from the Minor Hell of the Forest of Sword-Leaves.

Having emerged, they run about, seeking a dwelling, seeking shelter, seeking an island of safety, seeking a place of refuge, and seeking a place of protection; they then approach the Minor Hell of Five Hundred Yojanas of Foxes and Wolves.

Having entered that place, due to the retribution of their various unwholesome karmas, they are born as foxes and wolves within that hell—fierce, blazing, coarse, and hideous, snarling with terrifying ferocity. They bite the flesh from the bodies of the sentient beings in that hell, trampling them with their feet and tearing at them with their mouths, devouring them piece by piece, while also uttering cries of distress and letting out great, thundering roars.
Within those [hells], they undergo even the most severe sufferings.

As long as their lives have not yet ended—as briefly described before—they must experience, in their entirety and in successive order, all the torments brought about by the actions of humans and non-humans.
"Furthermore, monks!
Those sentient beings within that hell, after an immeasurable period of time, emerge from that minor hell of Foxes and Wolves.

Having emerged, they run about, seeking a dwelling, seeking an island, seeking shelter, seeking a place of protection, and seeking a place of refuge, until they arrive at the Small Hell of Cold Ice, which is five hundred yojanas in extent.

Having entered that place, due to the retribution of their various unwholesome karmas, a sudden cold wind arises, blowing a harsh, coarse, and intensely painful chill that strikes the bodies of the sentient beings in that hell; their skin is all split open, and once the skin is split, it next splits the flesh; once the flesh is split, it next splits the tendons; once the tendons are split, it next splits the bones; and once the bones are split, it finally splits the marrow.

When their marrow is shattered, they undergo therein extreme and severe suffering, the most agonizing and piercing of pains, which they cannot endure; consequently, their lives come to an end right there.
This is the very first and greatest, named the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva), along with the other sixteen minor hells.
"Furthermore, monks!

As for the second great hell, Kālasūtra, it is likewise surrounded by sixteen minor hells, each five hundred yojanas in extent; from the Black Sand Hell down to the sixteenth and final Cold Ice Hell, they constitute a single retinue.
"Monks! Within this context, what is the cause and condition by which this great hell is named 'Black Rope' (Kālasūtra)? Monks!"

Within that great Black Rope Hell, all sentient beings—those being born, those already born, those emerging, and those dwelling there—due to the retribution of their various unwholesome karmas, have coarse black ropes suddenly appear in the air above them, blazing with fierce flames and burning intensely with heat.
For example, from the ground up to the heavens, throughout that space, great black clouds arise and pervade it in such and such a manner.

Likewise, within the Great Hell of Black Rope, all sentient beings, as a result of their various unwholesome karmic retributions, see great black ropes with fiercely blazing flames emerge in the sky above. These fall upon the bodies of those sentient beings in hell. Once they have fallen upon their bodies, they burn the skin of the hell-beings; having burned the skin, they burn the flesh; having burned the flesh, they burn the tendons; having burned the tendons, they burn the bones; having burned the bones, they penetrate to the marrow. Once the marrow has emerged and is burning, great flames continue to erupt from it.

Within that state, they undergo fierce suffering and extremely heavy suffering. Because of their sinful karma, as long as their life has not yet ended, and until those evil and unwholesome karmas have been exhausted—not having been extinguished, transformed, eliminated, or completed—they must experience the full consequences of everything they created, whether in past human or non-human existences.
"Furthermore, monks!

All those sentient beings within that great hell of Black Rope—whether they have been born there, are currently being born, abide there, or are manifested there—do so as the result of the retribution for their various unwholesome karmas."

Then the wardens of hell seize those various sentient beings from that hell and throw them down upon a ground of blazing, hot iron. Once they have been laid flat on their backs until the flames are intensely fierce and raging, the wardens measure them all over with glowing iron cords. Having measured them, they use iron adzes and axes of blazing, radiant flame to hack the bodies of those sentient beings in the hell, cutting them into two parts, or three, four, five, or even ten, twenty, fifty, or a hundred parts.

For example, suppose there is a skilled carpenter or a carpenter’s apprentice who takes various pieces of wood, places them upon the ground, and then uses black cords to mark out measurements. Having completed the marking, he uses sharp adzes and axes to divide them into two parts, three, four, or five parts, or again into ten, twenty parts, or even a hundred parts, in such and such a manner.
"O bhikṣus!

Furthermore, it is the same for all sentient beings within that great hell of Black Rope (Kālasūtra). The wardens seize those beings and throw them down upon the ground of glowing, blazing iron; having laid them on their backs, they measure out paths with black iron cords and then use saws and axes to hack their bodies into various segments, just as before."

Within that state, they experience even excruciating and most severe suffering; yet, as long as their lives have not ended and those unwholesome karmas have not been exhausted, they must fully undergo all the consequences resulting from the deeds they committed while in human form in the past.
"Furthermore, monks!
Among all the sentient beings within that great hell of Black Rope—whether they are born there, transformed there, or even those who dwell there—"

At that time, the wardens seize those sentient beings and throw them down upon the ground of blazing, glowing-hot iron. Having thus taken them up, they lay them on their backs on the ground and measure their bodies with black iron cords. They then use iron saws of fierce, blazing flames to saw through the bodies of those hell-beings; having cut once, they cut again, until they have cut them greatly; then they tear them apart, having torn them once, they tear them again, until they have torn them greatly. They may hack or sever them, and having hacked and severed them, they hack and sever them yet again, or even great hacking and severing.

It is, for example, like a skilled carpenter in the world, or one of his disciples, who takes various pieces of wood, places them upon the ground, and uses black cords to mark out the lines. He then saws them apart with a sharp iron saw; having cut them once, he cuts again until they are greatly divided; next he splits them further, splitting them repeatedly until they are greatly split; then he cuts them through, and having cut them through, he cuts them yet again, even cutting them through on a large scale.
"Thus it is, thus it is, O bhikṣus!

Within that great hell of Black Rope (Kālasūtra), all those sentient beings—whether born there, currently existing there, or even dwelling there—the wardens seize them and throw them down upon the ground of glowing, blazing iron. Having made them lie prostrate on the ground, they measure out paths with black iron cords and then, using iron saws of fierce, blazing flames, they split their bodies apart. Having split them, they split them again until they are greatly split; having torn them, they tear them again until they are greatly torn; having cut them, they cut them again until they are greatly cut; having severed them, they sever them again until they are greatly severed."
Within those realms, they undergo even the most severe sufferings until their lives come to an end;
as briefly described above, they experience fully all that was done by them while in human form.
"Furthermore, monks!

Within that great hell of Black Rope (Kālasūtra), all those sentient beings who have been born there and even those currently dwelling there, are seized by the hell-wardens. With red-hot iron anvils blazing with fierce flames, they cause those beings to strike one another."

When they strike them, it burns their hands, burns their feet, or burns both hands and feet; it burns their ears, burns their noses, or burns both ears and noses; it burns their limbs, burns their joints, or burns all their limbs and joints.
Within that [hell], they undergo even the most severe and agonizing sufferings.
Before their lives have come to an end—as briefly described above—they experience in full all the consequences resulting from the deeds committed while in human form.
"Furthermore, monks!

Within that great hell of Black Rope (Kālasūtra), for the sake of all sentient beings dwelling there, a great black rope appears in the sky above, blazing with intense and fierce flames, which falls directly onto the bodies of those sentient beings in that hell."

When they fall into the Black Rope Hell, the bodies of those sentient beings are bound; having been bound, they are bound again and even more severely bound; having been constricted, they are constricted again and even more severely constricted.
After they have been bound and tightened, they are once again blown open by the wind.

When the wind opens them, the sentient beings in that hell have their skin flayed from their bodies; having flayed the skin, their flesh is next flayed; having flayed the flesh, their tendons are then pulled out, even unto breaking the bones; and once the bones are broken, the marrow is blown away.
At that time, during that interval, they undergo even the most severe suffering.
As long as their life has not yet ended—as briefly described above—they must experience all of it in succession until those evil and unwholesome karmas are fully exhausted.
"Furthermore, monks!

Those sentient beings within that hell, after an immeasurable period of time and a long journey, emerge from that Black Rope Great Hell. Having emerged, they run about, seeking cover, seeking shelter, seeking an island, seeking a place of refuge, and seeking a place of protection. They enter the Black Sand Minor Hell, which is five hundred yojanas in extent; having entered it, and briefly speaking, even as described above until reaching the sixteenth Cold Ice Hell, once they have entered those hells, they undergo various kinds of suffering until their lives come to an end."
"Furthermore, monks!

The Saṃghāta Great Hell is likewise surrounded by sixteen minor hells, each five hundred yojanas in length and breadth. Beginning from the Kālasūtra minor hell and continuing as previously described, up to the very last, the Arbuda Cold Ice Hell."
"Monks! Within this context, what is the cause and condition by which that great hell is named Saṃghāta? Monks!"

Furthermore, for the sake of all those sentient beings within that Saṃghāta Great Hell—whether they are being born, have been born, are emerging, are being transformed, or even those who remain—two mountains arise, named White Sheep and Mouth-Eater, blazing with extremely fierce and violent flames.
At that time, those sentient beings in hell enter within those mountains.

Once they have entered, the two mountains then grind against each other, strike against each other, and rub against each other; having thus closed, ground, struck, and rubbed, the mountains return to their original positions.

For example, there are two types of lightning called *vikhanu* and *prativikhanu*. When these two meet, rub against each other, grind against each other, and strike one another, having thus met, rubbed, and struck, they each return to their original place.
"In this way, monks, it is so!
Those two mountains, having come together, rubbed against, scraped against, and struck one another, and having collided, each disperses and returns to its original place; it is just like this."

Furthermore, among those beings in the hells, when they are crushed, ground, and beaten by the closing of the mountains, their bodies flow entirely with pus and blood until only skeletons remain; at that time, they undergo even the most severe suffering.
Since their lives have not yet ended, it should be understood that this applies briefly to all stages in the sequence as described above. "Furthermore, monks!

Regarding all those sentient beings within the Saṃghāta Great Hell—whether they are born there or already dwelling there—the hell-wardens seize those beings and, using great iron stones ablaze with fierce flames, they strike the hell-beings down and place them upon a hot ground, making them lie on their backs. Upon those iron stones, they take other stones to cover them, grinding them like a worldly millstone. Thus they grind them, grinding again and again, crushing them into powder; once they are powdered, they grind them even more finely."
While they were grinding it, they ground it further and more heavily; having ground it, they ground it again, grinding it extensively until it became dust.
Once it had become dust, they further reduced it to fine powder.
When they are thus ground into various kinds of dust and powder, they see nothing but pus and blood flowing out, while only empty skeletal remains and fine dust persist.
Within that state, they undergo even the most extreme and heavy suffering.
Since their lives have not yet ended, the brief description above should be understood as the sequence. "Furthermore, monks!

Within that Saṃghāta Great Hell, all those sentient beings who are born, exist, or even dwell there—the hell-wardens seize them and throw them into large iron vats of glowing red-hot iron, which blaze with intense, unceasing flames."

Once they have been cast into the trough, they are crushed just as sugarcane and sesame seeds are pressed in the world; thus they are crushed, crushed again and again, being subjected to such great pressure.

When they are thus pressed, one sees on their sides only pus and blood flowing out, and on one side only the dregs of bones remaining within; they undergo great and severe suffering, as briefly described above.
Since their life-span has not yet ended, they undergo various kinds of suffering that are extremely intense. "Furthermore, monks!

Among all the sentient beings within that Saṃghāta Great Hell—whether they are those being born, those already born, or even those currently dwelling there—the hell-wardens seize those beings and hurl them into iron mortars ablaze with fierce flames; they then take up iron pestles that are uniformly and intensely hot and pound them, pounding them again and again until they have been pounded thoroughly."
In this manner, they built again; having built, they built once more, until it was a great construction.
Once the tamping and building were complete, they further crushed it into powder, and then crushed it into even finer powder.
When they have thus been pounded, crushed, and ground into dust, only pus and blood flow out continuously to one side, while on the other side only the remains of bone fragments are left.
Among them, they undergo extremely severe and heavy suffering, as briefly described above.
Thus, until their lives come to an end, they fully experience all manner of sufferings therein.
"Furthermore, monks!
Within that Saṃghāta Great Hell, there are all those beings of the various hells—those who have been born, those who exist, and even those who dwell therein."
At that time, in the space above, a great iron elephant spontaneously appeared; it was blazing and fierce, even unto a single direction where its flames were intensely brilliant.

For the sake of those sentient beings in that hell, from the crown of their heads down to their insteps, an elephant tramples their skulls with its two feet; having trampled them once, it tramples again, and continues to trample until they are thoroughly crushed.

When those elephants trample upon them, they cause all the pus and blood from the bodies of the sentient beings in that hell to flow out entirely, until on one side there remain only the skeletal remains.
Therein they undergo great and severe suffering, as briefly described above.
Until their lives have come to an end, they experience it all in this successive order. "Furthermore, monks!
Then those beings within the Saṃghāta Great Hell, after passing through immeasurable time upon the long path, emerge from the Saṃghāta Great Hell.
Having emerged, they run straight ahead in flight until they reach a place of refuge within the Black Cloud Sands (Kṛṣṇābhra-saikatā), a minor hell five hundred yojanas in extent.
Having entered, they undergo all manner of sufferings even unto the Arbuda (Cold Ice) Hell.
"Furthermore, monks, within that Great Hell of Raurava (Screaming),
there are also sixteen minor hells, each five hundred yojanas in extent, ranging from Kālasūtra (Black Sand) down to the final Arbuda (Cold Ice) Hell."
"Monks! Within this interval, what is the cause and condition for designating that place as the Great Hell of Screaming? Monks!"

Furthermore, within that Great Hell of Screaming, among those beings who have been born, exist, or even dwell there, the hell-wardens drive those beings into various iron cities; these cities are ablaze with glowing, fierce iron flames, their radiant light and fire being intensely brilliant.

Because those beings therein undergo even severe suffering, being oppressed by manifold afflictions, they gather together and constantly cry out loudly; therefore, it is called the Hell of Screaming (Raurava).

Within that hell, the houses, rooms, carriages, and litters are all made of iron; the watchtowers, gardens, and ponds are likewise entirely of iron, filled with glowing embers and blazing fires, radiating intense light and penetrating through everything in every direction.

Those sentient beings who have committed offenses are driven into it and cast therein; oppressed by various sufferings that are unbearable, they even cry out, and for this reason it is called the Hell of Screaming (Raurava).
Within that place, they undergo great and severe suffering, as briefly described above.
Since their lives have not yet ended and their evil and unwholesome karma has not been exhausted, they must experience it in its entirety, following this sequence.
"O monks! Those sentient beings in that hell, after passing through an immeasurable time upon the long path, emerge from that Great Hell of Wailing."

Having emerged, they run away; as briefly described before, they continue until they seek a place of refuge and arrive at the Black Cloud Sand (Kṛṣṇābhra-vāluka) minor hell, five hundred *yojanas* in extent. Having entered it, as previously described and as briefly recounted, they eventually reach the final cold-hell, the Hell of Ice (Himā), where their lives end and they undergo all manner of suffering.
"Furthermore, monks!

Within that Great Crying Hell (Mahāraurava), there are also sixteen minor hells as its retinue, all of which are five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, ranging from the Black Sand Hell down to the final Cold Ice Hell."
"Monks! Within that interval, by what cause and condition is it called the Great Screaming Great Hell? Monks!"
Within that Great Crying Hell, all sentient beings— those who have been born there and those who dwell there—
are seized by the hell-wardens and cast entirely into iron chambers that are fiercely hot, even unto a state of continuous, violent, and blazing flames.

Within that [hell], they undergo extreme and agonizing suffering, so intense and unbearable that it is difficult to endure; as these various afflictions converge, they subsequently let out great cries of lamentation. For this reason, that hell is called "Great Crying" (Mahāraurava).
Within that hell, there are iron houses, iron chambers, iron carriages, iron pavilions, and iron towers; therein, glowing coals boil and overflow.
Within them, those beings undergo extreme suffering, as briefly described previously.
Since their life-span has not yet been exhausted, they continue to experience these states in succession until they are fully undergone. O bhikṣus!
After traversing the long and distant path for immeasurable time, those beings in the various hells emerge from the Great Howling (Mahāraurava) Great Hell.
Having emerged, they run away; to summarize briefly, they seek a place of refuge and protection, arriving at the Black Cloud Sand (Kṛṣṇābhrasikatā) minor hell.
Having entered it, they proceed through all the way up to the final sixteenth cold-ice hell, where they die and undergo all manner of sufferings.
"Furthermore, monks!

Within that Great Hell of Burning Heat, there are also sixteen minor hells as its retinue. Each of these hells is, as previously described, five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, extending from the Black Sand Hell down to the final Cold Ice Hell."
"Monks! Within this context, what is the cause and condition for designating that place as the Great Hell of Burning Torment (Tapana)? Monks!"

Within that Great Hell of Burning Torment, among those sentient beings who have been born, are being born, or even currently dwell there, the wardens seize them and cast them into iron cauldrons with their heads pointing straight down and their feet pointing upward; they are boiled and surged by intense heat, amidst nothing but the flames and fiery waters of perpetual scalding.
Because those beings are burned and boiled therein, it is therefore called the Hell of Heat and Torment (*Tapana*).
Within that hell, there are various iron cauldrons, iron jars, iron basins, iron vats, iron wash-basins, iron griddles, and iron tripods, all of which are blazing intensely with fierce flames.
Within that [hell], they are either burned or boiled; therefore it is called "Torment of Heat. Therein they undergo extremely severe and heavy suffering.
As long as their life has not yet ended and those evil and unwholesome karmas have not been exhausted, they must experience all of this in such a sequence.
"O bhikṣus!
Those beings within that hell, after passing through immeasurable time upon the long and distant path, emerge from that Great Hell of Burning Heat."

Having emerged, they run and flee in haste, seeking a place of refuge and protection; they head toward the Black Cloud Sand Minor Hell, and so forth, briefly including even the Cold Ice Hell. There, their lives end, and they undergo all manner of suffering.
"Furthermore, monks!

Within that Great Hell of Intense Heat (Pratāpana), there are also sixteen minor hells, each five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, ranging from the Minor Hell of Black Sand (Kālasūtra) to the final Minor Hell of Cold Ice (Himā).
Within this context, for what reason is it called the Great Hell of Intense Heat (Mahātapana)? O Bhikṣus!

In that Great Hell of Intense Heat, among those sentient beings who are born, exist, and even dwell there, the wardens seize them, grasp them by the head and cast them down with their feet upward, placing them within iron cauldrons. Fierce fires blaze intensely, until flames of heat surge forth in every direction.
Within that place, after they have experienced extreme heat and great torment, they undergo further intense torment; therefore, it is called the Hell of Blazing and Greatest Torment.
Within those glowing iron cauldrons, basins, pots, pans, and kettles, they suffer from burning heat and affliction, experiencing extreme and piercing agony.

Once cast therein, they are scorched, boiled, roasted, and fried by the fires of hell; they endure various torments, suffering upon suffering. For this reason, it is called the Hell of Most Fierce Heat and Extreme Affliction.
Within that place, they undergo intense suffering and affliction, as briefly described above.
Until their lives come to an end, they experience such suffering in this successive manner.
"O Bhikṣus!

Those beings within that hell, having passed through immeasurable time on a long and arduous path, emerge from that intensely hot and extremely agonizing great hell. They flee and run away—briefly described—they seek a place of refuge and protection, arriving at the minor hell of Black Sand, and so on, until they reach the final Cold Ice Hell. Yet, as their life has not yet ended, they continue to undergo various sufferings in succession, just as before."
"Furthermore, monks!

Within that great Avīci hell, there are also sixteen minor hells as its retinue, surrounding it on all sides. Each of these hells is five hundred yojanas in extent, beginning with Kālasūtra-saṃvartanī and ending finally with the Śīta-hima hell."
"Monks! What is the cause and condition by which that intermediate place is called the Great Hell of Avīci? Monks!"

Within that Avīci Great Hell, among the various sentient beings—those who have been born, those currently existing, those emerging, and those dwelling there—due to the retribution of their evil and unwholesome karma, wardens spontaneously appear. Each of them seizes the bodies of the hell-beings with their hands and hurls them onto the ground of glowing, blazing red-hot iron. As flames shoot straight upward, fiercely intense and all-consuming, they cast the beings face-down; then, taking up sharp knives, they pull out the sinews from the ankles, continuing all the way to the hair, drawing them out until heart and marrow are pierced through. The suffering is beyond description.

Once they have been thus extracted, they are then made to travel in iron chariots that blaze with fierce flames and are intensely hot, being driven across an iron ground extending for immeasurable yojanas.

Wherever they go, the path is entirely composed of glowing, red-hot iron; having gone, they go again, following their own mental impulses without pausing for even a moment. Wherever they wish to go, they proceed as they please, according to their desires, wherever they may travel and wherever they may arrive.
When they were thus about to take him away—when they intended to take him away, when they desired to take him away—the flesh and blood of their bodies immediately vanished, leaving nothing behind.
For this reason, they undergo severe and piercing suffering, most heavy and intense suffering, and suffering that the mind finds unpleasant.

As long as their life has not yet ended, and until their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted—not extinguished, not dispersed, not transformed, and not shifted—they must experience in its entirety everything that was done by them in former lives, whether as humans or non-humans.
"Furthermore, monks!

Within that great Avīci Hell, for all those beings who are born, have been born, are being transformed, or are dwelling there, as a result of the retribution of their evil and unwholesome karma, a great mass of fire suddenly arises from the eastern direction—blazing with a brilliant color, possessing extreme and fierce flames, shining intensely and uniformly."
