In this same sequence, from the south, the west, the north, and all other directions, there arise great masses of fire in each quarter, blazing with fierce flames that are entirely intense and brilliant.

Within that place, they are surrounded on all four sides by masses of the four great fires, which gradually close in upon them and converge together, causing all sentient beings to undergo various sufferings, even unto the experience of those most severe and agonizing pains.
Since their life-span has not yet ended, as briefly described above, they undergo all [these sufferings] within that hell.
*Qishi yinben jing*, Scroll Three.
*Qishi yinben jing*, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Dharmagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on the Hells, Part Two:
"Furthermore, O Bhikṣus!"

In that great Avīci hell, among those beings who are born, exist, and even dwell there, due to the retribution of their evil and unwholesome karma, flames emerge from the eastern wall and shoot directly toward the western wall.
Having arrived, they remained there; from the western wall, rays of light issued forth and shot directly toward the eastern wall, where they arrived and remained;
from the southern wall, rays of light issued forth and shot directly toward the northern wall;
from the northern wall, rays of light issued forth and shot directly toward the southern wall.
From below it ascends, and from above it shoots downward; they intersect horizontally and vertically, surging and piercing one another;
the hot light blazes with fierce flames as they surge and boil against each other.
Within that place, they cast sentient beings into these six kinds of great masses of fierce fire, causing them to be stuck therein and to undergo extremely severe and agonizing suffering.
"Since their life has not yet ended—and to speak briefly—until those unwholesome karmas have been completed and exhausted, they must experience [the results] in their entirety during that interval.
Furthermore, monks!"

Within that great Avīci hell, all those beings who have been born, exist, or even dwell there, because of the retribution for their evil and unwholesome karma, after passing through immeasurable time on the long path, see the eastern gate of the prison suddenly open of its own accord.
At that time, the various sentient beings in that hell, having seen and heard the sound of the gates opening, ran toward that place; they ran and ran again, running with great speed, thinking:
"Now that we have reached that place, we shall surely be liberated."
"We have now reached that place; it shall be most auspicious for us.
As those beings ran in this manner—running again and again, running with great speed—the flames on their bodies grew even more intensely blazing.
It is, for example, like a powerful and strong man in the world who runs against the wind carrying a great torch; that torch, moreover, burns even more fiercely and intensely as he goes.

In this way, as they run, having run they run again; as they run in this manner, all the limbs and joints of their bodies burn with even greater intensity. When they lift their feet, their flesh and blood disperse; when they set their feet down, that flesh grows back once more.
Furthermore, as they thus run about and draw near the gate, for their sake the gate closes of its own accord.
At that time, within that hell, upon the ground of glowing red-hot iron, the sentient beings become utterly faint and collapse face-downward amidst the blazing flames.

Once they have fallen prostrate therein, their skin is immediately scorched; after the skin is scorched, the flesh is scorched; after the flesh is scorched, the tendons are scorched; after the tendons are scorched, the bones are scorched; after the bones are scorched, it reaches the marrow. As soon as the marrow is exposed, smoke issues forth; once the smoke has issued, more smoke emerges, and then great clouds of smoke billow out.
Therein, they undergo extremely severe suffering in succession.

As long as their lives have not yet ended—briefly described as before—they must fully experience all those evil and unwholesome karmas that have come from their past actions while in human or non-human forms, until such karma is exhausted.
"Furthermore, monks!

Within that Great Hell of Unrelenting Torment (Avīci), those beings who have been born, exist, or even dwell there, due to the retribution of their various unwholesome karmas, pass through immeasurable time along the long path. At that time, the southern gate, the western gate, and even the northern gate of that hell open up once again in this manner."
At that time, the various sentient beings in that hell, hearing the sound of the opening, ran toward the gate; having run, they ran again, even running with great speed, and thought to themselves:
"We shall surely attain liberation from this place now; we will certainly be completely freed at this moment."
As they were thus running with great speed, their bodies became even more intensely ablaze.
It was as if a strong man were holding a large torch of dry grass in his hand and running against the wind; as he ran, that torch would not only burn, but become even more fiercely blazing.
In this manner, those sentient beings run and run again, even running with great speed.

As they run in this way, their bodies become increasingly ablaze; when they lift and throw down their feet, their flesh and blood are scattered, yet as they wish to set their feet down, the flesh and blood regenerate.

When they reached the gate, it closed shut again; within that place, upon a floor of glowing red-hot iron with blazing, intense flames, they ran on in one direction alone. Being unable to escape, their minds became frantic and confused, and they fell prostrate to the ground face down.

Once they have fallen to the ground therein, their skin is immediately scorched; once the skin is scorched, their flesh is scorched next; once the flesh is scorched, their bones are scorched, even penetrating to the marrow. Everything blazes forth with smoke issuing out; that smoke billows and surges, emitting crimson light as the smoke and flames intermingle, and the torment of heat is doubled.
Within that [hell], they undergo extreme and severe suffering, as briefly described above.

This continues until their lifespan has reached its end, and until their evil and unwholesome karma has been extinguished, abandoned, transformed, and dispersed; until then, they must experience the full consequences of everything they previously committed while in human or non-human forms.
"Furthermore, monks!

Among all the sentient beings dwelling within that Great Hell of Avīci, as they are being burned by the fires of that hell due to the retribution of their various unwholesome karmas, whatever forms they perceive with their eyes are all forms that are not pleasing to their minds; those forms that would be pleasing do not appear before them."
These are not what the mind desires, nor are they things that are good; they are forms that are unlovely and unwholesome, which constantly oppress and afflict.

The sounds heard by the ear, the odors smelled by the nose, the flavors tasted by the tongue, the tangibles felt by the body, and the mental objects conceived by the mind—all these are phenomena that are not pleasing to the mind.
If that which is not pleasing to the mind, not a desirable phenomenon, should appear before them, every such object is unwholesome.
Because of these causes and conditions, they constantly experience extremely heavy, coarse, and harsh suffering; because their color is foul, so too is their touch.

Until their lifespan has come to an end, and until their evil and unwholesome karma has subsided and been extinguished, they shall fully experience the consequences of all the various evil deeds they committed in the past while in human or non-human forms.
"Furthermore, monks,
for what other reason is that great hell Avīci called the Great Hell Avīci?
"O bhikṣus!

Within that great hell of Avīci, there is not even for a moment, nor for as long as the snap of a finger, any time when one can experience even temporary pleasure; therefore, that great hell is called Avīci."
In this manner, they experience suffering in its full extent. O Bhikṣus!
Those beings in that Great Avīci Hell travel through immeasurable time upon the long road until they finally emerge from that Great Avīci Hell.

Having emerged, they run; having run, they run again, even running at full speed, seeking a dwelling, seeking shelter, seeking an island, seeking a place of refuge, and seeking a place of protection, they arrive at the Black Cloud Sands (Kṛṣṇābhrasandhi) minor hell, five hundred yojanas in extent.
Having entered [the hells], and so forth, to speak briefly, he finally reaches the sixteenth cold-hell, where he fully experiences various sufferings and there his life comes to an end.
Regarding this, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
“If a person creates karma through body, speech, and mind, having created it, they head toward the evil realms.”
Thus one shall live in the Saṃjīva Hell, a place of terror that makes the hair stand on end.
Having passed through countless billions of years, though dead, one must immediately revive again;
enemies and foes each take their revenge upon one another, all because sentient beings have killed one another.
If one gives rise to an evil mind toward one's parents, or toward the Buddha, Bodhisattvas, or the assembly of Śrāvakas,
such persons shall all fall into the Black Rope Hell, where they will undergo most severe and intense suffering.
They instruct others in right conduct only to lead them astray; seeing those who are kind and friendly, they inevitably destroy their bonds.
Such people all fall into the Black Rope Hell, for they were double-tongued, foul-mouthed, and full of lies.
Delighting in committing the three kinds of grave evil karma, Failing to cultivate the sprouts of the three kinds of roots of goodness—
These deluded people fall into the Saṃghāta Hell, Where they suffer for a long time within it.
Or those who harm sheep, horses, and various oxen, or various kinds of beasts such as chickens and pigs,
and kill all other species of insects and ants— such persons fall into the Saṃghāta Hell.

The signs of fear in the world are manifold; because they oppress and afflict people with these, those beings fall into hells such as the Grinding Mountain, where they suffer the torments of being pounded by pestles and mortars and crushed under hammers.
Because of the evil proclivities of greed, hatred, and delusion, they distort correct principles and cause them to deviate;
by judging right as wrong and violating the laws and discipline, they are wounded by the wheel of swords and blades.
If one relies on power and status to plunder others, seizing them whether they are strong or weak,
and thus inflicts such various oppressions, that person will be trampled by iron elephants.
Those who delight in killing and harming sentient beings, whose hands and bodies are smeared with blood and whose minds are cruel,
and who constantly perform such impure deeds— they shall be born in the Raurava hell.
Because they have caused various kinds of affliction and distress to sentient beings, they are frequently boiled in the Raurava Hell;
within that hell there is also the Mahāraurava, which results from a mind of flattery, crookedness, and craftiness.
Enshrouded by the dense forest of various views, Sunk in the ever-thickening net of craving,
Constantly performing such most base deeds, They shall fall into the Great Howling Hell.
If one arrives here in this Great Screaming Hell, a place of blazing iron cities that makes the hair stand on end,
the iron halls and iron houses therein will utterly incinerate all who enter them.
If, while engaged in various worldly affairs, one causes much distress and agitation to sentient beings,
they shall be born in the Hell of Burning Heat, where they will undergo various torments for immeasurable time.
If one constantly vexes and offends the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the world, as well as parents, elders, and the aged,
causing them no joy, they shall all fall into the realm of burning affliction.
They take no pleasure in cultivating the pure karma for rebirth in heaven, and they are constantly separated from their beloved kin;
those who delight in performing such deeds shall all enter the Hell of Burning Heat.
Those who direct evil toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, as well as toward virtuous people, parents, and others,
or who harm other venerable ones, fall into the Heat Torment hell and are constantly boiled there.
Constantly and frequently committing various evil deeds, never having once given rise to a single virtuous thought—
such a person heads toward the Avīci hell, where they shall undergo immeasurable suffering and affliction.
If one proclaims the true Dharma as non-Dharma, and proclaims all that is non-Dharma as the true Dharma,
thereby providing no benefit to those who are virtuous, such persons shall all enter Avīci.
The Sañjīva and Kālasūtra—these two hells; Saṃghāta, Raurava, and the three together as five;
Tapana and Pratāpana form seven together; and the Avīci is the eighth.
These eight are the great hells, Fierce, blazing, and agonizing, difficult to endure;
Because they are produced by those who have committed evil deeds, Within them there are sixteen minor hells.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!
You should now know that between those two worlds, there are yet ten other hells situated therein."
What are these ten? They are:
the Arbuda hell, the Nirarbuda hell, the Ababa hell, the Hahava hell, the Atata hell, the Kukkula hell, the Utpala hell, the Padma hell, the Puṇḍarīka hell, and the Kumuda hell.
"Monks! Between those [realms], there are these ten kinds of hells. Monks!"
For what cause and for what reason is that Arbuda hell named "Arbuda"? O monks!
Within that Arbuda hell, the beings there possess physical forms and bodies such as these, resembling bubbles of foam; therefore, it is named Arbuda.
Furthermore, what is the reason why that *nirarbuda* is called *nirarbuda*, monks?
Within that *nirarbuda* hell, the various sentient beings there obtain such physical forms and bodies that they are like pieces of flesh; for this reason, it is called *nirarbuda*.
Furthermore, for what cause and by what condition is that Āhu Hell named Āhu?

O monks! Within that great hell of Āhu, when the various sentient beings there are tormented by severe suffering and oppression, they cry out and shout, "Āhu! Āhu!"—it is such great suffering—that it is therefore called Āhu.
Furthermore, for what cause and by what condition is that [hell] named Huhuva?
O monks! Within that Huhuva hell, when the various sentient beings are tormented by the extreme sufferings of that hell, they cry out and shout "Huhuva"; therefore, it is named Huhuva.
Furthermore, for what cause and by what condition is that *Aṭaṭa* Hell named *Aṭaṭa*?

O monks! Within that *Aṭaṭa* Hell, when the various sentient beings are oppressed by extreme suffering and distress, they utter the cry "Aṭaṭa"; yet they are unable to even extend their tongues from their own mouths. For this reason, it is named *Aṭaṭa*.
Furthermore, for what cause and for what reason is that [hell] named Sāṅkāṭika?
O monks! Within that Sāṅkāṭika hell, the fire is of such a color as to resemble the Sāṅkāṭika flower; therefore, it is named Sāṅkāṭika.
Furthermore, for what cause and for what reason is that [hell] named Utpala?
O monks! Within that Utpala Hell, the fire is of such a color as to resemble the Utpala flower; therefore, it is named Utpala.
Furthermore, for what cause and for what reason is that Kauṇḍa hell named Kauṇḍa?
O monks! Within that Kauṇḍa hell, the fire has this color, like the Kauṇḍa flower; therefore, it is named Kauṇḍa.
Furthermore, for what cause and by what condition is that [hell] named Puṇḍarīka? O monks!
Within that Puṇḍarīka hell, the fire has this color, like the puṇḍarīka flower; therefore, it is named Puṇḍarīka.
Furthermore, for what cause and by what condition is that *pātāma* hell named *pātāma*? Monks!
Within that *pātāma* hell, the fire has a color like that of a *pātāma* flower; therefore, it is named *pātāma*.

“Monks! Suppose, for example, in the kingdom of Kośala, there were twenty *kharika*—a *kharika* being, in the language of Sui, twenty *hu*—of black sesame seeds piled high without being leveled. Then, suppose a man were to come along once every hundred years and remove a single sesame seed from within that heap. [In this manner, the heap would eventually be exhausted.]”
Proceeding in this manner for a full hundred years, one takes a single grain of black sesame and throws it out. Monks,
when those twenty khārikas of black sesame seeds filling Kośala have been completely exhausted by such throwing, I say that the lifespan of one Arbuda has not yet come to an end.
Furthermore, calculating roughly by these numbers: twenty such lifespans in the Arbuda hell constitute one lifespan in the Nirarbuda hell;
twenty lifespans in the Nirarbuda hell constitute one lifespan in the Ababa hell;
and twenty lifespans in the Ababa hell constitute one lifespan in the Hahava hell.
Twenty *huhuva* make one *aṭaṭa*; twenty *aṭaṭa* make one *sāta-kātyaya*;
twenty *sāta-kātyaya* make one *utpala*.
Twenty *utpala* make one *kumuda*;
twenty *kumuda* make one *puṇḍarīka*;
twenty *puṇḍarīka* make one *padma*.
Twenty *paduma* [kalpas] constitute one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*). "O Bhikṣus!

If sentient beings dwell in the location of the Paduma Hell even as far as a hundred *yojana*s away—where one *yojana* is forty *li* according to the Sui measurement—they are still scorched by the flames of that hellfire."
If they dwell at a distance of fifty yojanas, all sentient beings will become blind and sightless;
if they dwell at a distance of twenty-five yojanas, the flesh and blood of all sentient beings will naturally break apart and disperse.
"O monks! That bhikṣu Kokālika, having conceived a mind of slander and a turbid, evil mind toward Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, was immediately reborn after death in that Padma Hell."
Having been born in that place, flames issue from his mouth, reaching a length of ten *zhǔ* (with one *zhǔ* being two feet).
Upon his tongue, there naturally appear five hundred plows, which constantly till it.

"O monks! Elsewhere, I have never seen anyone cause such self-harm as this: namely, by conceiving impure thoughts toward fellow practitioners of the holy life—due to self-destruction, due to an evil mind, due to a mind of non-benefit, due to a lack of compassion, and due to a lack of purity."
"O bhikṣus!

For this reason, you should cultivate acts of loving-kindness through body, speech, and mind toward those who lead the holy life (brahmacarya). As I have seen, those who maintain acts of loving-kindness through body, speech, and mind day and night always experience peace and happiness."

Therefore, you bhikṣus, all of you should act in accordance with what I have seen and taught; you should constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness day and night, and you should train yourselves in this manner.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"When people of the world are born, An axe naturally emerges upon their tongues;
Because of the evil they speak from within their mouths, They in turn harm and cut their own bodies."
One does not praise those who deserve praise, yet speaks of the beauty of those who deserve reproach;
this is called a dispute within the mouth, and because of such dispute, there is no pleasant feeling.
If a person wins wealth through gambling, this is but a minor dispute in the world;
yet to give rise to a turbid mind toward one of pure conduct is called a great quarrel of the mouth.
In this way, there are thirty-six hundred thousand *nirarbuda* hells,
as well as five *arbuda* hells; one falls into those *padma* hells because of having reviled the noble ones,
due to having committed evil through the karma of speech and mind.
“Monks! Within that realm, there are further winds called ‘Tormenting Heat. Monks!”

If those winds were to come to these four worlds, then all sentient beings within these four continents—whether born or dwelling there—all would be scattered, extinguished, destroyed, and brought to nothingness.
Just as, for example, reeds or rushes, once they have been cut down and deprived of water,
wither and perish; even so, monks,

when those winds called "Tormenting Heat" come from that intermediate realm into these four realms, all sentient beings within these four continents will simultaneously wither and perish, leaving nothing behind.
Because those winds are obstructed by these two mountains, Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa,
they do not reach this place, O bhikṣus!
Those Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains are able to provide such supreme benefit, acting as a support for all sentient beings within the four continents and the four worlds.
"Furthermore, monks!

Moreover, in the midst of those worlds, there are winds that blow upon the hells, burning, boiling, and cooking the flesh, fat, marrow, and bones of sentient beings; they produce various impurities of foul stench, smoke, and roaring sounds."
"O Bhikṣus!

When that wind arrives here in this world-system of four continents, then all sentient beings within that world-system of four continents, even those who are stationary, will all become blind and lose their sight, because its breath is so foul-smelling and violent."
However, because they are obstructed by the two mountains, Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa, they do not come here due to that obstruction. O monks!

Those two mountains, Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa, are able to bring about the greatest benefit for all sentient beings within these four continents, as they establish the karmic basis upon which those beings depend.
"Furthermore, monks! Moreover, within that realm, there is yet another great wind called Saṃghāta-saṃghāta (Saṃghāta-saṃghāta), which in the Sui language means 'conjunction'."
"O Bhikṣus!

If that wind were to come into this world-system, it would be able to lift up the four great continents, the eighty-four thousand minor continents, as well as all other great mountains and Sumeru, the king of mountains, raising them from the earth by one krośa—four cubits being called one bow, and one thousand bows being called one krośa. Having lifted them, it could cause them to be scattered and destroyed; even if they were raised two, three, four, five, six, or seven krośas from the ground, once lifted, it could cause them all to be dispersed and destroyed."

Even up to a height of one *yojana*, he lifts it up and scatters and destroys it as before; likewise, he lifts up and destroys [earth] at heights of two, three, four, five, six, and seven *yojanas*, causing it all to be dispersed. Even up to a height of one hundred *yojanas*, having lifted it up, he disperses and destroys it; and even up to heights of two, three, four, five, six, and seven hundred *yojanas*, having lifted them up, he shatters, disperses, and destroys them, just as before.

Even up to a height of one thousand *yojanas*, having lifted it up, he scatters it into dust and destroys it; and even up to heights of two, three, four, five, six, and seven thousand *yojanas*, having lifted them all up, he disperses and destroys them.
"O bhikṣus!
It is as if a strong and powerful man were to take a handful of parched barley in his hand, lift it high up, and then, in mid-air, scatter the powder so that it is completely shattered."
"So it is, so it is, O bhikṣus!

In that world, there is a most powerful and violent *saṃghāta* wind; if it were to come here into this realm of four continents, then at that time the four great continents of this realm, along with the eighty-four thousand minor islands, the other great mountains, and Sumeru, the king of mountains, would be lifted up from the earth by one *krośa*, scattered and destroyed—briefly described as before—and even up to seven thousand *yojanas* of the earth, having been lifted up, would be reduced to dust and destroyed."
"O bhikṣus!
It is solely because they are obstructed by those two mountains, Mount Cakravāḍa and Mount Mahācakravāḍa, that due to this obstruction they do not come here."

"O monks! Those two mountains, Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa, possess such majestic power and capability for great benefit, acting as a support for all sentient beings within the four continents and the four worlds."
"Furthermore, monks!

To the south of Jambudvīpa, beyond the intermediate spaces of that world, there is the dwelling place of King Yama’s palace. It covers an area six thousand yojanas in length and breadth, surrounded by sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold networks of bells. Outside these, seven rows of tāla trees encircle it, of various beautiful colors and composed of the seven treasures—namely, gold, silver, vaidūrya, sphaṭika, red pearls, musāragalva, and aśmagarbha—accomplished through these seven precious substances."
In each of those four directions there are various gates; at each of these gates there are defensive towers, watchtowers, palaces, gardens, and lotus ponds.

Within those lotus ponds and gardens there are various kinds of trees, each with various leaves, various flowers, and various fruits, filled everywhere with the pervasive fragrance of diverse scents, while various birds each sing their own songs.
Furthermore, monks!

At another time and on another occasion, due to the retribution of his evil and unwholesome karma, King Yama will find that at the three periods of the night and the three periods of the day, molten red copper juice spontaneously appears before him.

At that time, the king’s palace immediately transforms into iron; all the previously existing objects of the five sensory pleasures that were present before him vanish and no longer appear. If he is within the palace, they arise in such a manner right there within the palace.

At that time, when King Yama saw this, he was struck with fear and unease; his hair stood on end, and he immediately went outside. If he was already outside the palace, he would likewise be born outside once more.
At that time, King Yama felt fear arise in his heart; trembling and restless, the hairs on his body all stood erect at once, and he immediately fled into the inner chambers.

At that time, the jailers seized King Yama and immediately threw him down upon a floor of hot iron, which was blazing fiercely with a single mass of flames. Having thrown him down so that he lay supine, they used iron tongs to pry open his mouth and poured molten copper into it.

At that time, King Yama’s lips and mouth were scorched; having scorched his lips and mouth, he next scorched his tongue; having scorched his tongue, he then scorched his throat; having scorched his throat, he then scorched his large and small intestines, which were successively consumed by fire until they emerged from below.
At that very time and on that occasion, King Yama thought to himself:

"All those sentient beings who, in their past lives, committed evil deeds of body, evil deeds of speech, and evil deeds of mind—all of them undergo such various forms of physical suffering and mental distress, in places that are not pleasing to the heart, just like the beings in the hells."
I am now likewise so, as are others—those beings who have performed similar deeds together with King Yama. Alas!
May I, upon casting off this body and dying from here, fall into the realm of union and be born meeting them once more among human beings.
At that time, I shall attain faith and understanding within the teaching of the Tathāgata.

At that time, having attained faith and understanding in that place and being fully endowed with it, I shall shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and, having attained right faith and understanding, go forth from the home into homelessness.

At that time, having gone forth, it was not long before the Saṅgha was harmonious. For whatever purpose a son of good family, having attained right faith and understanding, goes forth from the home life, he personally realizes and attains the fruit of the supreme holy life within this very life.

Having completed these preparations, he made this vow: "I shall now proceed; I have now exhausted birth and death, I have established the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and that which was to be done has been fully accomplished; I shall no longer undergo rebirth in future worlds."
"O Bhikṣus! At times, King Yama may give rise to such thoughts of seeking and cultivating wholesome mindfulness.

During those times, the palace where King Yama dwells once again becomes composed of the seven treasures, manifesting various forms, and the five celestial sensual pleasures appear before him, all fully complete."
At that time, King Yama further thought to himself:

"May all sentient beings who have performed wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind each receive such peace and happiness as I do now—like the yakṣas dwelling in the sky—and like those other kings of Yama who have gathered here with me through the common karma of their actions."
"Monks! There are three kinds of celestial messengers in the world.
What are the three?
That is to say: aging, illness, and death.
Monks, there is a certain kind of person who, through self-indulgence, engages in unwholesome conduct of body, as well as unwholesome conduct of speech and mind.

And when that person has performed unwholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, by reason of those causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they head toward a miserable destination and are reborn in hell.
The jailers then drove those beings away and immediately led them before King Yama, saying:
"O Heavenly King!
This man, while formerly among humans, was wanton and self-indulgent; he failed to harmonize his conduct and gave rein to his body, speech, and mind, performing evil deeds."
However, because they committed evil deeds with their body, speech, and mind, they have now been born here.
Therefore, O Heavenly King!
Your excellent instruction and your excellent reprimand are well-placed.
Then King Yama asked that man: "O good man!
When you were formerly in the human world, the first divine messenger appeared, providing excellent instruction and excellent reproof; did you not see that divine messenger appear at birth?"
He replied: "O Deva!
Truly, I have not seen it."
At that time, King Yama spoke again, saying: "O man!

Did you not see when, in a former life in the world, while you had a human body—whether as a woman or as a man—you manifested the signs of old age? When you were a decrepit elder (*mahallaka*), your teeth fell out and your hair turned white; your skin became slack and wrinkled, covered with spots like sesame seeds; you walked with a hunchbacked and crooked back, limping and stumbling so that your steps did not follow your body, always leaning to one side; the skin of your neck became loose and sagged like a cow's dewlap; your lips and mouth were parched and dry, and your throat and tongue were rough and withered."
The body is bent and hunched, his strength is frail and thin, and he pants with audible gasps like one pulling a saw.
He nearly falls forward at every step, walking while leaning on a staff; having left the prime of youth behind, his flesh and blood have utterly wasted away.
Are you emaciated, treading the path toward future lives, with movements so feeble that you have lost the physical form of your youth?
Have even your body and mind become constantly trembling, such that all your limbs and joints are entirely exhausted and weary?
That person replied:
"O Deva! I truly saw it."
Then King Yama spoke again:
"You foolish man, you lack wisdom.
Having previously seen such signs as these, why did you not reflect in this way: "
“Within my own body now, there is this very dharma and this very condition; I have not yet escaped such a dharma, and I am currently possessed of this very dharma of aging.”
Since I have not yet attained liberation, I should now perform subtle and sublime wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, so that I may experience the retribution of long-term benefit and peace.
Then, that man replied: "O Deva!
I truly did not have such a thought."
"Why is this? Because their minds were unrestrained and they practiced heedlessness.
Then, King Yama spoke again:
"O foolish man, if it is as you say, then because of your own indolence and your practice of negligence, you have failed to cultivate wholesome karma of body, speech, and mind."

For this reason, throughout the long night, you shall experience great suffering and affliction, devoid of any peace or happiness; therefore, you must fully undergo the retribution for these crimes of heedlessness, receiving such evil karmic results as that man of negligence did.

Furthermore, O noble sir, as for this retribution of suffering resulting from evil karma, it was not created by your mother, nor by your father, nor by your brothers, nor by your sisters, nor by the king, nor by the gods, nor even by your ancestors of the past. Rather, O noble sir, you yourself committed these evil deeds within your own person; now they have gathered together, and you alone must undergo this retribution.

"Then, King Yama of that world, having fully and skillfully instructed him with this first divine messenger and having rebuked him, further proceeded to instruct and rebuke him with the second divine messenger, saying: 'O man!'"
"Do you not see that the second messenger has appeared in the world?
He replied, "O Deva!"
"I truly did not see it.
The king spoke again, saying: "O man!"

Do you not see that in former times, when one was born as a human being in this world, the four great elements were in harmony; yet once they fell into discord, whether it be the body of a woman or the form of a man, afflicted by severe and agonizing illness, one might lie upon a small bed or a large couch, defiling one’s own body with excrement and urine, wallowing in filth without any autonomy.
Whether lying down, rising, walking, or sitting, he was always supported by others; some washed and wiped him, some carried him out, some gave him drink, and others provided him with food.
That person replied:
"O Deva! I truly saw it."
The king spoke again:
"O man! Seeing this as you do, if one were skillful and wise, how could they not think in such a way?"
"I too now possess such a dharma; I too now possess such an occurrence; I likewise have not yet escaped such a state of affliction; I too am subject to such an afflicted condition."

Since one has not yet escaped [saṃsāra], one should realize for oneself: "I too may now perform various wholesome karmas—whether wholesome karma of body, speech, or mind—for my own great benefit and state of supreme peace throughout the long night of the future."
That person replied: "O Deva!
I truly did not entertain such thoughts; it was because I acted with negligence due to a lazy mind."
The King spoke again:

"O man! Since you are now one who acts with negligence, being lazy and indolent, and do not perform wholesome deeds—whether by body, speech, or mind—how can you obtain benefit and the retribution of peace and happiness for the long night?"

Therefore, you should practice wholesome deeds. If you act with negligence, then because of that negligence, this evil karma of yours was not created by your father, nor by your brothers, nor by your sisters; it was not made by kings or gods, nor by your ancestors of old, nor was it produced by any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
"This evil karma was committed by you yourself; therefore, you must undergo this retribution yourself.

At that time, King Yama, having instructed and rebuked him with these words using the second divine messenger in due order, proceeded to instruct and rebuke that man further with the third divine messenger, saying:
"O foolish man, when you were in the human world as a human being, did you not see the third divine messenger appear in the world?"
He replied: "O Deva!
Truly, I did not see it."
Then King Yama spoke again to him, saying:
"O man! Have you not seen in that world when women or men, at the time of their death, are placed upon a bed and carried outside, covered with cloth of various colors?"

Furthermore, they have constructed various kinds of canopies, awnings, and curtains that surround them on all sides; they are encircled by their kinsmen and retinues. Having cast off all their necklaces and ornaments, they raise their hands and dishevel their hair, or take ashes and dust to smear upon their heads. In the utmost state of grief and distress, they wail and weep, crying out "Alas! or "Too much! or "O our nurturer! They raise their voices in loud shrieks, beating their breasts in lamentation, uttering various words so piercing and choked with sobs—do you see all this?
That man said: "O Deva!
I truly saw it."
Then King Yama spoke again to him, saying:
"O man! Since you have already witnessed such things as these in the past, why did you not think to yourself thus: "

"I too now possess such a nature; my body also possesses such a condition. Since I have not yet escaped such a condition, I too am subject to death; I possess the nature of death and have not yet attained liberation from it."
I shall now also perform various wholesome deeds—whether wholesome deeds of body, speech, or mind—for the sake of bringing me great benefit and peace for the long night.
Then, that man replied to the deva, saying:
"I truly did not do it.
For what reason?"
"Because of negligence.
Then, King Yama spoke again to him, saying: "O man!"

Since you are now one who acts with negligence, because of this negligence you do not perform wholesome deeds, nor do you accumulate other virtues—namely those of body, speech, and mind—which would bring you benefit and provide you with peace and happiness for a long night; therefore, such a state as this has come to pass for you now.
Relying on heedless conduct and because of that heedlessness, you have brought this evil and unwholesome karma upon yourself.

This evil karma of yours was not created by your parents, nor by your brothers, nor by your sisters; it was not created by the king or the gods, nor by your ancestors of the past, nor by śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
“O man! This evil karma of yours was created and accumulated by you yourself; having obtained this retribution, you must now experience it yourself.
Then, King Yama, having fully instructed, rebuked, and exhorted that man with these words of the third divine messenger, immediately cast him aside.
Then, the jailers seized the man’s arms in various ways, turned his head downward and held his feet upward, and immediately cast him into the various hells.
At that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
“Once sentient beings have committed evil deeds, After death they fall into the miserable realms.
When King Yama sees them arrive, He rebukes them with a heart of compassion:”
"When you were formerly among humans, did you not see old age, sickness, and death?
These are the messengers of the gods who have come to inform you; why are you so heedless as to remain unaware?"
Though body, speech, and mind are defiled by various dusts, If one does not practice giving and precepts to discipline oneself,
How can such a person be called "possessing consciousness," Yet fail to create the causes for benefit?
At that time, after King Yama, acting according to the Dharma, had thus rebuked the sinner, the latter gasped for breath, his heart filled with terror; trembling with fear, he spoke these words:
"Because in the past I associated with evil friends, I heard of wholesome deeds but did not take pleasure in performing them."
Enshrouded and obscured by greed and hatred, you do not cultivate what benefits yourself and thus harm your own body.
"Since you have not cultivated the causes of various virtues, but have only created all manner of evil karma, you shall today reap the fruit of that folly;
you will undergo those karmic retributions within the hells."
All such evil karmas as these were not created by the father nor by the mother,
nor by śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, nor by kings nor by devas.

This is solely what you have created yourself; because these seeds of evil karma are impure, and since you have personally committed these various evil deeds, you must now individually undergo their bitter fruits.
When that king, having sequentially rebuked the transgressors with these three messengers,
the King Yama at that time abandons those sinful beings and departs.
At that time, those who dwell in the realm of Yama immediately seize those men and lead them away toward hell,
that most terrifying place where one's hair stands on end.
On its four sides facing one another are four gates; the four cardinal and four intermediate directions are all well-ordered.
The walls of all the courtyards are made of iron, and iron is used to form railings encircling them on all sides.
The ground is made of fiercely blazing, scorching iron; its flames are magnificent and intense, mingling with smoke and fire.
Seen from afar, it is terrifying and already strikes the heart with alarm; its fierce, blazing, and dazzling radiance is difficult to approach.
Just as within a range of one hundred yojanas, a great fire blazes and completely fills the space,
so too are the multitudes of sentient beings therein being burned, all due to the causes of evil they committed in the past.
Rebuked by the celestial messengers, yet with minds heedless and lacking self-awareness,
they now repent for the long night, all because of their former base intentions.
All you wise people, if you see a celestial messenger come to instruct you, you should be diligent and not be negligent;
thus has the King of Sages, skilled in teaching, well explained.
Having seen and heard this, one must feel dread;
among all states of birth and death, there is nothing that surpasses nirvāṇa, wherein all manner of afflictions are exhausted without remainder.
Upon reaching that state of peace, one finds happiness; thus perceiving the Dharma, one attains tranquility.
That is to say, having transcended all enemies, one naturally becomes pure and attains Nirvana.
*Sūtra on the Origin of the World*, Scroll Four;
*Sūtra on the Origin of the World*, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Dharmagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Five: On the Nāgas and Garuḍas "Furthermore, monks,
all nāgas have four modes of birth."
What are the four? First, birth from eggs;
second, birth from a womb; third, birth from moisture; and fourth, birth by transformation. These are called the four modes of birth for nāgas.
"O bhikṣus!
Those garuḍas are also born in four ways: namely, from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, and by transformation; these are called the four modes of birth of those garuḍas."
"O Bhikṣus!

At the bottom of the great ocean, there is the palace of the Nāga King Sāgara, measuring eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, perfectly equal on all sides. It is adorned all around with sevenfold walls and sevenfold railings, featuring sevenfold rows of precious bells interspersed with jeweled nets."

Furthermore, it was surrounded by seven tiers of *tāla* trees, their branches spreading wide to cast a dense shade. Their exquisite colors were beautiful to behold, and they were adorned with various jewels—namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate—all composed of these seven precious substances.
In each of those four directions there are various gates; at those gates there are multi-storied pavilions, watchtowers, and battlements, as well as gardens and ponds.
Upon the ground and within the ponds, there were various kinds of flowers and grasses, each arranged in orderly rows.
Furthermore, there were many trees with diverse leaves and blossoms, various fruits, manifold fragrances, and all manner of birds, each calling out its own song.

"O Bhikṣus! Between those two mountains, Sumeru and Khadiraka, there is the dwelling place of the palaces of the two great Nāga Kings, Nanda and Upananda. That place is six thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls and sevenfold railings; as described briefly before, up until the various birds each sing their own songs."
"O Bhikṣus!
To the north of that great ocean, for all the dragon kings and all the garuḍa kings, there is a great tree; the name of that tree is Kūṭaśālmali, which in the language of Sui means 'Coarse Cluster'."

That great tree has a circumference of seven *yojanas* at its base; it extends twenty *yojanas* into the earth and rises one hundred *yojanas* above ground. Its branches and foliage completely cover fifty *yojanas*. Its courtyard is five hundred *yojanas* in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls and moats, as briefly described before, even down to the various birds, each of which sings its own song.
"O Bhikṣus!

To the east of that great Jātikusumālī tree, there dwell the palaces of the egg-born nāgas and the egg-born garuḍas; each palace is six hundred yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, as described above in brief, even unto the various birds each singing their own songs."

"On the southern side of that great Kūṭaśālmali tree, there dwell the palaces of the womb-born nāgas and the womb-born garuḍas; these are also each six hundred yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, as briefly described before, up to the point where various birds each sing their own songs."

To the west of that great *kūṭaśālmalī* tree, there dwell the palaces of moisture-born nāgas and moisture-born garuḍas; these too are each six hundred yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, described in brief as previously mentioned, up until the various birds each sing their own songs.

To the north of that great *kūṭaśālmalī* tree, there dwell various palaces of spontaneously born nāgas and spontaneously born garuḍas; these are each six hundred yojanas in length and breadth. They have sevenfold walls, described in brief as before, up to the point where various birds each sing their own songs.

“O bhikṣus! When that king of the garuḍas born from eggs desires to seize an egg-born nāga, he immediately flies toward the eastern branch of the great tree Kūṭaśālmalī. Having looked down at the ocean, he then fans the great sea with his two wings, causing the waters to part for two hundred yojanas.”
Once the ocean waters have parted, the bird immediately seizes the egg-born nāgas and brings them out, using them as it pleases and eating them as it pleases. Monks!
These kings of the egg-born garuḍas can only seize and eat egg-born nāgas for their own use; they cannot seize nāgas born from a womb, nor those born from moisture, nor those born by transformation.

“Monks! When those Garuḍa kings born from the womb wish to seize dragons born from eggs, they immediately fly toward the eastern branch of that great Caṭasāla tree, look down at the great ocean, and with both wings, fan the great ocean until the waters part for two hundred yojanas. Thereupon, they seize the egg-born dragons in their beaks and bring them out to eat as they please.”

Furthermore, when the garuḍa king born from an egg wishes to seize an egg-born nāga, he immediately flies toward the southern branch of that great Jāṭāsura-mālī tree, looks down upon the great ocean, and fans the sea with his two wings. The waters part for four hundred yojanas, whereupon he seizes the egg-born nāga in his beak and brings it out to eat as he pleases.
"O Bhikṣus!

Those Garuḍa kings born from the womb can only capture dragons born from eggs and dragons born from the womb for their own use; they cannot capture dragons born from moisture or those born through transformation."

“Monks! When those garuḍa kings born from moisture wish to seize a nāga born from an egg, they fly up onto the eastern branch of that great Caṭasalmali tree. With their wings they fan the great ocean until the waters part for two hundred yojanas. Having parted them, they seize the egg-born nāgas and consume them according to their appetite.”

Furthermore, when a moisture-born garuḍa wishes to seize a womb-born nāga, it immediately flies toward the southern branch of that great Caṭasalmali tree. With its wings it fans the great ocean until the waters part for four hundred yojanas. Having parted them, it seizes the womb-born nāga with its beak and consumes it as it sees fit.

Furthermore, when a moisture-born garuḍa wishes to seize a moisture-born nāga, it flies toward the western branch of that great tree, the Caṭasalmali, and fans the great ocean with its wings until the waters part for eight hundred yojanas; it then seizes the moisture-born nāga in its beak to consume as its food.

"O monks! Those garuḍas born from moisture can only seize dragons born from eggs, dragons born from wombs, and dragons born from moisture, taking them as they require and consuming them as they please; however, they cannot seize dragons born through transformation."

"O bhikṣus! When those garuḍas born by transformation wish to seize a nāga born from an egg, they fly toward the eastern branch of that great tree, the Caṭaka-sāmalī. They then flap their wings against the great ocean until the waters part for two hundred yojanas, whereupon they immediately seize the egg-born nāga in their beaks and consume it as they see fit."

Furthermore, when a *nirmāṇakāya* garuḍa wishes to seize a *jarāyuja* nāga, it immediately flies toward the southern branch of that great *kūṭaśālmalī* tree and fans the great ocean with its wings, causing the waters to part for four hundred *yojanas*. Thereupon, the *nirmāṇakāya* garuḍa seizes the *jarāyuja* nāga in its beak as food, using it as required.

Furthermore, when a golden-winged garuḍa born by transformation wishes to seize a dragon born from moisture, it immediately flies toward the western branch of that great Caṭasalmali tree. It fans the great ocean with its wings until the waters part for eight hundred yojanas, whereupon it instantly seizes the moisture-born dragon as food to consume as it pleases.

Furthermore, when the miraculously born (upapāduka) King of the Garuḍas wishes to seize a miraculously born nāga, he immediately flies toward the northern branch of the great Jāṭāśamari tree, looks down at the ocean, and fans the great sea with his two wings. The waters part for him to a distance of one thousand six hundred yojanas, whereupon he seizes the miraculously born nāga as food, using it as required.
"Monks! All these nāgas are entirely devoured as food by those garuḍas. Monks!"
There are other nāgas whom that garuḍa cannot capture.
These include the Nāga King Sāgara, who has never been startled or shaken by that king of the garuḍas;
furthermore, there are the Nāga Kings Nanda and Upananda—these two nāga kings, and others like them, are likewise not taken by that garuḍa.
Furthermore, the Naga King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Naga King Anavatapta, and others are likewise not seized by that Garuḍa King.
"O Bhikṣus!
Furthermore, there are other nāga kings who likewise are not seized by those garuḍas, namely: Mātula and Cakravāka; Takṣaka and Karkoṭaka; Jīmūta and Vāsuki; Śaṅkhapāla and Kambalāśvatara."
"O Bhikṣus!
There are yet other dwelling places of various nāgas; within those realms, they likewise are not devoured by the garuḍas."
“Monks! What are the causes and conditions for those beings in that realm who are born among the nāgas?”
"O bhikṣus!

There are sentient beings who cultivate the causes for being a nāga, observe the precepts of a nāga, give rise to the mind of a nāga, and form the intention of a nāga. Having performed such karma, because they are matured by those causes and conditions, they shall be born among the nāgas."

Furthermore, there is another class of beings who cultivate the causes for becoming a garuḍa, uphold the precepts of a garuḍa, give rise to the mind of a garuḍa, and direct their thoughts toward being a garuḍa; by these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they shall immediately be reborn among those garuḍas.

Furthermore, there is another class of beings who cultivate the causes of various animals, observe the precepts of various animals, give rise to the minds of various animals, practice the karmic deeds of various animals, and differentiate the intentions of various animals. Because they have thus cultivated the various causes of animal precepts, initiated such karmic actions, and perfected their mentalities through these manifold conditions, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they are immediately reborn among those various mixed animals.

Furthermore, there is another class who cultivate the causes of cattle, the precepts of cattle, the karma of cattle, the mind of cattle, and the intention of cattle—as briefly described before—and up to their various discriminations; for these reasons, they are born among cattle.

Furthermore, there is another kind who cultivate the nature of a chicken, the precepts of a chicken, the karma of a chicken, the mind of a chicken, and the intention of a chicken; as briefly explained before, up to the point of discriminating the mind and karma of a chicken—by these causes and conditions, they shall be born among chickens.

Furthermore, there is another class of beings who cultivate the causes for becoming an owl, receive the precepts of an owl, give rise to the mind of an owl, perform the actions of an owl, and harbor the intentions of an owl. Because they have cultivated the karma of an owl, received its precepts, given rise to its mind, and harbored its intentions, by these causes and conditions, upon the relinquishing of the body, they shall be reborn among owls.
"O bhikṣus!

Furthermore, there is another kind [of practitioner] who cultivates the 'Moon Vow' (candramasa-vrata), or cultivates the 'Sun Vow' (sūrya-vrata), the 'Constellation Vow' (nakṣatra-vrata), or the 'Elder Vow' (vṛddha-vrata); or they cultivate the 'Silence Vow' (mauna-vrata); or they cultivate the 'Vow of the Great Power Deity' (mahābala-deva-vrata); or they cultivate the 'Vow of the Great Man' (mahāpuruṣa-vrata); or they cultivate the 'Vow of Entering Water' (udaka-praveśa-vrata); or they cultivate the 'Vow of Offering to the Sun' (sūryopasthāna-vrata); or they cultivate the 'Vow of Serving Fire' (agni-sevana-vrata); or they practice asceticism in various defiled places."
Having cultivated these practices, he forms this thought:

"May all these precepts that I have cultivated—the lunar precepts, the solar precepts, the precepts of the constellations and so forth, as well as the precept of silence, the precepts of the Great Power Deities, the precepts of the Great Man, the water precepts, the fire precepts, and the various such precepts of asceticism and austerity—[bear fruit]."
"I shall become a deva, or perhaps receive the retribution of a deva.
Thus he made this perverse vow. "O bhikṣus!

Furthermore, there is another class of persons, such as men (*pudgala*), who give rise to wrong aspirations; regarding them, I shall now say that they will head toward two destinations: either rebirth in hell or rebirth among animals.
"O monks! Furthermore, there is a class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
'The self and the world are eternal.'"
"This alone is the truth; all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"Both the self and the world are entirely impermanent."
"This alone is the truth; all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"The self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal."
"This alone is the truth; all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"The self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal."
"This alone is the truth; all else is false. "O bhikṣus!
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas, brahmins, and others who hold such a view and speak thus:"
"The self and the world are finite;
this alone is true, all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"I and the world are infinite;
this alone is true, all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"Both the self and the world are either finite or infinite;
this alone is the truth, and all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
“Both the self and the world are neither finite nor infinite;
this alone is true, all else is false. “O bhikṣus!”
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"The life-principle is identical to the body.
This alone is true; all else is false."
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"The life-principle is one thing and the body is another.
This alone is true; all else is false."
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"There is a life-principle and there is a body.
This alone is true; all else is false."
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"There is no life-principle and no body.
This alone is true; all else is false."
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"The Tathāgata exists after death."
‘This alone is the truth; all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
‘After the Tathāgata’s death, existence does not exist.’
"This alone is the truth; all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, he either exists or does not exist."
"This alone is the truth; all else is false.
Furthermore, there is another class of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, it is neither that existence exists nor that existence does not exist."
"This alone is the truth; all else is false. "O monks!
Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:"
"Both the self and the world are eternal;
this alone is true, all else is false"—
those who hold such a view will, regarding the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), conceive of them as the self and conceive of them as the world.
Within the departure from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), they should form the view of a self and the view of a world.
For this reason, they form such views and make such assertions as: "The self and the world are eternal."
"This alone is the truth; all else is false. Monks!
Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
Regarding those who say, "The self and the world are impermanent;
this alone is true, all else is false," they should cultivate the view of non-self and the view of no-world within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Within the departure from all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), one should cultivate the view of non-self and the view of no world.
For this reason, they speak thus:
"The self and the world are impermanent."
"This alone is the truth; all else is false. Monks!
Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
"Both the self and the world are eternal and non-eternal;
this alone is true, all else is false"—
those who hold such a view will, regarding the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), possess the view of a self and the view of a world.
Within the departure from all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), there must be the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of a world (*loka-dṛṣṭi*). For this reason, they speak thus:
"The self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal."
"This alone is the truth; all else is false. Monks!
Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
Regarding those who say, "The self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal;
this alone is true, all else is false," they will maintain views of a self and views of the world within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Within the departure from all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), there may still be the view of a self (*ātman*) and the view of a world (*loka*).
For this reason, they speak thus:
"The self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal."
"This alone is the truth; all else is false. "O monks!
Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:"
Regarding those who say, "The self and the world are finite;
this alone is true, all else is false," they speak as follows:
"Life has limits; the person has limits.
From the initial conception within the womb is life; after death, the enshrouding, burial, and interment constitute the person.

A superior person, from the first birth and reception of the fourfold body, undergoes seven falls, seven cycles of transmigration, seven runnings, and seven traversals, thereby fulfilling their life and entering the assembly of life."
Therefore, they speak thus:
"The self and the world are finite.
This alone is true; all else is false."
"O monks! Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
'The self and the world are infinite.'"
"This alone is the truth; all else is false. They speak thus:
"Life is boundless; the person is boundless."
From the initial conception within the womb, that is life; after death, the enshrouding, burial, and interment constitute the person.

The superior person, from the very first birth and reception of the fourfold body, undergoes seven cycles of falling back, seven transits, seven runnings, and seven traversals, whereby they shall accomplish life and enter the assembly of life.
Therefore, they speak thus:
"The self and the world are infinite.
This alone is true; all else is false."
“Monks! Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
‘The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite.’”
"This alone is true, all else is false.
Those who speak thus say:
"The life-principle (jīva) is neither finite nor infinite."
This person, from the initial moment of entering the womb until death and subsequent burial, is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

A superior person (*āryapudgala*), however, from the first reception of the fourfold body, undergoes seven cycles of falling back, seven cycles of transmigration, and seven cycles of wandering and running; having completed these, they shall achieve their life-span and enter the assembly of those destined for it (*jīvitasaṃskāra*).
Therefore, they speak thus:
"The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite.
This alone is the truth; all else is false."
“Monks! Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
‘The self and the world are neither non-finite nor non-infinite.’”
"This alone is true, all else is false. They speak thus:
"The world is neither non-finite nor non-infinite."

From the initial reception of the body, there are four kinds; one falls seven times, transmigrates seven times, and having run and wandered seven times, one shall then achieve life and enter the assembly of life.
Therefore, they speak thus:
"The self and the world are neither non-finite nor non-infinite.
This alone is true; all else is false."
“Monks! Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
‘That life is that very body.’”
"This alone is true; all else is false.

Those who speak thus perceive a self within this body and perceive a life-principle within it, and they likewise perceive a self and a life-principle within other bodies; for this reason, they declare:
"That which is the life-principle is that which is the body."
"This alone is the truth; all else is false. "O bhikṣus!
Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:"
Regarding those who say, "The life-principle is distinct from the body; this alone is true,

all else is false," they will perceive a self within the body and perceive a life-principle therein, and they will likewise perceive a self within a distinct body and perceive a life-principle therein.
Therefore, they speak thus:
"The life-principle is distinct from the body;
this alone is true, all else is false."
“Monks! Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
‘The life-principle (jīva) and the body (śarīra) are one and the same.’”
Those who say, "This alone is true;
all else is false," will perceive a self and a life-principle within their own bodies, and they will likewise perceive a self and a life-principle within other bodies.
Therefore, they speak thus:
"The life-principle and the body exist;
this alone is true, all else is false."
"Monks! Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
'The life-principle is not the same as the body.'"
"This alone is true;
all else is false"—those who speak thus do not perceive a self within the body, nor do they perceive a life-principle; nor do they perceive a self or a life-principle in any other body.
Therefore, they speak thus:
"The life-principle is not the body.
This alone is true; all else is false."
"Monks! Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
'The Tathāgata exists after death.'"
"This alone is true;
all else is false"—those who hold such a view in the world maintain that the life-force (āyus) both persists and departs, moving toward and following the cycle of saṃsāra.
Therefore, they speak thus:
"After the Tathāgata’s passing, existence will continue to exist.
This alone is true; all else is false."
"Monks! Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
'After the Tathāgata has passed away, he does not exist.'"
"This alone is true; all else is false"—those people in the world speak thus:
"In this place there is the arrival of life; in that place there is the cessation of life."
Therefore, they speak thus: "After the Tathāgata’s passing, there is no existence.
This alone is true; all else is false."
"Monks! Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
'After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, he either exists or does not exist.'"
"This alone is true; all else is false"—thus do they speak regarding what they perceive:
"When life ceases here, one runs to another place, proceeding through the cycle of transmigration."
Therefore, they speak thus:
"Whether the Tathāgata exists after death, or does not exist after death—
this alone is the truth, and all else is false."
"Monks! Among them, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and speak thus:
'After the Tathāgata has passed away, existence neither exists nor does not exist.'"
"This alone is true; all else is false.
Those who hold such views regarding the world say:
"When a person's life is cut short and destroyed here, it is likewise cut short and destroyed when transferred to that other place."
Therefore, they speak thus:
"After the Tathāgata’s passing away, there is neither existence nor non-existence.
This alone is the truth; all else is false."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!
I recall that in the past there was a king named Ādarśamukha (Mirror-Face)."
At that time, King Ādarśamukha once desired to engage in playful diversions with a group of men born blind; he immediately issued a proclamation:
"Gather many men who were born blind."
Having gathered them, he said to those blind men:
"O you who were born blind, do you happen to know the form and appearance of an elephant? What is its shape like?"
Then those blind men answered together:
"O Heavenly King!
We have been born blind and truly never knew the form or appearance of an elephant."
The king spoke again, saying:
"Since you have never known an elephant before, do you wish now to know its shape and appearance?
Then, those blind men replied in unison:
“‘O Heavenly King!
We truly do not know them. If we might receive the favor of Your Majesty, we wish to learn the appearance and characteristics of elephants.
At that time, King Ādarśamukha immediately issued an order to summon an elephant trainer and said to him:”
"Go quickly to that elephant stable, fetch an elephant, and place it before me to show to these blind men.
At that time, the elephant trainer, having understood the king's intention, immediately brought the elephant and placed it before the royal palace.
The king said to those groups of blind men,
"This is the elephant. Then,
each of the blind men felt the elephant with his own hands.
At that time, the elephant trainer said to the group of blind men, "Touch the elephant and report back to the king according to what you find.
Then, among the blind men, some felt the trunk, some the tusks, some the ears, and others the head, neck, back, flanks, thighs, feet, and tail; having felt these parts in this manner, they proceeded.
Then the king asked, "You who were born blind,
have you already come to know the form, appearance, and characteristics of the elephant?
They, all born blind, answered the king in unison:
“O Great King!
We have now come to know the various forms of elephants.
At that time, the king questioned them once more, saying:
"You blind ones, since you have already examined the elephant, if you know it, what kind of thing is the elephant?
At that time, among the group of blind men, there was one who felt the trunk with his hand and addressed the king, saying: "O Great King! [The elephant is like this...]"
"The elephant's shape is like a rope.
The one who had touched its tusks replied:
"O Heavenly King!..."
Its appearance is like a wooden stake.
The one who had touched the elephant’s ear replied:
‘O Great King!...’
Its appearance is like a winnowing basket.
The one who had touched the elephant’s head replied:
‘O Great King!’”
The elephant is like a water jar.
One who had touched the elephant’s neck replied,
‘O Great King!’”
The elephant is like a house beam.
The one who had touched the elephant’s back replied,
‘O Great King!’”
The elephant is like the ridgepole of a house.
The one who had touched the elephant’s flank replied:
‘O Great King!’”
The elephant’s shape was like a grain basket.
One who had touched the elephant’s thigh replied:
‘O Great King!’”
Its form is like a tree.
The one who had touched the elephant’s leg replied:
‘O Great King!’”
Its appearance is like a mortar.
The one who had touched the elephant’s tail replied:
‘O Great King!’”
"The elephant is like a broom.
Each of those blind men answered in this way. "Great King, such is the elephant; Great King, such is the elephant," they said, and further addressed him:
"Great King, I know the elephant to be thus."
Then the king said to the group of blind men:
"You do not even know whether this is an elephant or not; how much less can you know the form and characteristics of an elephant?

At that time, each of those blind men clung to his own view and quarreled with one another. Each covered his face with his hands, each contending with the others, each disparaging the rest, and each claiming, "I am right."
At that time, King Ādarśamukha, seeing those blind men thus contending with one another, laughed aloud in joy.
Then the king spoke these verses:
"These groups of blind men were born without eyes, Yet they crossly dispute with one another over all matters."
"Without having received even a single word of instruction from a teacher, how could one know the various parts of an elephant's body? "O bhikṣus!

In this way, and in this manner, all those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world are likewise; they are unable to know, as it truly is, the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering."

Since they do not know things as they truly are, you should know that for a long night they will together give rise to strife and contention, wandering through saṃsāra, mutually disparaging one another and mutually reviling one another. Having given rise to strife and contention, they will persist in their rivalry without ceasing; each with his own hand covering his face, they are like a group of blind men who together cause mutual distress and confusion.
Regarding this, it is said in verse:
"If one does not know that Noble Truth of Suffering, One cannot also know the cause, the Accumulation of Suffering;
Nor can one know all the various states of suffering in the world, Nor the state where suffering is extinguished without remainder."
Not knowing this place as the Path, how much less could they know the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering?
Thus their minds are not yet liberated, nor have they attained the state of liberation through wisdom.
Since they are unable to discern and contemplate clearly, their destination leads only toward birth, old age, and death;
having not yet attained liberation from the bonds of Māra, how could they reach that realm where nothing exists?

“Monks! If there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others who can know the noble truth of suffering as it truly is, and who know as they truly are the noble truths of the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering—they should train themselves accordingly. For a long night, they should practice in harmony, each rejoicing without contention, following the same training like water and milk, dwelling together in a state of mutual concord, manifesting the peaceful abode of the noble Dharma taught by the Teacher.”
In this regard, a verse says:
"If one can know that all these possess suffering, And the various places where suffering arises,
Having realized that everything is entirely suffering, One should cause it all to be extinguished without remainder."
Having realized that cessation is attained through the Path, one reaches the state where suffering is extinguished;
thereupon, one is able to fully realize liberation of mind and attain the state of liberation through wisdom.
Thus one can reach the limit of all states of existence;
in this way, one does not arrive at birth, old age, or death, forever attaining liberation from the net of Māra, and eternally departing from all realms of worldly existence.
6. The Chapter on Asuras. *Qishi jing*, Chapter Six, Part One. At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!..."

To the east of Mount Sumeru, after passing one thousand *yojana*s, beneath the great ocean lies the palace residence of the Asura King Vemacitra. This place measures eighty thousand *yojana*s in length and breadth; it is surrounded by seven tiers of walls and adorned on all sides with seven tiers of railings, extending even to seven tiers of golden and silver bell-nets. Outside these, seven rows of *tāla* trees encircle it everywhere, beautiful to behold and composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, *sphatika*, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.
The walls of that city are one hundred yojanas high and fifty yojanas wide.
Between each of those walls, at intervals of five hundred yojanas, gates are established; those gates are thirty yojanas high and twelve yojanas wide.
At each of those gates, there were various defensive watchtowers and battlements, as well as gardens and ponds.

Within these gardens and ponds grew various kinds of trees; the trees had various leaves, the leaves bore various flowers, the flowers produced various fruits, and the fruits possessed various fragrances, the scent of which wafted far and wide.
Furthermore, there were various kinds of birds of diverse species, each calling out with voices that were harmonious and elegant, producing all manner of sounds. "O Bhikṣus!

Within the great wall of that Asura realm, a palace was specially established for the Asura King Vemacitra; its name is Śamāvatī. That city is sixty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, surrounded by sevenfold walls made of the seven treasures, such as lapis lazuli and the rest."
The walls of that city are one hundred yojanas high and fifty yojanas wide; the walls are spaced five hundred yojanas apart, with gates established at the intervals between them.
Those gates are thirty yojanas high and twelve yojanas wide;
they are also equipped with watchtowers, defensive parapets, and upper chambers.

There are various gardens and groves, as well as ponds, pools, and lotus-ponds; there are various kinds of trees with various leaves, various flowers, and various fruits, all fragrant with diverse scents. There are various birds, each singing its own song, their voices harmonious and elegant, producing a variety of sounds.

“O Bhikṣus! In that city of Śrāvastī, at the very center of the king’s residence, there was an assembly hall established for the Asura King Vemacitra, named Saptamukha. It was five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, adorned with sevenfold railings and decorated with exquisite ornamentation.”

Furthermore, there are seven layers of golden and silver bell-nets, and outside these, seven rows of *tāla* trees encircle the four directions; they are of various beautiful colors, most lovely to behold, and each is composed entirely of the seven treasures, including even such gems as musaragalva and agate.

On each of the four sides there are various gates; these gates are equipped with watchtowers and defensive bulwarks, variegated and beautiful to behold, fashioned from the seven precious gems, including even musaragalva and agate. Their lower sections are interspersed with blue vaidūrya, soft, fine, and smooth to the touch, like kācilindika cloth.
“Monks! In the very center of that assembly place where the seven-headed asuras gather, there is a pillar made of jewels that arises spontaneously, twenty yojanas in height.”

Beneath that jeweled pillar, a precious throne was established for the Asura King Vemacitra; it was one yojana in height and half a yojana in width, variegated in color, beautiful to behold, and exceedingly delightful. It was composed of the seven treasures, including even *śaṅkha* and *musāragalva*, and was so soft, fine, and smooth to the touch that it was like *kācalindika* cloth.

On both sides of that seat, there are sixteen dwelling places for minor asuras, variegated and beautiful to behold, likewise accomplished from the seven precious gems, including even musaragalva and agate; they are soft and pleasing to the touch, like kācilindika cloth.

“O bhikṣus! To the east of the assembly hall of the seven-headed asuras, there is the palace residence of the asura king Vemacitra. It is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold nets of bells.”
