Outside, there are seven rows of *tāla* trees that completely encircle it on all four sides; they are of various beautiful colors, most lovely and delightful, and are likewise composed of the seven treasures, namely gold, silver, *vaiḍūrya*, *sphaṭika*, and so forth, up to *musāragalva* and *aśmagarbha*.
On each of the four sides there are various gates, and those gates are equipped with watchtowers, defensive bulwarks, terraces, pavilions, gardens, ponds, and various flower-filled pools.

There are various kinds of trees with various leaves, as well as various flowers, various fruits, and various fragrant incenses; there are various birds, each singing its own song, their voices harmonious and elegant, producing all manner of sounds.
“O bhikṣus! To the south, west, and north of that assembly place of the seven-headed asuras, there are respective palatial residences where various minor asura kings dwell.”

That place is nine hundred yojanas in length and breadth, or eight hundred, seven hundred, six hundred, five hundred, four, three, two, or even as small as one hundred yojanas in length and breadth. It has sevenfold walls, and so forth, as briefly described, with various kinds of birds each singing their own songs.
"O Bhikṣus!

Furthermore, to the east, south, west, and north of the assembly place of the seven-headed Asuras, there are the palatial dwellings of various minor Asuras. These places measure ninety yojanas in length and breadth; some are eighty, seventy, sixty, fifty, forty, thirty, twenty, or even as small as twelve yojanas in length and breadth. They are surrounded by sevenfold walls, and to speak briefly, they contain various birds, each chirping its own song."
"O Bhikṣus!

To the east of the assembly hall of the seven-headed Asuras, there is a park belonging to the Asura King Vemacitra called the Śāla Forest. This forest is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and it is composed of the seven precious substances such as agate, featuring sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold networks of bells."

On each of the four sides there are various gates, and those gates are equipped with watchtowers of diverse and beautiful colors, all fashioned from the seven precious substances, including even musaragalva and agate.
“O bhikṣus!

To the south of the assembly hall of the seven-headed asuras, there is a grove belonging to the asura king Vemacitra called the Śamālī Forest. This forest is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and it is composed of sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets of bells, and the seven precious jewels such as agate.”

On each of the four sides there are various gates, and those gates are equipped with watchtowers of diverse and beautiful colors, all fashioned from the seven precious substances, including even musaragalva and agate.

“O Bhikṣus! To the west of the assembly hall of the seven-headed Asuras, there is a grove belonging to the Asura King Vemacitra called the Kovidāra Forest. This forest is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and it is composed of the seven precious substances, such as agate, with sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold nets of bells.”

On each of the four sides there are various gates, and those gates are equipped with watchtowers and battlements of diverse and beautiful colors, all fashioned from the seven precious substances, including even musaragalva and agate.
“O bhikṣus!

To the north of the assembly hall of the seven-headed asuras, there is a grove belonging to the asura king Vemacitrin called the Nandana Forest. This forest is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold networks of bells, all composed of the seven treasures such as agate and the rest.”

On each of the four sides, there are various jeweled gates securely established; these gates are equipped with watchtowers of diverse and beautiful colors, even being composed of treasures such as musāragalva and aśmagarbha. These gates alone lack upper chambers, while all other features are identical [to those of the palace].

“O bhikṣus! Between the Śāla grove and the Śamālī grove, in the space between these two groves, the asura king Vemacitrin has a great lake named Nanda, which is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.”
The water is cool, light, delicious, and free from turbidity; it is limpid, pure, and ever-clear.

It is interspersed with seven layers of precious bricks, seven layers of paved slabs, seven layers of railings, and seven layers of bell-nets. Surrounding these on the outside are seven rows of *tāla* trees, encircling the area in every direction; they are of various beautiful colors and composed of the seven treasures, including even *musāragalva* and *aśmagarbha*.
On each of the four sides, there are stairways of various beautiful colors, also accomplished from the seven precious substances, such as agate and others.

Furthermore, various kinds of flowers grow there, namely the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka*. Those that are like fire have the color, shape, and radiance of fire; those that are gold have the color, shape, and radiance of gold; those that are blue have the color, shape, and radiance of blue; those that are red have the color, shape, and radiance of red; those that are white have the color, shape, and radiance of white; those that are green have the color, shape, and radiance of green; all are as round as chariot wheels.
Its radiance illuminates one *yojana*, and its fragrance likewise perfumes one *yojana*.
Within that pond, various lotus roots grow, as large as the axles of chariots; when cut, they exude a sap white in color like milk, with a sweet taste like pure honey.

“O bhikṣus! Between the two groves of Kūṭadanta and Nandanavana, for the asura king Vemacitra there is a great tree named Sujātāpāṭala. Its trunk is seven yojanas in circumference; its roots extend twenty-one yojanas into the earth; it rises a hundred yojanas above ground; its branches and foliage cover fifty yojanas; and it is five hundred yojanas in total height and breadth.”

Outside of that, there are likewise seven layers of walls; to speak briefly, they extend all around in an encircling perimeter, variegated and beautiful to behold, composed of the seven treasures, including even *musāragalva* and *aśmagarbha*.

On all four sides there are likewise gates made of the seven precious substances, and those gates are further equipped with watchtowers, defensive bulwarks, and pavilions; to speak briefly, up to various kinds of birds, each singing its own song.
*Sūtra on the Origin of the World*, Scroll Five;
*Sūtra on the Origin of the World*, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Dharmagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
The Chapter on Asuras, Part Two: "O Bhikṣus!
At the place where the seven heads of the asuras assemble, there are two forked paths through which that king travels back and forth for his pleasure."
At the location of the palace of the Asura King Vemacitrin, there were two branching paths, just as before;
at the locations of the palaces of the various minor Asura kings, there were likewise two branching paths;
and at the dwelling places of the various minor Asura kings, there were also two branching paths.
The Śāla grove also has two branching paths;
the Śalmali grove also has two branching paths;
the Kovidāra grove also has two branching paths.
The Nandanavana grove likewise has two branching paths;
the Nandā lake likewise has two branching paths;
and the great Saptaparṇa tree likewise has two branching paths.
All were as described before; they moved back and forth through the seven interconnected peaks. "O Bhikṣus!
That Asura King Vemacitrin desired to go toward those groves of Sāla trees, the Śamālī, the Kovidāra, and the Nandana gardens, to bathe, sport, wander about, and enjoy himself."
At that time, he thought of those minor Asura kings and thought of the minor Asuras.
Then, those minor Asura kings and the minor Asuras likewise conceived this thought:
"The Asura King Vemacitra has his mind set upon us."

Having understood this, they immediately adorned their bodies with various kinds of precious necklaces and ornaments. Once each was fully decorated, they mounted various vehicles and together proceeded toward the gate of the palace of Vemacitra, the Asura King. Upon arrival, they entered and stood before the hall of Vemacitra, the Asura King.

At that time, the Asura King Vemacitra, seeing those various minor Asura kings and the hosts of minor Asuras approaching, immediately adorned his own body with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments; having thus adorned his body, he mounted his vehicle.

At that time, the minor asura kings and the various minor asuras surrounded him on all four sides, acting as his attendants in front and behind, escorting him toward the Sālavana grove, the Śamālīvana grove, the Kovidāravana grove, the Nandanavana grove, and others.
Having arrived there, they stood before the Nanda Grove.
Monks! In that Nanda Grove, there are three wind-circles that blow naturally to adorn the grove.
What are the three?
They are the opener, the purifier, and the blower.
What is meant by "the opener"?
A wind-wheel comes, opening and closing the various gates.
What constitutes purity?
A wind-wheel comes, sweeping those groves and gardens so that the ground becomes pure.
What is meant by "blowing"?
A wind-circle arises and blows upon the various flowers of those garden trees, causing them to scatter and drift in all directions. Monks!
Within that Nandana grove, various kinds of exquisite flowers were scattered by the wind, falling as deep as the knees; there were various fragrances, their sweet scent pervading the entire grove.

At that time, Vemacitra, the King of the Asuras, together with the various minor Asura kings and their retinues of lesser Asuras, surrounded him and entered the Nandana grove. Having entered, they bathed, observed the sights, and sported, dwelling there as they pleased.
The various asuras, in those groves and gardens, bathe and sport for one month, two months, or three months, dwelling there at their pleasure and departing each according to where they wish to go.
“Monks! That Asura King Vemacitra is constantly accompanied by five other Asuras who remain at his side to protect and guard him against all evil matters.”
What are the five? First is named Anumoda;
second is named Bhava; third is named Mada; fourth is named Mucilinda; and fifth is named Vaihāyasa.
"O monks! That Asura King Vemacitra has these five kinds of asuras who constantly remain by the side of the Asura King Vemacitra for the purpose of guarding him."
"O Bhikṣus!
Above the palace of that Asura King Vemacitrin, there exists a mass of seawater ten thousand yojanas deep, which is naturally sustained by four kinds of winds."
What are these four?
They are: first, abiding; second, dwelling securely; third, not falling; and fourth, being a firm master.
Sustained by this wind, it remains eternally still and unmoving.
“O bhikṣus! A thousand yojanas to the south of Sumeru, the king of mountains, beneath the great ocean, lies the palace and dwelling place of the asura king Saṃjñeya.”

That place is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls; in brief, it is just like all that belongs to the asura king Vemacitra, and you should know that each detail therein is as described for him.

Furthermore, all the masses of water above this royal palace are likewise sustained by four kinds of wind-wheels: first, abiding; second, securely abiding; third, non-falling; and fourth, the firm master.

“O bhikṣus! One thousand yojanas to the west of Sumeru, the king of mountains, beneath the waters of the great ocean, there is the palace and dwelling place of the asura king Śāpāla (translated in the Sui language as ‘Illusionary Transformation’). It is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls; in brief, it possesses all the various features of the asura king Vemacitrin, and you should know that every detail herein is as described for him.”

Furthermore, all the masses of water above this royal palace are likewise sustained by four kinds of wind-wheels: first, abiding; second, securely abiding; third, non-falling; and fourth, the firm master.

"O Bhikṣus! To the north of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, at the same distance as described above, beneath the waters of the great ocean, there is the palace and dwelling place of Rāhu, the Asura King. Its dimensions, both length and breadth, are as previously stated; its walls, gate-towers, pavilions, and battlements are likewise."
In the gardens and various ponds, there are all kinds of trees with various leaves, various flowers and fruits, and various fragrant scents; there are various birds, each singing its own song.
"O Bhikṣus!

In that place, there is a city belonging to Rāhu, the Asura King; the king dwells in that city, which is named Māpadevi (in the language of Sui, 'Tranquil Lord'). Its dimensions and its magnificent adornments are also as described above."

There are seven layers of walls, seven layers of railings, seven rows of *tāla* trees, and seven layers of networks of bells surrounding it on all sides; they are of variegated and beautiful appearance, composed of the seven treasures, including even *musāragalva* and *aśmagarbha*.
The height, depth, and breadth of those walls are also as previously described.
Those walls likewise have various gates;
the height, depth, and breadth of each of those gates are exactly as before.

Furthermore, upon all the multi-storied pavilions, defensive towers, gatehouses, gardens, ponds, and lotus pools at those gates, there were also various trees with diverse leaves, diverse flowers and fruits, and diverse fragrances; there were also various birds of many kinds, each calling out its own song.

“O bhikṣus! Where King Māpadya dwells in that city of Māpadya, there is a gathering place for the asura king Rāhu, also named ‘Seven Heads. Its length and breadth are as previously described; it is surrounded on all sides by sevenfold railings, networks of bells, and rows of tāla trees, which are beautiful to behold with their variegated colors and adorned with the seven precious substances, including musāragalva and aśmagarbha.”

On each of the four sides there are various gates; those gates are also equipped with watchtowers, which are of diverse colors and beautiful to behold, composed of the seven precious substances, including even musaragalva and agate.
The lower part of that place is inlaid with celestial *musāragalva* (agate), and its ground is soft, so that touching it is like the touch of *kācalindika* cloth.
In the center of that place stands a jeweled pillar, its height, width, and breadth being as described above.

Beneath that pillar, a high seat was prepared for Rāhu, the Asura King; its height, dimensions, and adornments were each exactly as described before, variegated and beautiful to behold, fashioned from the seven treasures, including even musaragalva and agate. It was soft, fine, and smooth, such that touching it was like touching kācilindika cloth.

To the left of that seat, sixteen minor asura kings were each provided with their own exquisite high seats, variegated and beautiful to behold, fashioned from the seven precious gems, including even musaragalva and agate.
On the right side it is likewise; there are high seats for sixteen minor asura kings, also as described above, with a softness to the touch like that of kācilindika cloth.
“Monks! To the east of the dwelling place of the Asura King Saptasiras, he established a separate palace residence for the Asura King Rāhu.”

The dimensions of that place, both length and breadth, were each exactly as described before. It was surrounded on all four sides by sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets of bells, and even sevenfold rows of *tāla* trees, all of which were encircling it completely. These were of various beautiful colors, composed of the seven treasures, including even *musāragalva* and *aśmagarbha*.
On each of the four sides there are various gates; at those gates are multi-storied pavilions and defensive watchtowers.
There are gardens and groves, various ponds, springs, and marshes, with all kinds of trees possessing diverse leaves, flowers, fruits, and fragrant scents.
Furthermore, there are various kinds of diverse birds, each calling out its own song; their voices are harmonious and elegant, most delightful. "O Bhikṣus!

To the east, west, south, and north of that dwelling place of the Asura King Saptasīrṣa, there are respective palatial residences for the minor Asura kings. These places are nine hundred yojanas in length and breadth, or eight hundred, or seven hundred, or six, five, four, three, two, and even as small as one hundred yojanas. All of them have sevenfold walls and railings, and to speak briefly, they contain various kinds of birds, each calling out its own song."

"O monks! To the east, south, west, and north of that dwelling place of the Asura King Saptasiras, there are also separate palatial residences for those various minor Asuras. These places are ninety yojanas in length and breadth; some are eighty, seventy, sixty, fifty, forty, thirty, twenty, or even as small as twelve yojanas in length and breadth. They are surrounded by sevenfold walls, and so forth, until one reaches the detail that various kinds of birds each sing their own songs."
"O Bhikṣus!

To the east of the assembly hall of the seven heads of the Asura King is a park belonging to the Asura King Rāhu, named Śāla Forest. Its length and breadth are each as previously described; it has sevenfold walls and sevenfold railings, and so forth, up to being composed of the seven treasures, including agate."

On each of the four sides there are various gates; these gates are all equipped with watchtowers and battlements, variegated in color and beautiful to behold, even being composed of the seven treasures such as musaragalva and agate, and are exceedingly delightful.

“Monks! To the south of the assembly hall of the seven heads of that asura king, there is a park belonging to the asura king Rāhu, called the Śamālī Forest. Its dimensions and adornments are all as described above; it has sevenfold walls and seven rows of tāla trees, beautiful with their variegated colors, and likewise constructed from the seven treasures, including even musāragalva and aśmagarbha.
"On all four sides there are various gates; those gates have watchtowers and turrets, even up to those made of the seven treasures, including agate. Monks!..."

To the west of the assembly hall of the seven-headed Asura King is a park where the Asura King Rāhula resides, named the Kovidāra Forest. The dimensions of this forest, as well as its sevenfold walls and so forth, are all composed of the seven treasures including agate, exactly as described above.

On each of the four sides there are various gates, and those gates are also equipped with watchtowers and battlements, adorned with diverse decorations and variegated colors that are beautiful to behold, even being embellished with treasures such as musaragalva and agate; they are exceedingly delightful.

“O Bhikṣus! To the north of the assembly hall of the seven heads of that Asura king, there is a park and residence belonging to the Asura King Rāhula, named Nandanavana Forest. That forest is as long and wide as previously described, with sevenfold walls, and so forth, composed of the seven treasures including agate.”

On each of the four sides there are various gates, and those gates are also equipped with watchtowers and battlements; they are adorned with various ornaments and diverse colors that are beautiful to behold, even being embellished with treasures such as musaragalva and agate, and are exceedingly delightful.

“O bhikṣus! Between those two places, the Śamāli and the Sāla groves, there is a lake belonging to Rāhu, the king of the asuras, named Nanda; the length and breadth of that lake are as previously described.”
The water is cool, soft, light, and sweet; it is pure and free from turbidity.
It is paved with seven layers of bricks made of the seven precious substances, and adorned with panels of the seven precious substances interspersed throughout.

There are seven layers of railings and seven layers of networks of bells, surrounded on all sides by seven rows of *tāla* trees; they are of various beautiful colors and composed of the seven treasures, including agate.
Furthermore, its four sides have various stairways that are exceedingly delightful, also fashioned and adorned with the seven treasures.

Moreover, various flowers grow there—*utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka*. These flowers are fire-colored, fire-shaped, and possess the radiance of fire; briefly stated, they are as described above, including those water-colored, water-shaped, and possessing the radiance of water, which brightly illuminate the four directions.
The fragrance was rich and pervasive, universally perfuming all things.
There were also lotus roots, their juice white and their flavor sweet; eating them was as delicious as pure wax honey.

“O Bhikṣus! Between the two groves of Kūṭāgāra and Nandana, there is a great tree belonging to that Asura King Rāhu; the name of this tree is Sujātāpāṭala. Its dimensions and various adornments are all as described above, including the sevenfold walls and railings made of the seven treasures such as mother-of-pearl and agate, which are exceedingly delightful. To speak briefly, up to the point where various kinds of birds each sing their own songs, their voices being harmonious and elegant, bringing joy to those who hear them.”

“Monks! The assembly hall of that seven-headed Asura King is adorned as previously described; there are also branching paths and thoroughfares for coming and going, intended for the Asura King Rāhula to travel to and from his palace.”
Furthermore, for the various minor asura kings and the various minor asuras, there are also branching paths for the purpose of coming and going.
There are likewise branching paths leading toward the Śamālī and the Kovidāra trees.
There are branching paths leading to Mount Nandana, Lake Nanda, and the Pāṭala tree of Suvarṇaprabhāsa, all providing access for coming and going so that they may enjoy themselves in play.

“Monks! When that Asura King Rāhu wishes to go toward the Sālavana grove, the Nandanavana grove, and other such places to bathe, sport, and go out for sightseeing, at that time he directs his thoughts to the Asura King Vemacitra.”
At that time, the asura king Vemacitrin thought to himself:
"The asura king Rāhu has set his mind upon me, wishing to sport with me."
At that time, after the asura king Vemacitrin had formed this thought, he further called to mind his various minor asura kings and the hosts of minor asuras.
At that time, those minor Asura kings and their retinues of minor Asuras conceived this thought:
"The Asura King Vemacitra has turned his thoughts toward us; we should go to him."

They immediately adorned their bodies with various kinds of precious necklaces and ornaments; having thus decorated themselves, they each mounted their respective vehicles and proceeded toward the abode of the Asura Vemacitra. Upon arrival at the gate of that palace, they stood there in a disciplined and orderly fashion.

At that time, having seen that all the minor asura kings and the various hosts of minor asuras had assembled, the asura king Vemacitra adorned himself, donned various necklaces and ornaments, and mounted his various vehicles. Together with the minor kings and the asura hosts, surrounded on the left and right and escorted from before and behind, he proceeded toward the asura king Rāhu; having arrived, he halted there.
"At that time, Rāhu, the Asura King, again thought of the two Asura Kings, Vala and Śambara.
Then, those two Asura Kings, Vala and Śambara, likewise thought:
'Rāhu, the Asura King, is now thinking of us.'"

Having understood this, they each further called to mind their respective minor asura kings and their various hosts; once these had also taken notice, they gathered together and approached in full regalia. Each went toward the two asura kings, Dhr̥tarāṣṭra and Śambarasura; having arrived, they adorned themselves with necklaces and mounted their vehicles, and surrounded by their retinues, they proceeded toward Rāhu Asura. Upon arrival, they each took up positions according to where they belonged.
At that time, Rāhu, the Asura King, seeing that Vemacitra, the Asura King, and the others had all assembled like clouds, thought of the various minor Asura kings and their respective retinues.
Having learned of this, they too each adorned themselves with ornaments and mounted their vehicles, arriving before Rāhu, the king of the asuras, and stood there solemnly.

Then, King Rāhu, having seen them, adorned his own body with various necklaces and ornaments, and mounting various vehicles, surrounded by his retinue, joined King Vemacitra and the asura kings Saṃjaya, Śabala, and others, along with the hosts of minor asura kings. Gathering like clouds in procession, they headed toward the Sāla Grove, the Śamālī Grove, the Kovidāra Grove, and the Nandana Grove. Having arrived, they stood for a short while before [the Lord].
“Monks! Within that Nandanavana grove, there are naturally three kinds of wind-circles (*vāyu-maṇḍala*).
What are these three?
What are called "opening," "purifying," and "blowing.
Among these, the "opening" wind-circle opens wide all the gates;
the "purifying" wind-circle sweeps clean all the grounds.
The "Blower" refers to the wind-circle that blows upon the various flowering trees. Monks!

Within that Nandana grove, exquisite and beautiful flowers are scattered everywhere, covering the ground; the fragrance of those flowers perfumes the entire garden, which is richly adorned and full of manifold wonders to behold.

At that time, Rāhu the Asura King, along with Vemacitra the Asura King, Valguka the Asura King, Śabara the Asura King, and others—accompanied by their minor kings, retinues, and hosts of lesser asuras—surrounded him and entered the Nandana Grove.

Having entered, they bathe, sport, and experience pleasure; they gaze upon various sights, whether walking, standing, lying down, or sitting, proceeding wherever they wish and acting according to their own inclination.
"O Bhikṣus!
That Rāhu, the Asura King, is likewise constantly accompanied by five other Asuras who protect his evil deeds; their names are as previously stated."
The seawater above Mount Sumeru—its extent, breadth, depth, and thickness—is sustained by four kinds of winds so that it does not fall away, as was explained above.
Chapter Seven: The Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings *Qishi Jing*, Chapter Seven: The Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings "O Bhikṣus! [The Four Heavenly Kings are as follows...]"

On the eastern flank of Mount Sumeru, King of Mountains, forty-two thousand yojanas above the ground at the summit of Mount Yugandhara, lies the city and residence of the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra. This city is named Bhadraśreṇī; it is six hundred yojanas in length and breadth, and is surrounded by sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold networks of bells.

Furthermore, it was surrounded on all sides by seven rows of *tāla* trees, beautiful to behold with their variegated colors, all adorned with the seven treasures—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, *sphatika*, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.
On each of the four sides there are various gates, and those gates are equipped with watchtowers, defensive bulwarks, and palatial pavilions, as well as gardens and various ponds.
Within those flower groves are trees of many kinds, with various leaves, various flowers and fruits, and various fragrant scents.
There are various kinds of birds, each calling out its own song; their voices are harmonious and most delightful. "O Bhikṣus!

On the southern slope of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, at a height of forty-two thousand yojanas above the earth, on the summit of Mount Yugandhara, there is the city and residence of the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka. The city is named Suprabha; its dimensions and adornments are exactly as previously described for the residence of the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and so forth, up to the various birds, each calling out its own song."

“Monks! On the western flank of Mount Sumeru, King of Mountains, at a height of forty-two thousand yojanas above the earth and at the summit of Mount Yugandhara, there is the city and residence of the Deva King Virūpākṣa; the city is named Sudarśana.”

In length and breadth, each feature of its adornment is exactly as previously described regarding the abode of the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra; to speak briefly, even down to the various birds, each chirping its own song, their voices harmonious and most delightful.

"O Bhikṣus! On the northern slope of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, at a height of forty-two thousand yojanas above the earth and from the summit of the Yugandhara Mountains, there are three city-walls belonging to the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, which serve as his dwelling place."
What are these three?
The first is called Vaiśravaṇa; the second is named Ghaṭotkaca; and the third is named Aṭapāṇḍa.
Each is six hundred yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls and sevenfold railings; to speak briefly, there are various kinds of birds, each singing its own song.
"O Bhikṣus!

With the exception of the palaces of the Moon Devaputra and the seven great palaces of the Sun Devaputra, all other celestial palaces belonging to the various devas under the Four Great Kings have dimensions ranging from forty yojanas in length and breadth, or thirty, twenty, or twelve; even the smallest are still sixty yojanas in length and breadth. Each is likewise surrounded by sevenfold walls and railings, as described briefly before, up to the point where various birds sing of their own accord."
“O bhikṣus! Between those two palaces, Vaiśravaṇa and Ghaṭāpati, there is a pool of water belonging to King Vaiśravaṇa; that pool is named Nādikī, and it is forty yojanas in length and breadth.”
The water is harmoniously blended, cool, refreshing, light, and soft; its taste is sweet and delicious, fragrant, pure, and unclouded.

On the four sides of the pond, there are seven layers of brickwork and seven layers of precious planks, arranged with distinct clarity, along with seven layers of railings and seven layers of bell-nets.

There were also seven rows of *tāla* trees surrounding it on all sides; they were of various beautiful colors, composed of the seven treasures, including even such gems as *musāragalva* and *aśmagarbha*.
On each of the four sides, there were stairways, likewise adorned with the seven precious substances.
Within those ponds, various flowers—such as the utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka—spontaneously grew.

The flowers were the color of fire, the shape of fire, and the radiance of fire; likewise, they were the color of water, the shape of water, and the radiance of water. When the flowers bloomed, they spread out as vast as a chariot wheel.
Their light illuminated half a yojana, and their fragrance perfumed one yojana.
There are lotus roots as large as chariot axles; when cut, they exude a sap white as milk, which is sweet and delicious to eat, with a flavor as sweet as honey.

“O Bhikṣus! Between the two palaces of Ghaṭāpati and Aṭaṇḍa, there is a park belonging to King Vaiśravaṇa where he dwells; the name of that park is Kapiñjala. It is forty yojanas in length and breadth, exactly equal on all sides. It is surrounded on all sides by sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, and so forth, up to seven rows of palm trees. It is of various beautiful colors, as described briefly before, and is composed of the seven precious gems.”
As for the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, in his residence of Bhadraśreṣṭha, there are two forked paths for the coming and going within the city walls;
as for the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, in his residence of Sudarśana, there are likewise two forked paths for the departing and arriving within the city walls;
as for the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa, in his residence of Sudarśana, there are two forked paths for the departing and arriving within the city walls.
In the city of Aṭaṇḍa, the residence of King Vaiśravaṇa, there are two forked roads;
likewise, in the cities of Viśālamati and Ghaṭapāṇi, there are also two forked roads at each location.
Furthermore, in the palatial residences of all the minor devas who are the retinues of the Four Great Kings, there are likewise two forked roads for their coming and going.
The Nandīni Pond and the Kāpivanta Garden, and so forth, each have two-way paths for coming and going. "O Bhikṣus!
When the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa wishes to go to that Kāpivanta Garden to sport and bathe, he immediately calls to mind the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra within his heart."
At that time, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra also thought to himself:
"The Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa has me in his thoughts.
Having known this, he immediately called to mind the minor heavenly kings and the celestial hosts belonging to his own realm.
At that time, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his retinue belonging to the eastern quarter thought to themselves:
"The Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra is thinking of us."

Having understood this, they each adorned their bodies with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments, mounted various vehicles, and proceeded to the presence of the Great Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra; having arrived, they stood to one side before him.
At that time, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra adorned himself and donned various necklaces and ornaments.

Having mounted his carriage, he was surrounded by his retinue of minor kings and celestial hosts, who escorted him as he proceeded to the presence of the Great Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa; having arrived, he stood before King Vaiśravaṇa.
"At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa thought of the two great heavenly kings, Virūḍhaka and Virūpākṣa.
Then, those two kings thought thus in their minds:
'The King Vaiśravaṇa is thinking of us.'"
Having known this, each of them immediately called to mind the minor deva kings and their respective retinues whom they governed.
At that time, those minor kings and their celestial hosts also thought to themselves:
"Our Great King is calling us to mind; we should go there with all speed."

Having understood this, they each adorned their bodies with necklaces and ornaments, and together proceeded to the abodes of the two heavenly kings, Virūḍhaka and Virūpākṣa; having arrived, they stood there.

At that time, the two celestial kings, knowing that the minor kings and the other hosts of devas had gathered and arrived, each adorned themselves, donned various necklaces and ornaments, and immediately mounted their vehicles. Surrounded by the assembly, they all proceeded together to the palace of the Great Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa; having arrived, they halted together before him.
At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa, knowing that the celestial hosts of the two kings had already assembled, further called to mind the minor deva-kings and their various retinues whom he himself led.
At that time, the minor kings of the northern quarter and their celestial hosts conceived this thought:
"The Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa now thinks of us."
Having understood this, they each donned various necklaces of many jewels; having thus adorned their bodies, they went before the Great Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa and all stood there together.

At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa, having adorned his own body with various kinds of precious necklaces and ornaments, mounted a variety of celestial vehicles, and accompanied by the four great kings—Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, and others—each surrounded by their respective hosts of heavenly kings, all proceeded together toward the Caitraratha Garden. Having arrived, they halted before the garden.
"O Bhikṣus!
Within that Caitraratha Grove, there naturally arise three wind-circles: first, the opening; second, the purifying; and third, the blowing."
"Opening" means opening the gates of that garden;
"purifying" means purifying the grounds of that garden;
"blowing" means blowing upon the trees of that garden, so that all the flowers flutter and drift away.
"O Bhikṣus!
In that Caitraratha Grove, various flowers accumulate up to the knees, and their manifold fragrances pervade everywhere.

At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, King Virūḍhaka, and King Virūpākṣa—along with all the minor kings and their retinues—enter the Caitraratha Grove together, bathe, sport, and enjoy every kind of pleasure."
Within that garden, for perhaps one month, two months, or three months,
having finished bathing, they sport and enjoy pleasures, traveling wherever they desire and proceeding as they please.
"O Bhikṣus!
That Vaiśravaṇa also has five yakṣa-king deities who constantly follow him, remaining close at hand to his left and right for the purpose of guarding him."
What are these five? First is named Five-Fathoms;
second is named Wilderness; third is named Golden Mountain; fourth is named Long Body; and fifth is named Needle-Hair.
"O bhikṣus!
When the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa comes and goes for his pastimes, he is always protected by these five yakṣa deities.
Chapter 8: The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven The Sūtra on the Arising of the World, Chapter Eight (Part One): The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven "O bhikṣus!"

Upon the summit of that King of Mountains, Sumeru, there is the abode of the palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa gods; it is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth. It is surrounded on all sides by sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets of bells, and sevenfold rows of *tāla* trees, which are of various beautiful colors and composed of the seven treasures—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, *sphatika*, red pearls, *musāragalva*, and *aśmagarbha*.
Its walls are four hundred yojanas high and fifty yojanas wide; these walls are each separated by five hundred yojanas, and between them stand various gates.
Those gates are thirty yojanas high and ten yojanas wide.
On both sides of the gates, there are watchtowers, battlements, pavilions, and various types of carriages.

Furthermore, there are various ponds and flowering groves with diverse trees, diverse leaves, diverse flowers and fruits, and diverse fragrant scents; there are diverse birds, each singing its own song, their voices harmonious and most delightful.
Furthermore, at each of those gates, there are always five hundred yakṣas for the purpose of guarding the Trāyastriṃśa devas. O bhikṣus!

Within that enclosure wall, for the sake of the King of the Trāyastriṃśa devas, there is a city named Sudarśana. That city is sixty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, surrounded by sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold networks of bells, and sevenfold rows of tala trees, encircling it on all sides. It is beautiful to behold with its various colors and is adorned with the seven treasures, including even musāragalva and aśmagarbha.

The walls of that city are one hundred yojanas high, and fifty yojanas wide at the top. The city ramparts are likewise each five hundred yojanas apart from one another, and between them stand various gates; each gate is thirty yojanas high and ten yojanas wide.

At those various gates, there were likewise watchtowers, battlements, and pavilions; there were ponds and flower groves with various kinds of trees, various leaves, various flowers and fruits, various fragrant incenses, and various flocks of birds, each singing its own song.
At each of those gates, there are five hundred yakṣas who serve as guardians for the Trāyastriṃśa devas. "O bhikṣus!

Near that celestial palace, by the side of the city of Sudarśana, there is a palace where the great nāga-elephant king Airāvaṇa resides. That palace is six hundred yojanas in length and breadth, and it likewise has sevenfold walls, railings, and so forth, up to various kinds of birds, each singing its own song."
"O Bhikṣus!

Within the great enclosure wall of that city of Sudarśana, there is a hall for the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa devas called the Sudharmā Hall. That place is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, surrounded on all sides by sevenfold railings, sevenfold networks of bells, and sevenfold rows of tāla trees. It is of various beautiful colors, composed of the seven precious substances, including even musāragalva and aśmagarbha."
On each of the four sides there are various gates, all equipped with watchtowers, battlements, and defensive towers of diverse colors, fashioned from the seven precious gems.
The ground is composed entirely of blue lapis lazuli, soft and smooth to the touch, like kācilindika cloth.
In the midst of it stands a precious pillar twenty yojanas high.

At the base of this pillar, a throne has been established for Śakra, Lord of the Devas; it is one yojana high and half a yojana wide, of variegated and beautiful appearance, composed of the seven treasures including musāragalva and aśmagarbha, soft, fine, and smooth to the touch, as described before.

On both sides of that seat, there were sixteen thrones for minor heavenly kings who attended and guarded it; they were composed of the seven treasures, beautiful in their variegated colors, and smooth and supple to the touch, no different from what was described before.

“O bhikṣus! For the sake of Śakra, Lord of Devas, a palace was established within the Sudharmā Hall—the assembly hall of the devas. That palace was one thousand yojanas in extent, with sevenfold walls, and even the various birds each sang their own songs.”
"O Bhikṣus!

In the Sudharmā Hall, the assembly place of the devas, there are palaces where various minor kings reside in the east, west, south, and north. They measure nine hundred yojanas in length and breadth; some are eight, seven, six, five, four, three, or two [hundred], while the smallest are one hundred yojanas wide. Each has sevenfold walls, and even the various birds each sing their own songs."

To the east, west, south, and north of the Sudharmā Hall, the assembly hall of the devas, are the various small celestial palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa devas. They measure ninety yojanas in length and breadth, or eighty-seven, eighty-six, eighty-five, eighty-four, eighty-three, eighty, or seventy; the smallest of them is twelve yojanas in width. Each is surrounded by sevenfold walls, and even the various birds each sing their own songs.

"O Bhikṣus! To the east of the Sudharmā Hall, the assembly hall of the devas, there is a park belonging to the King of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, named Pāruṣyaka. It is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth; briefly described, it features sevenfold walls made of the seven treasures, such as agate and so forth."

On each of the four sides there are various gates; these gates are equipped with watchtowers, which are multicolored and beautiful to behold, even being composed of the seven precious gems, including agate.
"O Bhikṣus!
Within that Pāruṣyaka Garden there are two great rocks: one named Bhadra and the other named Subhadra.
They are composed of celestial agate, each measuring fifty yojanas in length and breadth; they are soft, fine, and smooth, such that touching them is like touching kācilindika cloth."

“O Bhikṣus! To the south of the Sudharmā Hall, the assembly hall of the devas, there is a park belonging to the King of the Thirty-three, named Citraratha. This park is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and its sevenfold walls are composed of everything up to agate.”
On each of the four sides there are various gates; those gates are all equipped with watchtowers and battlements, variegated and beautiful to behold, even being fashioned from agate.
Within that garden there are also two rocks: the first named Variegated Color (*Citra-varṇa*) and the second named Well-Variegated Color (*Sucitra-varṇa*).
They are composed entirely of celestial blue lapis lazuli; each is fifty *yojanas* in length and breadth, soft, fine, and smooth, such that touching them is like touching *kācilindika* cloth.

“O bhikṣus! To the west of the Sudharmā Hall, the assembly hall of the devas, there is also a garden belonging to the King of the Trāyastriṃśa devas called Citraratha. This garden is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold walls, and so forth, being composed of the seven precious substances.”
On each of the four sides there are gates, all equipped with watchtowers, battlements, and defensive platforms, all made of the seven precious substances.
Within that Grove of Various Impurities (Miśrakāvana), there are also two stones: the first is named Sudarśana, and the second is named Upasudarśana.
They are composed of celestial *pārijātaka* [trees], each fifty *yojana* in length and breadth; they are soft, fine, and smooth, such that touching them is like the touch of *kācalindika* cloth.

“O Bhikṣus! To the north of the Sudharmā Hall, the assembly place of the devas, there is a park belonging to the King of the Trāyastriṃśa gods called Nandana. This park is one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and its sevenfold walls are composed of the seven treasures, including agate.”
On each of the four sides there are gates, each equipped with watchtowers, battlements, and defensive galleries, all likewise adorned with the seven precious substances. O Bhikṣus!
Within the Nandana Grove, there are also two rocks: one named Nandana and the other named Sunandana.
They are made of celestial silver, each fifty yojanas in length and breadth, soft and lustrous, and to the touch they are like kācilindika cloth.
“O bhikṣus! Between the two gardens, Pāruṣyaka and Citraratha, there is a lake belonging to the King of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, named Nandana, measuring five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.”
The water is cool, light, soft, and sweet; it is pure and free from turbidity.
It is lined on all four sides with bricks made of the seven treasures, interspersed with seven layers of precious planks.
It was surrounded on all sides by seven tiers of railings and, likewise, seven rows of *tāla* trees, forming a pleasing sight with their variegated colors.
Furthermore, at each of its four corners, there were stairways, all adorned with the seven precious substances.
Within it were various flowers: blue lotuses (utpala), red lotuses (padma), yellow lotuses (kumuda), and white lotuses (puṇḍarīka).
These flowers had the color, shape, and radiance of fire, and even the color, shape, and radiance of water; their length, breadth, and size were all like those of chariot wheels.
Its radiance illuminates one *yojana*, and when the wind blows, its fragrance perfumes one *yojana*.
There are various lotus roots as large as chariot axles; when cut, their sap flows out, white in color like milk, and its taste is sweet and delicious like pure honey.

“O Bhikṣus! Between the Caitraratha Grove and the Miśrakāvana Grove, for the sake of the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there is a great tree named Pārijātaka-kovidāra. Its roots extend seven yojanas in circumference; briefly stated, its branches and leaves spread everywhere, covering an area five hundred yojanas in length and breadth. It has sevenfold walls, and so forth, until: various birds each sing their own songs.”
"O Bhikṣus!

Beneath the great tree Pāriyātra-kovidāra, there is a great stone named Paṇḍakambala. It is composed of celestial gold, measuring fifty yojanas in length and breadth, soft and lustrous, like touching a kācilindika cloth."
“Monks! Regarding that interval, for what cause and for what reason is the assembly hall of the devas where they gather called ‘Sudharma’ (The Hall of Good Dharma)? Monks!”

In that Sudharmā Hall, the assembly place of the devas, once the Kings of the Thirty-three have gathered and taken their seats, they discuss therein only subtle, refined, and profound meanings; they contemplate them with discernment, weighing and examining them. Since these are mostly essential worldly matters and principles of true reality, it is for this reason that the heavens call it the Assembly Place of the Sudharmā Hall.
Furthermore, for what reason is the park named Pāruṣyaka? “Pāruṣyaka” means ‘rough and harsh’ in the language of Sui. Monks!

When the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enters the Rough and Harsh Garden and sits upon the two rocks, Bhadra and Subhadra, he discusses nothing but worldly, coarse, evil, and unwholesome speech and jesting; therefore, it is called Pāruṣyaka.
Furthermore, for what reason is it called the Citrapāṭalīvana (Variegated Car Park)? Monks!

Once the kings of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have entered the Citrapāṭalīvana, they sit upon two rocks—the Citra and the Sucitra—and discuss various worldly matters concerning diverse forms and appearances. For this reason, it is called the Citrapāṭalīvana.
Furthermore, for what reason is it called the Garden of Intermingling (Saṃkīrṇa)? O Bhikṣus!

Within the Garden of Intermingling, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of every month, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven releases all the ladies of his inner palace to go toward that garden. He causes them to mingle with the hosts of the Trāyastriṃśa devas, so that they may frolic and play together without obstruction, indulging in their pleasures at will and experiencing the five celestial desires, fully endowed with merit as they roam about and enjoy themselves.
For this reason, the hosts of devas in that place collectively call that garden the *Saṃkīrṇa* (Miscellaneous) Garden.
*Qishi yinben jing*, Scroll Six.
*Qishi yinben jing*, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Dharmagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven:
"O Bhikṣus!..."
Furthermore, for what reason is that grove named "Joy" (Nandana)?

O monks! Once the King of the Thirty-three Gods has entered that Joy Grove, he sits upon two stones, the Joyful and the Well-Joyful. His mind experiences joy; his thoughts are filled with joy; he reflects again and again, his heart experiences delight, and having experienced delight, he experiences further delight. For this reason, it is called the Joy Grove.
"O bhikṣus!
Furthermore, for what reason and by what cause is that tree named the Pāriyātra-kovidāra tree?
O bhikṣus!"

Beneath that Pārijāta-kovidāra tree dwells a devaputra named Manda, who day and night constantly enjoys himself in play, fully endowed with and harmoniously united with the various fivefold sensual pleasures of that heaven; for this reason, the gods call that place the Pārijāta-kovidāra tree.
"O Bhikṣus!

Furthermore, whenever the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven are in urgent haste, they never depart from that Mount Gandhamādana; rather, having merely made offerings with respect and reverence, they go wherever they wish."
Why is this? Because this rock was the place where the Tathāgata dwelt in the past;
those devas took it to be a caitya-stūpa, and because all the world—including gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—makes offerings to it.
“Monks! There are gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven who can see the Pāruṣyaka Grove with their eyes alone, but their bodies cannot enter it.
Because their bodies do not enter, they are unable to experience the full enjoyment of the fivefold sensual pleasures there.”
Why is this? Because the karma in that place is superior; since they cultivated inferior roots of goodness in their previous lives, they are unable to enter.
There are those among the Thirty-three Gods who can see the Pāruṣyaka Garden and whose bodies may also enter it.
Having thus entered, they fully experience the bliss of a single essence, endowed with the harmonious merits of the various fivefold sensual pleasures of the devas. Why is this?
Because their roots of goodness are superior and preeminent. "O Bhikṣus!

There are certain gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven who cannot see the Citraratha Garden with their eyes, nor can they enter it; furthermore, they are unable to experience the pleasure of being of one essence with the perfect merits of the five sensory desires of that garden."
Why is this? It is because their roots of goodness are distinct.

Furthermore, there are those in the Heaven of the Thirty-three who, though able to see the Citrapāṭalīvana Garden with their eyes, are unable to enter it with their bodies, nor can they experience the bliss of being of one essence with the complete and harmonious merits of the five desires of that garden.
Why is this? It is because their roots of goodness vary in degree of excellence.
Furthermore, there are those among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven who, having already been able to see the Citraratha Grove with their eyes, are also able to enter it with their bodies.
Having entered therein, they fully experience the joy of the harmonious union of those various fivefold sensual desires as being of one essence.
Why is this? It is because their roots of goodness have become superior and preeminent.

“Monks! All those gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are able to see the Caitraratha Grove, and they all enter it. Having entered, they all together experience the perfect bliss of a single essence, which consists of the harmonious merits of the various fivefold sensual pleasures within that grove.”
Why is this? Because in that place there are no distinct roots of goodness, practices, or the like. O bhikṣus!

There are gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven who are unable to see the Nandana Grove, nor are they able to enter it; furthermore, they are unable to experience the perfect bliss of the unified essence resulting from the combination of the various fivefold sensual pleasures within that grove.
Why is this? It is because the karmic conditions created in previous lives that resulted in those rebirths were distinct.

Furthermore, there are those among the Trāyastriṃśa gods who are able to see the Nandana Grove, yet they may not enter it; nor can they fully experience the bliss of the unified essence of the various five sensual pleasures and their harmonious merits within that Nandana Grove.
Why is this? Because their karma differs in that place.

Furthermore, there are those among the Trāyastriṃśa gods who are able to see the Nandana Grove; their bodies also enter it. Having entered, they fully obtain the various merits of the harmonious union of the five sensual pleasures and experience all such bodily joys together.
Why is this? Because in that place, when they perform various wholesome karmas, there is no distinction in the process of their cultivation. "O Bhikṣus!"
At the site of the Sudharmā Hall, the assembly place of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, there are two forked paths;
at the site of the palace of Śakra Devendra, there are two forked paths;
and at the sites of the palaces of the various minor deva kings, along with their respective officials and retinues within the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, there are likewise two forked paths.
At the location of the palace of the great nāga-elephant king Airāvaṇa, there are likewise two branching paths;
in the Pāruṣyaka Garden, there are likewise two branching paths;
and in each of the Citraratha Garden, the Caitraratha Garden, the Nandana Garden, the ponds, and so forth, there are likewise two branching paths for each.
The great tree Pāriyātra-kovidāra also has two forked paths. "O Bhikṣus!

When Śakra, the King of Devas, wishes to go toward the Caitraratha garden, the Miśrakāvana garden, the Nandana garden, and so forth, to bathe, enjoy himself, and sport, he then directs his mind toward the great nāga-elephant king Airāvaṇa."
The great nāga-elephant king Airāvaṇa also had this thought:
"The Heavenly King Śakra is thinking of me.
Having known this, he emerged from his palace and immediately manifested a transformation, assuming thirty-three heads.
Each of his heads was transformed into six tusks;
upon each tusk were transformed seven ponds; within each pond were seven lotuses;
and upon each lotus were seven jade maidens.
Each of these jade maidens, in turn, had seven daughters of her own as attendants.
At that time, after the great dragon-elephant king Airāvaṇa had manifested such supernatural transformations, he proceeded to where King Śakra was, and upon arrival, stood before him.
"At that time, Śakra, King of the Gods, thought of the thirty-two minor kings of the gods, as well as the assemblies of the thirty-two devas.
Then, those minor kings and the assemblies of devas also gave rise to this thought:
'Śakra, King of the Gods, is now thinking of us.'"

Having understood this, they each adorned their bodies with various kinds of exquisite necklaces and ornaments, mounted various types of carriages together, and proceeded toward the presence of Śakra, Lord of the Devas; having arrived, they each stood before him.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having seen this, immediately adorned his body in various ways and donned many necklaces and ornaments. Surrounded on all sides—front, back, left, and right—by hosts of devas, he ascended the dragon-elephant king Airāvaṇa. Śakra, King of Devas, sat directly upon the central head, while on each of the left and right sides there were sixteen minor deva kings, all riding upon the transformed heads of that same dragon-elephant king Airāvaṇa, each sitting in their respective place.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, leading his retinue of celestial hosts, proceeded toward the Pāruṣyaka and Citraratha groves, as well as the Miśrakāvana and Nandanavana gardens; having arrived, he halted there.

Within each of the four gardens, such as Nandana and the others, there are three kinds of wind-circles that sustain them: namely, the opening, the purifying, and the blowing winds; these are briefly explained as before, referring to the opening of gates, the purification of the ground, and the blowing of flowers, and so forth.
"O Bhikṣus!
In those groves, flowers have been blown about until they cover the ground up to the knees, and their fragrance permeates everywhere.

At that time, Śakra, together with the minor deities and surrounded by his retinue of the Thirty-three Gods, enters the Citraratha and Nandana gardens and other such places; there he sports and enjoys pleasures, wandering at will, sometimes reclining and sometimes sitting."
At that time, Śakra, King of the Devas, desiring to obtain a jeweled necklace, immediately called to mind the devaputra Viśvakarman.
Thereupon, that devaputra manifested various precious necklaces and offered them to the King of the Devas.
If the retinues of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and others require necklaces, Viśvakarman transforms them all into such ornaments and provides them.

For those who wish to hear sounds and music, there are various birds that produce all manner of voices; these sounds are exceedingly harmonious and elegant, causing the gods to rejoice in listening to them.

At that time, the devas experience such pleasures for one day up to seven days, or one month up to three months; they enjoy various forms of delight, bathing and sporting, moving, standing, sitting, or lying down, traveling east and west as they please.
"O bhikṣus!
Śakra, the King of Devas, has ten sons who constantly act as his guardians.
What are these ten?"
First is named Indrakaka; second, Gopaka; third, Binduka; fourth, Bindubhaka; fifth, Aghaṭaka; sixth, Ṭaṭotka; seventh, Śivaka; eighth, Hulugīna; ninth, Naṭaka; tenth, Hulubhaka.
"O Bhikṣus!
Śakra, the Lord of Devas, is constantly protected by these ten sons of devas, who always follow at his left and right, never departing from him, for the sake of guarding him."

"O Bhikṣus! In the land of Jambudvīpa, among the water-born flowers that grow for the sake of all people, those which are most supreme, exquisite, and exceedingly lovely are the so-called *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers;

the fragrance of these flowers is dense, soft, and beautiful. As for the land-born flowers, the most excellent are the so-called *atimuktaka*, *campaka*, *pāṭala*, *sumana*, *vārṣika*, *mallikā*, *mādhūkakāntika*, *sāntika*, *yūthikā*, *śukrasārikā*, and *tānusa-kāñcika* flowers."
"O Bhikṣus!

Among the people of Aparagoyānī, there are water-born flowers that are most excellent, namely: the utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka flowers; their fragrance is rich and pervasive, wafting everywhere to permeate those who encounter it.

As for their land-born flowers, those that are most fragrant and beautiful are: the atimuktaka, campaka, pāṭala, sumana, vārṣika, mallikā, mādhūkadantī, sātī, yūthikā, śukrasārikā, and dhānuṣkāriṇī flowers."
"O Bhikṣus!

Among the people of Pūrvavideha, there are water-born flowers that are most excellent, namely the utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka flowers; they are exceedingly radiant and their fragrance wafts everywhere.
As for the land-born flowers that are most excellent, they are the atimuktaka, campaka, pāṭala, sumana, vārṣika, mallikā, mādhūka, sātaka, yūthikā, śukrasārika, and dhānuṣkāriṇī flowers."
“Monks! Among the people of Uttarakuru, there are water-born flowers that are most excellent, namely the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, which possess fragrant and soft scents.

As for their land-born flowers that are most excellent, they are the *atimuktaka*, *campaka*, *pāṭala*, *sumana*, *vārṣika*, *mallikā*, *mātuluṅgikā*, *sākuṇḍikā*, *yūthikā*, *śukrasārikā*, and *dhānuṣkāriṇī* flowers, among others.”

“O bhikṣus! Those nāgas and garuḍas likewise each possess aquatic flowers, the most excellent of which are the utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka; their fragrance is pervasive, and they are soft and exquisite.

As for their terrestrial flowers, the most excellent are the atimuktaka, campaka, pāṭala, sumana, vārṣika, mallikā, mādhūkapuṣpa, saptaparṇa, yūthikā, śukrasārikā, karkārava, and mahākarkārava, among others.”

“O bhikṣus! Those asuras likewise each possess various water-born flowers, the most exquisite of which are the utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka; their fragrance wafts everywhere, being exceedingly delightful.”

As for the flowers that grow on land, those that are most excellent are as follows: the *atimuktaka* flower, the *campaka* flower, the *pāṭala* flower, the *sumana* flower, the *bāliśika* flower, the *mallikā* flower, the *mātuluṅgikā* flower, the *sākuṇḍikā* flower, the *yūthikā* flower, the *cūṭaśakalikā* flower, the *dhanuṣkāra* flower, the *karkārava* flower, the *mahākarkārava* flower, the *pundarīka* flower, the *mahāpundarīka* flower, the *mandārava* flower, and the *mahāmandārava* flower, and so forth.

“O bhikṣus! The Four Great Kings and the various classes of devas possess water-born flowers that are exceedingly beautiful, upright, lovely, and subtle—namely, the utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka flowers—which are extremely fragrant and very soft in substance.”

The flowers growing on land are subtle, exquisite, and lovely, namely: the *atimuktaka* flower, the *campaka* flower, the *pāṭala* flower, the *sumana* flower, the *vārṣika* flower, the *mallikā* flower, the *mātuluṅgikā* flower, the *sākuṇḍikā* flower, the *yūthikā* flower, the *śukrasārikā* flower, the *tānuśaka* flower, the *kakkāralī* flower, the *mahākakkāralī* flower, the *bimbiṭa* flower, the *mahābimbiṭa* flower, and so forth.

“Monks! Among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there are water-born flowers that are exceedingly beautiful, exquisite, and delightful—namely, the utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka flowers. Their fragrance is most intense, and their substance is very soft.”

The flowers growing on land are subtle, exquisite, and lovely, namely: the *atimuktaka* flower, the *campaka* flower, the *pāṭala* flower, the *sumana* flower, the *vārṣika* flower, the *mallikā* flower, the *mātuluṅgikā* flower, the *sākuṇḍikā* flower, the *yūthikā* flower, the *śuktimatī* flower, the *dhānuṣkāriṇī* flower, the *karkaṭharī* flower, the *mahākarkaṭharī* flower, the *bimbi* flower, the *mahābimbi* flower, the *mandārava* flower, the *mahāmandārava* flower, and so forth.

Just as all the flowers belonging to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven exist, so it is for the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven, and likewise for the Mārakāyika Heaven; one should know that they are each equal and without difference in this successive order.
“Monks! There are seven kinds of physical forms among the people of the world.
What are these seven?
"O bhikṣus!

There are people who have the color and form of fire, the color and form of gold, the color and form of blue, the color and form of red, the color and form of white, the color and form of yellow, and the color and form of black—just like the constant colors of Māra and Brahmā."
"O Bhikṣus!
Human beings in this world possess these seven kinds of colors; the asuras likewise possess these same seven colors;
and the hosts of devas also possess these seven kinds of colors, just like the constant colors of Māra and Brahmā."
“Monks! The devas possess ten distinct qualities.
What are these ten?
"O bhikṣus! First, the coming and going of the various devas is boundless;
second, the coming and going of the various devas is unimpeded."
Third, the movements of the devas are neither slow nor rapid;
fourth, the footsteps of the devas leave no tracks;
fifth, the bodies of the devas are free from affliction and fatigue.
Sixth, the bodies of the devas have form but cast no shadows;
seventh, the devas have neither excrement nor urine;
eighth, the bodies of the devas produce neither mucus nor saliva.
Ninth, the bodies of the devas are pure and subtle, being devoid of fat, marrow, skin, flesh, blood, sinews, bones, veins, and the like;

tenth, the bodies of the devas can manifest as long or short, blue, yellow, red, or white, large or small, coarse or fine, according to their will—all of them being upright, most excellent and marvelous, and causing all who behold them to feel love and joy.
The bodies of the various devas possess these ten kinds of inconceivable qualities.
O bhikṣus! Furthermore, the bodies of the various devas are replete and not hollow; they are entirely level and full.
His teeth were white, square, and closely set; his hair was blue-black and perfectly even.
It was soft and lustrous, and his body naturally radiated light.
Possessing supernormal powers, he could soar through the void, and his eyes did not blink.
Their necklaces are natural and their garments are free from dust and grease. "O Bhikṣus!
The people of Jambudvīpa have a lifespan of one hundred years, though there are those who die prematurely within that span."
The people of Aparagoyānī have a lifespan of two hundred years, though there are also those who die prematurely;
the people of Pūrvavideha have a lifespan of three hundred years, though there are also those who die prematurely;
the people of Uttarakuru have a fixed lifespan of one thousand years, with no premature deaths.
The sentient beings in the world of Yama have a lifespan of seventy-two thousand years, yet there are also those who die prematurely;
the various nāgas and garuḍas have a lifespan of one kalpa, yet there are also those who die prematurely;
the lifespan of the asuras is equal to a thousand celestial years, yet they also die prematurely in the interim.
The life span of the gods of the Four Great Kings is five hundred years, though there are also those who die prematurely;
the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three have a life span of one thousand years;
and the gods of the Yāma Heaven have a life span of two thousand years.
The gods of Tuṣita Heaven have a lifespan of four thousand years;
the gods of Nirmāṇarati Heaven have a lifespan of eight thousand years;
and the gods of Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven have a lifespan of sixteen thousand years.
The gods of the Māra-kāyika heaven have a lifespan of thirty-two thousand years;
the gods of the Brahma-kāyika heaven have a lifespan of one kalpa;
and the gods of the Ābhāsvara heaven have a lifespan of two kalpas.
The gods of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven have a lifespan of four kalpas;
the gods of the Bṛhatphala Heaven have a lifespan of eight kalpas;
and the gods of the Asaṃjñisattva Heaven have a lifespan of sixteen kalpas.
The gods of the Heaven Without Heat have a lifespan of one thousand kalpas;
the gods of the Heaven Without Affliction have a lifespan of two thousand kalpas;
the gods of the Heaven of Good Vision have a lifespan of three thousand kalpas.
The gods of the Sudṛśa Heaven have a lifespan of four thousand kalpas;
the gods of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven have a lifespan of five thousand kalpas;
the gods of the Ākāśānantyāyatana Heaven have a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas.
The gods of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness have a lifespan of twenty-one thousand kalpas;
the gods of the Sphere of Nothingness have a lifespan of forty-two thousand kalpas;
and the gods of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception have a lifespan of eighty-four thousand kalpas.
During that interval, all will meet with untimely death. "O Bhikṣus!
The people of Jambudvīpa are three and a half cubits in height; their robes are seven cubits in width and three and a half cubits in length."
The inhabitants of Aparagoyānī and Pūrvavideha are equal in body size and clothing to those of Jambudvīpa.
As for the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, their bodies are seven cubits tall; their garments are fourteen cubits in width and seven cubits in height and length.
The bodies of the asuras are one yojana long; their garments are two yojanas in width and one yojana in height and length, weighing half a kāliśa.
The bodies of the Four Heavenly Kings are half a *yojana* in height; their garments are one *yojana* in width and half a *yojana* in length, with a weight of one *kāliśa*.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are one *yojana* in height; their garments are two *yojanas* in width and one *yojana* in length, with a weight of half a *kāliśa*.
The gods of the Yāma Heaven are two *yojanas* in height; their garments are four *yojanas* in width and two *yojanas* in length, with a weight of one-quarter of a *kāliśa*.
In the Tuṣita Heaven, the height of the body is four yojanas; the width of the garment is eight yojanas, and its length is four yojanas;

its weight is one-eighth of a karṣa. In the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the height of the body is eight yojanas; the width of the garment is sixteen yojanas, and its length is eight yojanas; its weight is one-sixteenth of a karṣa.

In the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the height of the body is sixteen yojanas; the width of the garment is thirty-two yojanas, and its length is sixteen yojanas; its weight is one-thirty-second of a karṣa.
The gods within the body of Māra are thirty-two yojanas in height; their robes are sixty-four yojanas wide and thirty-two yojanas long from top to bottom, yet weigh only one sixty-fourth of a karīṣa.
From this point upward, the height of the bodies of the various devas is exactly equal to their robes, without any difference. "O Bhikṣus!
Regarding all the commercial transactions of the people of Jambudvīpa, they are conducted either with money and wealth, or with grain and silk, or with living beings."
The people of Aparagoyānī engage in trade for their desires, using either cattle and sheep or *maṇi* jewels;
the people of Pūrvavideha, when conducting market transactions, use either wealth and silk, or the five grains, or *maṇi* jewels;
as for the people of Uttarakuru, they have no market trading, for all that they desire appears spontaneously.
"O Bhikṣus!
The people of Jambudvīpa, Aparagoyānī, and Pūrvavideha all have the customs of men marrying and women being wedded;
however, among the people of Uttarakuru, there is no sense of 'I' or 'mine. When the branches of trees bend down, the men and women unite; they have no system of marriage."
"O Bhikṣus!
Among the nāgas, garuḍas, and asuras, marriage and wedding ceremonies are, in brief, exactly like those of human beings.

The gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita heaven, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, and the Māra-kāyika gods all likewise have marriages and weddings; in brief, they are as described previously."
From this point upward, among those various devas, there is no longer any distinction between marriage or the sexes of male and female. "O Bhikṣus!
When the people of Jambudvīpa engage in sexual desire, their two organs meet and impurity is emitted; [but for the higher devas, it is not so]."
The people of Aparagoyānī, Pūrvavideha, and the inhabitants of Uttarakuru are all exactly like those of Jambudvīpa.
As for all the nāgas and garuḍas, when they engage in sexual desire, their two organs also meet; however, they satisfy their passion merely by emitting wind, and there is no impurity.

The asuras, the gods of the Four Great Kings, and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven engage in desire with their organs meeting; they satisfy their passion by emitting wind, just like the nāga kings and the garuḍas, being in every way identical and without difference.
The gods of the Yāma Heaven fulfill their desire by holding hands;
those of the Tuṣita Heaven fulfill their desire by mere thought;
and the gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven fulfill their desire by gazing intently.
In the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, desire is fulfilled through conversation;
among the various heavens of the Māra realm, desire is fulfilled by gazing at one another;
in all these cases, their hearts are fully satisfied, thereby accomplishing their sensual desires.
“Monks! Regarding the human world, the light of a firefly is not equal to the light of a lamp;
the light of a lamp, in turn, is not equal to the light of a torch.”
The brilliance of that torch-fire is not equal to the brilliance of that mass of fire;
the brilliance of that mass of fire does not equal the radiance of the stars and constellations in the heavens;
and the radiance of those stars and constellations, in turn, does not equal the brilliance of that lunar palace.
The brilliance of the lunar palace does not equal the radiance of the solar palace;
the illuminating radiance of the solar palace, in turn, does not equal the brilliance of the walls, palaces, and bodily ornaments of the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings;
and all the various radiances of the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings do not equal the radiance possessed by the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
The radiance of all the gods in the Heaven of the Thirty-three does not equal the radiance of the walls, palaces, and necklaces of the gods in the Yāma Heaven;
the various lights of the Yāma Heaven do not equal the radiance possessed by the Tuṣita Heaven;
and the various luminosities of the Tuṣita Heaven, in turn, do not equal the radiance of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
The radiance of all the gods in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations does not equal that of the gods in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations;
and the radiance of those in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations, in turn, does not equal the radiance of the body of Māra.
Compared to those below, the light from the walls, palaces, and necklaces of Māra’s body is most supreme, most exquisite, and uniquely unsurpassed.
“O bhikṣus! Those gods of the Māra-body realm do not equal those of the Brahma-body realm;
those of the Brahma-body realm, in turn, do not equal those of the Ābhāsvara (Radiant) realm.”
When that light is compared to the light of the Śubhakṛtsna devas, it does not equal theirs;
when the light of those Śubhakṛtsna devas is compared to the light of the Bṛhatphala devas, it does not equal theirs.

Regarding those gods of the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala) Heaven, this is a brief description; the same applies to the gods of the Untroubled Heat (Avṛha), Good Vision (Sudarśana), Good Appearance (Sudṛśa), and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. With the sole exception of their necklaces, everything else should be understood as previously described.
"O Bhikṣus!

Whether it be the world of devas, or the various Māras and Brahmās, or śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, or any other light existing in the world—if one wishes to compare them with the light of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, even hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Ganges-sands of such lights cannot be compared to it."
This light of the Tathāgata is most excellent, most wondrous, extraordinary, and supreme.
Why is this so? O bhikṣus!

The body of that Tathāgata—his immeasurable ethical conduct (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*); his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the practice of supernormal powers; his teaching (*deśanā*) and the wheel of teaching; and his locus of discourse (*deśanā-sthāna*) and the wheel of discourse—is in each case immeasurable and boundless.
"O Bhikṣus!
The Tathāgata possesses such immeasurable merits, fully endowed with all dharmas.
For this reason, the radiance of the Tathāgata is supreme and unsurpassed; you should uphold it as such."
“Monks! All sentient beings have four kinds of nutriment, which sustain the great elements so that they may endure, bring about existence, and provide mutual support.”
What are the four?
First, coarse and subtle edible food; second, contact-food; third, volition-food; and fourth, consciousness-food.
Which sentient beings should consume coarse morsel food and subtle food? O Bhikṣus!
The people of Jambudvīpa eat rice, parched grain, beans, fish, meat, and the like; these are called coarse morsel food.
Massaging, bathing, rubbing, and the application of oils and ointments—all these are termed subtle food.
As for the people of Aparagoyānī and Pūrvavideha, their coarse and subtle food is, in brief, similar to that of Jambudvīpa mentioned previously.
As for the people of Uttarakuru, they do not engage in plowing or sowing; rather, naturally ripened non-glutinous rice appears of its own accord, which they consume as coarse food.
Covering themselves [with leaves], bathing, and massage serve as their subtle nourishment.
“O monks! For all the nāgas and garuḍas, fish, turtles, tortoises, crocodiles, frogs, *qiuliu*, *chichi*, snakes, otters, *kumbhīra*s, and so forth constitute their coarse food;
various coverings and such constitute their subtle food.”
The various asuras take the exquisite flavor of the celestial *sudhā* as coarse food,
while they regard things such as coverings as subtle food.
The Cāturmahārājika devas and the other classes of devas all take that celestial *sudhā* flavor as their coarse food.
For the various covering beings and others, these are considered subtle.
For the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the essence of ambrosia (*sūdā-rasa*) constitutes their coarse food;
for the various covering beings and others, these are considered subtle.

To speak briefly, it is like the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; likewise, the Yāma Heaven, Tuṣita Heaven, Nirmāṇarati Heavens, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heavens all take the flavor of celestial *sudhā* as their coarse food, while various garments serve as their subtle food.

From this point upward, the various classes of devas all take the joy of dhyāna and the delight of the Dharma as their food; they take samādhi as their food and samāpatti as their food, no longer consuming coarse morsels or subtle nutriment.
“Monks! What kind of sentient beings take contact as nutriment? Monks!”
