There are sentient beings who are born from eggs—namely, geese, wild geese, swans, cranes, chickens, ducks, peacocks, parrots, mynas, doves, pigeons, sparrows, quails, magpies, and other such various species of sentient beings born from eggs. Because they possess these bodies by virtue of being born from eggs, all of them take touch as their food.
What kind of sentient beings take volition as their food?

If there are sentient beings who, through mental volition, nourish and moisten their sense faculties and increase their physical life—namely fish, turtles, snakes, frogs, and *kārakūṭas*, as well as all other classes of sentient beings who, through mental volition, benefit their sense faculties and increase their life—all such beings take volition as their food.
What kind of sentient beings take consciousness as their nutriment?
They are the various classes of sentient beings in the hells, as well as the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness and others.
All such sentient beings employ consciousness, taking it as their sustenance.
"O bhikṣus!
These four kinds of nutriment sustain the great elements of sentient beings and bring about their birth.
Regarding this, there is an udāna verse:"
"Flower-colors and all dharmas, lifespan and clothing as the fifth,
buying and selling, marriage, the two organs, and food make ten. O Bhikṣus!"
All sentient beings in the world possess these three kinds of unwholesome conduct. What are the three?
They are namely: bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct.
"O bhikṣus!

There is a certain class of beings who, having committed misconduct of body, speech, and mind, and having acted in such a manner, will—on account of those causes and conditions—at the breaking up of the body after death, fall into an evil destination and be born in hell."
In this process, as the final consciousness ceases there, the consciousness that first arises in continuity within the hell realms comes into being.
Simultaneously with that consciousness, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) arises; and conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) arise.

“Monks! Furthermore, there is another kind of person who, having committed evil deeds of body, speech, and mind, because of those causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, falls into an evil destination and is reborn among the animals.”
Within this process, when the final consciousness ceases there, the consciousness of a being among animals arises for the first time in succession.
At the very moment that consciousness arises, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) exists simultaneously; conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) arise.

“Monks! Furthermore, there is another kind of person who, having committed misconduct of body, speech, and mind, because of those causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, falls into an evil destination and is born in the world of Yama.”
In this process, when the final consciousness of that [person] ceases, the first moment of consciousness in the world of Yama arises in succession.
At the very moment that consciousness first arises, it simultaneously co-arises with name-and-form (nāmarūpa). Conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) arise.
"Monks! These are called the three kinds of unwholesome conduct;
they should be avoided. Monks!"
Furthermore, there are three kinds of wholesome conduct in the world.
What are these three? They are namely:
wholesome conduct of body, and wholesome conduct of speech and mind.

"Monks! There is a certain class of beings who perform wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind; having practiced in this way, by reason of those causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in the human realm."
There, at this point, the final consciousness ceases, and within the human realm, consciousness first arises in continuous succession.
At the very moment that consciousness first arises, it is born simultaneously with name-and-form (nāmarūpa). Because of name-and-form as a condition, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) arise.

“Monks! There is another type who, having performed wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, by reason of those causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, is reborn in a heavenly realm. There, consciousness ceases in this place, and the initial continuity of consciousness arises in that heavenly realm.”
When that consciousness arises, it simultaneously co-arises with name-and-form; because there is name-and-form, the six sense bases arise. Monks!
Among those in the heavens, whether as a celestial son or a celestial daughter, they are born while sitting cross-legged, or between the knees, the thighs, and the groin.
When first emerging, its form is like that of a twelve-year-old human child.
If it is a male deva, it is born upon the lap of a deva;
if it is a female deva, it is born within the thighs of a celestial jade maiden.
Once they have been born in this way, those devas immediately claim, "These are my children. It should be understood in this manner:
"O bhikṣus! For those who cultivate merit and are reborn in heaven, such is the law."
When they are first born, those devas and devīs, conditioned by the latencies of their own karmic causes, give rise to three kinds of thoughts:

first, they know from where they have died; second, they know that they are now born in this place; and third, they know what karma produced this birth and what meritorious reward it is, realizing, "Having had my body and life perish in that place, I have come to be born here."
Furthermore, he reflects thus:
"It is because of these three kinds of karmic fruits and the ripening of these three kinds of karma that I have come to be born here.
What are the three?"
That is to say: wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind.
Because the retribution of these three types of action has matured, at the breaking up of the body after death, they have come to this place.
Again, he formed this thought:
"May I, having died here now, be reborn among humans.
Having been thus reborn there, I shall once again cultivate wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind."
"Because I have practiced wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, after the dissolution of this body, I have returned to this life.
Having formed this thought, he immediately began to think of food.
When he thinks of food, there appear before him various jeweled vessels, naturally filled with celestial *sūdā* flavors, manifesting in all their variety.
Among the devas, if there is one who is superior, the flavor of that *sudhā* is of the whitest color;
if the deva is of middling karmic retribution, the flavor of that *sudhā* is red;
and if there is a deva of inferior merit, the flavor of that *sudhā* appears black.

At that time, the deva-son took celestial *sudhā* with his hand and placed it in his mouth; once the *sudhā* had entered the deva’s mouth, it immediately and gradually melted away and transformed of its own accord.
For example, if clarified butter or fresh butter is cast into a fire, it immediately melts away, leaving no form or shadow behind.
In this very same way, when the divine *sūdhā* flavor is placed in the mouth, it is naturally digested; it is just like that.

Having eaten the *sūdā*, if they become thirsty, there appears before them a celestial jewel-vessel filled with celestial wine. According to the superior, middling, or inferior merit [of the beings], it is white, red, or black in color; as briefly described previously, it enters the mouth and is digested, and its melting away is likewise.

At that time, when that devaputra had finished eating and drinking, his body—its proportions from head to toe, large and small—became exactly like those of the other long-resident devaputras and devakanyās.
“O monks! When the bodies of the devas and devīs have become full, they each go toward the edge of a pond according to their inclination.
Having reached the edge of the pond, they enter within that pool to bathe and purify themselves, experiencing joy and pleasure.”
Having emerged from the pond, he went to the side of the fragrant tree.

At that time, the branches of that fragrant tree naturally lowered, and various kinds of exquisite perfumes issued forth from within them, flowing into his hands; he immediately applied them to his body.

He proceeded again to the tree of garments; having arrived, just as before, it also bent down for him, and from within that tree there emerged various kinds of exquisite and wonderful garments. Once they reached his hands, he took them and put them on.
Having finished dressing, he went to the necklace-tree; it lowered itself in this manner until the ornaments flowed down into his hands, which he then fastened or put on to adorn his body.
Thus, they proceed again to the Mālya trees; as before, these bend low and flow forth various exquisite flower garlands.

Having taken them to adorn their heads, they then go toward the Bhājana trees, from which emerge various vessels made of diverse jewels that enter their hands according to their wishes. Taking these, they go to the Phala grove, where they fill them with various fruits, either eating them immediately or taking their juice to drink.

Proceeding thus, he went to the side of the musical-instrument trees; these trees also bent low, spontaneously producing various kinds of musical instruments. Taking them as he pleased, he either plucked, struck, sang, or danced; the sounds were exquisite and subtle, and he then proceeded toward the grove.
Having entered the garden, he immediately beheld therein countless, boundless hundreds, thousands, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of celestial maidens.
If one has not yet seen the woman, one possesses the knowledge and vision of past lives regarding karmic retribution:
"From what place did I come to be born here? Just as this body of mine now undergoes this retribution."
Because the fruits of their karma have ripened, at this time they clearly and distinctly remember their past lives as plainly as looking at the palm of one's hand.

Yet, upon seeing the celestial maidens and becoming infatuated with their forms, their wisdom of right mindfulness and discernment immediately perishes. Having lost their memory of their previous births, they become attached to present desires and cry out only:
"O celestial jade maiden!"
"O celestial jade maidens!
This is what is called the bond of sensual craving. Monks!
This is what is called the three kinds of wholesome conduct. "O Bhikṣus!

Within a single month, there are six upoṣadhas—upoṣadha (Sui: 'observing the fast,' also translated as 'increasing')—five days during the waxing moon and likewise five days during the waning moon. Thus, in these two months, the bright and the dark, there are three days for observing the fast in each."
What are the three days for observing the uposatha in the bright fortnight?
They are the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month.
The dark fortnight likewise has three days for observing the uposatha, corresponding in number to those of the bright fortnight.
What is meant by saying that in each of the two months—the bright and the dark—there are three days on which one observes the fast and precepts?
O Bhikṣus! In each of the two months, the bright and the dark, there are eight such days.
On that day, the Four Great Kings gathered their retinues and addressed them, saying:

"You should go and observe the four directions thoroughly: are there any among the people in this world who practice filial piety extensively, who support their parents, and who show reverence to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas?"
Do you revere and honor your elders and superiors?
Do you practice giving and observe the precepts?
Do you maintain the eightfold abstinences and observe the six fast days?

At that time, after the Four Heavenly Kings had thus instructed their messengers, those messengers, in accordance with the command of the heavenly kings, respectfully set out and descended to survey all the people of the world: in whose household do parents receive filial support;
which clans honor śramaṇas, brahmins, and others;
and in whose family do sons and daughters reverently serve their elders?
Who practices giving;
who observes the six fast days;
and who maintains the eight precepts?
"Who upholds the virtue of the precepts?
At that time, the messenger thus traveled throughout the world to observe.

He saw that among human beings, those who are filial and serve their parents are few; those who attend upon and honor śramaṇas are few; those who revere elder brāhmaṇas and show veneration toward elders are also few; their giving is meager, their observance of the fasts is infrequent, their protection of the precepts is incomplete, and their self-restraint is full of deficiencies.
At that time, having seen this, the celestial messenger immediately went to the abode of the Four Heavenly Kings and addressed them, saying:

"O Heavenly Kings, you should know that among all the people in the world, there are few who practice filial piety and support their parents; there are none who show much reverence to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; there are none who show much respect and honor to their elders, seniors, and those of virtue; there are none who extensively practice giving or observe the six fast days; and there are none who extensively uphold the prohibitive precepts or maintain the eightfold abstinences."
At that time, having heard these words from the messengers, the Four Great Heavenly Kings felt a sense of sorrow in their hearts and were not at all joyful. They replied to the messengers, saying:
"If it is indeed so in those worlds, then those people are most unwholesome."
Why is this so? The lifespan of human beings is extremely short;
living for but a brief time, one should cultivate all manner of wholesome deeds, so that in the next world one may attain peace and happiness.

Why is it that people in this world today do not practice filial piety and support for their parents to any great extent, and are even unable to observe the six fast days and the eight prohibitions to restrain their bodies and speech?
"This will greatly diminish my assembly of devas and cause the race of asuras to increase further and further.

Monks, if in that world many people are respectful and filial toward their parents, honor śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and other elders, practice generosity, delight in observing the six fast days, diligently establish meritorious deeds, and constantly maintain the eight prohibitions— if such things continue in succession— [the asuras will decline].
At that time, the celestial messengers, having observed this during their patrol, reported to the Four Great Kings:

"Your Majesties should know that among the people of the world, there are many who are filial and obedient toward their parents; many who show reverence to śramaṇas, brahmins, and their elders; and who delight in practicing generosity and diligently cultivate the merit of fasting."
At that time, when the Four Great Heavenly Kings heard these words from their messengers, their hearts were filled with great joy and they leaped for immeasurable delight, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! How most virtuous and noble it is that the people of the world are able to practice in such a manner."
Why is this? Those people have short lifespans and will soon pass on to the next world.

Yet now, amidst that human realm, they are able to provide filial support to their parents, respectfully serve śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the elders, take great pleasure in practicing generosity, and maintain the precepts and observe the fasts.
"In this way, the immeasurable retinues of the devas shall increase, while the classes of asuras shall diminish. "Monks,
what are the fourteenth days of the two months, the dark and the bright, that constitute the upoṣadha day?"
"O Bhikṣus!

On the fourteenth day of both the dark and light fortnights of each month, the Four Great Kings likewise summon the four Crown Princes of the heavens, causing them to descend and observe the extent of good and evil among beings, rejoicing or feeling sorrowful. A brief account of this is entirely as that which was spoken by the celestial messengers; the only difference is that it is the Crown Princes who descend in person."
"O Bhikṣus!
On the fifteenth day of both the dark and light fortnights, during the Upavasatha,
the Four Great Kings descend from their worlds in person to examine the good and evil [of beings]."

Having ascertained the extent [of these matters], he immediately went in person to the Sudharmā Hall, arriving at the assembly where the devas gather for discussion. Reaching the front of the hall, he faced Śakra and recounted the various matters of human good and evil, their frequency and their conformity or opposition.
At that time, Śakra heard that those among humans who cultivate merit were few; he immediately became somber and dejected, feeling unhappy as he thought, "How can this be?
The celestial hosts are diminishing, while the asuras are increasing."
If they hear that there are many among the human realm who act in accordance with the Dharma, they will rejoice and leap for joy immeasurably, saying:
"The assembly of our devas shall gradually increase."
Because on the sixth day of both the dark and bright fortnights, the various devas descend to observe the good and evil among humans, this day is named Upoṣadha.
*Qishi yinben jing*, Scroll Seven;
*Qishi yinben jing*, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Dharmagupta of the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on the Heaven of the Thirty-three, Part Two: “O Bhikṣus!
If at some time various followers of external paths, or perhaps Pāribbājaka wanderers, should come to your place and ask you, saying: "O elders!..."
For what cause and for what reason does one kind of person become terrified by non-human beings,
while another kind of person is not terrified by those same non-human beings?
"Regarding those non-Buddhists who ask such questions, you should respond to them as follows:
'Venerable elders! There is a cause and condition for this.'"

Why is this? Within the world, there is a class of people who habitually practice what is contrary to the Dharma; they possess false views and inverted views. Having practiced the ten unwholesome paths of action, spoken of unwholesome dharmas, and contemplated unwholesome dharmas, they are characterized by false views and inversion.
Because they have committed these ten unwholesome deeds, the deities who protect living beings gradually abandon them.
Of such a group, whether numbering a hundred or a thousand, only a single deity remains to provide general protection.
It is like a herd of cattle or a flock of sheep, numbering perhaps a hundred or a thousand, with only a single person standing by their side to guard them.
In just this way, because the protective deities are few, they are constantly terrified by non-human beings.
There is a certain class of people whose speech accords with the Dharma, who do not practice wrong views, and who do not hold perverted views.

Since they practice these ten wholesome actions, possessing right view and right speech, and cultivate virtuous karma, for each and every one of them, there come to be immeasurable—perhaps hundreds of thousands—of spirits who arrive together to provide protection.
By these causes and conditions, this person will not be terrified by non-human beings.
It is like a king or a royal minister, each of whom is guarded by a retinue of hundreds or thousands of attendants.
"O bhikṣus! Among the people of the world, there are those with such surnames and names; likewise, among the non-human beings, there are also various such names."
"O bhikṣus!

Among humans, there are mountains, forests, rivers, marshes, kingdoms, cities, towns, villages, hamlets, and dwelling places. Likewise, among non-humans, there are also such things as the names of houses and the seats of various kings."

“O bhikṣus! In all the streets, crossroads, winding alleys, and the like; whether in slaughterhouses or empty caves—none of these are devoid of life, for they are all abodes where various deities and non-human beings dwell.
Furthermore, within the valleys of the śītavana cemeteries and along the paths frequented by fierce beasts, there are likewise non-human beings.”
"Monks! In all trees, if they are one fathom in height and one foot in circumference, there are deities who dwell upon them, making them *caityas*."
In all the worlds, whether they be men or women, from the time of their birth until death, there are various celestial deities who constantly follow them wherever they go, never departing from them.
They only abandon it when they habitually practice evil or at the time of death; this brief explanation is as above.
"O Bhikṣus! The people of Jambudvīpa excel those of Godānīya in five respects."
What are these five? First, valor and strength;

second, right mindfulness; third, Jambudvīpa being the place where Buddhas appear in the world; fourth, Jambudvīpa being the land for cultivating practice; and fifth, Jambudvīpa being the place for practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
As for Aparagoyānī, it surpasses the people of Jambudvīpa in three respects.
What are these three?
First, abundance of cattle; second, abundance of sheep; third, abundance of mani-jewels in Aparagoyānī.
As for Jambudvīpa, it has five kinds of superiority over the people of Pūrvavideha, as briefly described above.
Pūrvavideha surpasses the people of Jambudvīpa in three respects.
What are these three?
First, because that continent is most exceedingly vast; second, because that continent extensively encompasses various sub-continents; and third, because that continent is most exquisite and subtle.
In Jambudvīpa, there are five matters in which it excels Uttarakuru; these five are as described above.
In Uttarakuru, there are three matters in which it excels Jambudvīpa.
What are the three?
First, that person is without the notions of "self" or "what belongs to self"; second, because their lifespan is exceedingly long; and third, because that person possesses superior practice.
In this Jambudvīpa, there are five matters in which its inhabitants surpass the various beings of the world of Yama, as previously described;
conversely, in the world of Yama, there are three matters in which its inhabitants surpass those of Jambudvīpa.
What are these three?
First, a long lifespan; second, a large physical form; third, the possession of natural clothing and food for sustenance.
Humans of Jambudvīpa have five kinds of superiority over nāgas and garuḍas, as previously described.
The nāgas and garuḍas possess three kinds of superiority over the people of Jambudvīpa.
What are these three?
First, their lifespan is long; second, their physical forms are large; and third, their palaces are vast.
The people of Jambudvīpa surpass the asuras in five respects, as previously described;
however, the asuras surpass the people of Jambudvīpa in three respects.
What are these three?
First, long life; second, superior physical form; and third, abundant experience of pleasure. These three matters are the most excellent.

“Monks! The gods of the Four Great Kings possess three things by which they excel: first, their palaces are lofty; second, their palaces are exquisite; third, their palaces possess the most excellent radiance.
The gods of the Thirty-three Heavens likewise possess three things by which they excel.”
What are these three?
First, long life; second, superior physical form; and third, abundant pleasure.

Just as with the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, one should know that the Yāma Heaven, Tuṣita Heaven, Nirmāṇarati Heaven, Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and the Māra-body Heavens likewise all possess these three kinds of excellence, just as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven excels the people of Jambudvīpa.
"In that Jambudvīpa, there are five kinds of beings who surpass the various classes of devas, as described above; you should know this by answering.
O Bhikṣus! Within these three realms, there are thirty-eight classes of sentient beings."
What are these thirty-eight kinds?
O monks! Within the realm of desire there are twelve kinds; within the realm of form there are twenty-two kinds; and within the formless realm there are four kinds.
"O monks! Among these, what are the twelve types of the desire realm? They are:

hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, asuras, the gods of the Four Great Kings, the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, and the Māra-kāyika gods; these are called the twelve."
What are the twenty-two types within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)?

They are: the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Brahmakāyika, Mahābrahmā, Ābhāsvara, Parīttābhā, Apramāṇābhā, Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Bṛhatphala, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Bṛhatphala, Asaṃjñisattva, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha. These twenty-two belong to the realm of form.

As for the four types within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they are the Heaven of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), the Heaven of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); these four categories belong to the formless realm.
“Monks! In this world, there are four kinds of clouds: white clouds, black clouds, red clouds, and yellow clouds. Monks!”
Among these four types, white clouds contain a predominance of the earth element;
black clouds contain a predominance of the water element;
and red clouds contain a predominance of the fire element.
"Where there are yellow clouds, there is an abundance of the wind element.
You should understand it in this way, monks!"
Furthermore, there are four kinds of great deities in the world. What are these four?
They are the great deity Earth, the great deity Water, the great deity Fire, and the great deity Wind.
"O Bhikṣus!
Once upon a time, the great earth deity Pṛthivī gave rise to this evil view, thinking to herself:
'Within the element of earth, there is no water element, fire element, or wind element.'"
"O monks! At that time, I went to the presence of that earth deity and said to that great earth deity:
'O Deva, do you truly hold such a wrong view as to claim that within the earth element there are no three other great elements—water, fire, and wind?'"
He replied to me, saying,
"It is truly so, World-Honored One.
I then spoke again, saying:
"O Deva, do not hold such an evil view. Why is this?
Within that earth element, there truly exist the water, fire, and wind elements."
"However, within that [aggregate], the earth element is the most predominant; therefore, the earth element alone receives the name. Monks!

I was able to know that the Great Deva Mahāpathavī had conceived such a thought, and I severed his wrong view, causing him to rejoice. Amidst all defilements, he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, realized the fruit and the path of awakening, became free from fetters and delusions, crossed to the further shore beyond doubt, was no longer subject to afflictions, did not rely on the teachings of others, and followed the practice of the Dharma in accordance with reality.
And he said to me:
"Venerable World-Honored One!
I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha."
"Venerable World-Honored One!
From this day forward, until the end of my life, I shall uphold the precepts of an upāsikā; I shall no longer commit killing, stealing, or other unrighteous acts."
"Take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and maintain them with purity. Monks!
On another occasion, the great water deity likewise had such a thought and gave rise to a wrong view, saying:
"In the water element, there is no earth element, nor fire or wind elements.
I understood his meaning, went to him, and asked the Deva Water: "Is it truly so?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
I spoke to him again:
“O Deva, do not hold such an evil view; within this water element, there are entirely the earth, fire, and wind elements. This was likewise said to the Deva of Fire and the Deva of Wind.
All of them held this same view. Having known this, the Buddha went to each of them and questioned them, and they all replied to the Buddha:
“It is truly so, World-Honored One.”

The Buddha opened their minds, and they all attained awakening and understanding; they took refuge in the Triple Gem and practiced in accordance with it entirely. A brief account is as previously described for the Earth Deity Mahādeva; only the one who had his doubts removed came to my side.
"Monks! These are called the four great deities. Monks!"
In the world there are clouds that rise from the earth and remain in the midst of space; some remain at a distance of one *krośa*, or two or three *krośas*, up to six or seven *krośas*.
"O Bhikṣus!
Furthermore, there are clouds that abide one yojana above in the empty sky, or two, three, four, up to five, six, or seven yojanas."
"O bhikṣus!

Furthermore, there may be clouds that remain suspended in the upper reaches of space at a height of one hundred yojanas, or even two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or up to a hundred yojanas."

Furthermore, there may be clouds that abide in the sky above the earth at a distance of one thousand yojanas, or two, three, four, five, six, or seven thousand yojanas, remaining there until the end of the kalpa.
“Monks! At times, a non-Buddhist named Pāribhājaka may come to you and ask this question:
‘Venerable sirs!’”
"By what causes and conditions does this sound arise within the clouds in the void?
"O bhikṣus! You should answer in this way:"
"There are three causes and conditions, through their mutual contact, that cause a sound to issue forth from within the mass of empty clouds.
What are these three?
O Venerable Elders!"
There may be a time when the wind element within the clouds comes into contact with the earth element, and because of this mutual friction, a sound spontaneously arises. Why is this so?
Just as fire is produced when the branches of trees rub against one another, even so, venerable elders,
this is the first causal condition for the production of sound.
Furthermore, Venerable One!

There may be a time when the wind element within the clouds rubs against the water element; because of this mutual friction, a sound naturally arises, just as described above. This is the second causal condition for the production of sound.
Furthermore, Venerable One!

There may be a time when the wind element within the clouds rubs against the fire element; because of this mutual friction, a sound naturally arises. To speak briefly, it is like two trees rubbing together until fire is produced. This is the third cause and condition for the arising of sound.
One should answer in this way. O bhikṣus!
You too should thus understand through detailed analysis.
“Monks! At some time, a non-Buddhist parivrājaka may come to you and ask this question:
‘Venerable sirs!’”
"By what causes and conditions does a sudden radiance arise as lightning within the clouds in the void?
"O bhikṣus! You should answer in this way:"
“Venerable elders!
There are two causes and conditions by which lightning flashes arise from within the clouds in the void.
What are these two?
First, there is lightning in the east, named Wu-hou (No Thickness);
in the south there is lightning, named Shun-liu (Following the Current);
in the west there is lightning, named Duo-guangming (Falling Radiance).
In the north there is lightning named Hundred-Birth Tree.
Venerable elders!

Furthermore, there may be a time when a thick flash of lightning from the east and a luminous flash of lightning from the west meet, coalesce, rub against one another, and strike each other. Because of this, light is produced from within the masses of clouds in the sky, which is called lightning; this is the first causal condition for lightning.
Furthermore, venerable elders!

If a flash of lightning from the south, moving with the current, were to encounter, adhere to, rub against, and strike a hundred flashes of lightning from the north, it would be because of such an occurrence that electric light is produced.

For example, when two pieces of wood rub together due to the wind, fire spontaneously emerges; once it has returned to its source, this is the second causal condition for lightning: light emerges from within a mass of clouds.

“Monks! In the sky, there are five causes and conditions that can obstruct the rain, such that the diviners cannot discern or know it, increasing their confusion; they predict that it must rain, yet the heavens do not send rain.”
What are these five? Monks!

There may be a time when, in the upper reaches of the sky, clouds arise and thunder rolls, producing the sounds "gaṭa gaṭa" and "gūchu gūchu"; or lightning flashes forth; or again, a cool, cold breeze blows. Such various phenomena as these are all signs of rain.
The diviners and astrologers all predicted that at this very time, rain would surely fall.
At that moment, Rāhu, the Asura King, emerged from his palace and, with both hands, seized those rain clouds and cast them into the ocean.
"O bhikṣus! This is the first cause and condition for the obstruction of rain.
Yet the astronomers and diviners do not see it, nor do they know it; their minds become filled with doubt, and though they record that the heavens will send rain, no rain eventually falls."
“Monks! There may be a time when clouds arise in the sky; within those clouds, there is the sound of ‘gaṭa gaṭa,’ lightning flashes forth, and a cool, cold breeze blows.”
At that time, the astronomers and diviners, having observed these signs, recorded that it would surely rain at that very moment.
Then, through the predominant power of the fire element, the rain clouds were incinerated and extinguished in that interval; this is called the second causal condition for the obstruction of rain.
Those astrologers, failing to see or understand this, become confused in their minds; they record that it will certainly rain, yet in the end it does not. "Monks!
There may be a time when clouds arise in the sky, and within those clouds there is the sound 'gaṭa gaṭa,' lightning flashes forth, and a cool, cold breeze blows."
At that time, the astronomers and diviners, having observed these signs, recorded that it was destined for rain at this very moment.

However, through the predominant power of the wind element, those clouds were blown away and cast onto the Kalinga desert, or cast onto the Tāṇḍaka desert, or cast onto the Maṇḍaga desert, or cast into the vast wilderness, or cast upon the sandy plains of Mālana; this is called the third cause and condition for the obstruction of rain.
Those astrologers, failing to see or understand this, become confused in mind; they predict that it will certainly rain, yet it does not rain. "Monks!
Furthermore, there is a time when clouds arise in the sky, and within those clouds, the sound 'gaṭa gaṭa' is made, lightning flashes forth, and cold breezes blow."
Regarding the prognostication of this, it is recorded that rain will certainly fall from heaven.

However, when those various devas who govern the rain become heedless, because of that heedlessness, those clouds are unable to bring down rain at the proper time. Since they do not fall at the proper time, the clouds naturally dissipate; this is the fourth causal condition for the obstruction of rain.
For this reason, the celestial astrologers become confused in their minds; they predict that it will certainly rain, yet in the end it does not. "Monks!
Furthermore, there are times when clouds arise in the sky, and the heavens produce the sound 'gaṭa gaṭa,' lightning flashes, and cool, cold winds blow."
Those astronomers have predicted that rain will surely fall.
Yet, among the people of this Jambudvīpa world, many act contrary to the Dharma; they are addicted to various sensual desires, mired in stinginess, greed, and envy, and are entangled by wrong views.
Because those people engage in evil conduct, practice what is contrary to the Dharma, are attached to sensual desires, and compete out of greed and envy, the heavens do not send down rain.
"O Bhikṣus! This is called the fifth cause and condition for obstructing rain.
Those who are experts in astronomy and divination do not see or know [this], and their minds become confused; they record that it will certainly rain, yet in the end it does not."
“Monks! These are called the five causes and conditions for the obstruction of rain.
Regarding this, there is a summary verse (udāna):”
Flowers, dharmas, form, and lifespan; clothing and buying and selling;
marriage, samādhi, and the four kinds of food and drink.
The two practices, the poṣadha, and the three realms named upper and lower.
The clouds and the various devas, etc., together with the *krośa*-sounding lightning.
Chapter Nine: On Battle. In the *Lokadhātunirdeśa-sūtra*, Chapter Nine, "On Battle," it says: "O Bhikṣus!..."
I recall that in the past, when the various devas were engaged in battle with the asuras, Śakra-devānām-indra addressed the thirty-two devas, saying:
"O worthy ones!..."
"You gods, when you engage in battle with the asuras, you should adorn yourselves well and take up your weapons skillfully.
If the gods are victorious and the asuras are defeated, you may seize the asura king Vemacitrin alive."
"Once he has been bound with the fivefold bonds, take him and place him before the Hall of Good Dharma, at the assembly site of the devas.
Having heard the command of Śakra, the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens followed it and carried it out.
At that time, the Asura King Vemacitra likewise addressed the Asuras, saying:

"If the devas fight with the Asuras and the devas are defeated, you must immediately seize King Śakra by force, bind him with the fivefold bonds, and lead him to the assembly place of the seven-headed Asuras, placing him before me."
At that time, the asuras also followed these instructions. O bhikṣus!

At that moment, because Śakra, King of the Devas, had won the battle, he captured the asuras alive, bound them with the fivefold bonds, and brought them before Śakra at the assembly hall of the Sudharmā deva-congregation.
At that time, King Vemacitra thought to himself:
"May all the asuras be at peace and well; I have no further need for these asuras."
"I am now here, together with the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens in one place, enjoying pleasures that are most delightful.
At the very moment King Vemacitra conceived this thought, he saw his fivefold bonds completely severed, and all the various merits of the five sensual desires of the gods appeared before him.
Furthermore, at times he thinks:
"I have no further need for the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
May all the devas remain safe and well; I shall return to the palace of the asuras."
"When he gave rise to this thought, his body was immediately bound again by the five fetters, and the merits of the five desires suddenly vanished. 'O bhikṣus!
That asura king Vemacitrin possesses such subtle fetters.'"
Those various bonds of Māra are even subtler than this.
Why is that? O bhikṣus!
When one engages in wrong reflection, one is immediately bound;
when one maintains right mindfulness, one is immediately liberated. Why is this so?
"O Bhikṣus!
To contemplate that there is a self is wrong contemplation;
to contemplate that there is no self is likewise wrong contemplation."

Even such reflections as "I shall be permanent," "I shall be impermanent," "I shall have form," "I shall be formless," "I shall have perception," "I shall be without perception," or "I shall be neither with nor without perception," are all erroneous thoughts.
"O monks! This wrong reflection is an abscess, it is a sore, and it is like a poisoned arrow.

Within this regard, the learned noble one who possesses wisdom recognizes this wrong reflection as being like a disease, like a sore, like an abscess, and like an arrow. Having reflected thus, he binds his mind in right mindfulness and does not follow the course of the mind; he makes the mind immovable, which brings great benefit."
"O monks! If one conceives of a self, that is a false conception, it is conditioned, and it is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

If one conceives of non-self, that too is conceptual proliferation. This extends to all things: whether with form or formless, with perception or without perception, or neither with nor without perception—all are conceptual proliferation."
"O monks! All conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is entirely a disease, like an abscess, like a wound, and like a poisoned arrow.
Within this regard, the learned noble ones who possess wisdom, having understood these various faults and dangers of conceptual proliferation, delight in the absence of conceptual proliferation."
Maintaining mental tranquility, one practices extensively. "O Bhikṣus!
I recall that in the past, when the celestial kings were about to engage in battle with the asuras, Śakra, the King of Devas, addressed the thirty-two devas of the four directions, saying: [...]"
"O worthy ones, you should properly prepare your bodies and all your weapons; now the asuras wish to come and fight.

If the devas are victorious, you may capture the asura king Vemacitrin alive, bind him with the fivefold bonds, and lead him before the Sudharmā Hall—the assembly place of the devas—to bring him into my presence."
The gods of the Thirty-three Heavens received the command of Śakra and carried it out accordingly.
The asuras were likewise instructed in this manner. O bhikṣus!
During that battle, the devas were victorious and bound the asuras with the fivefold bonds, leading them before the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā).

At that time, the asura king Vemacitrin, having been bound by the fivefold bonds in the presence of the celestial hosts, saw King Śakra entering the Hall of Good Dharma and taking his seat; he immediately spoke evil words, uttering various insults and slanders against the Lord of Devas.

The celestial king Śakra had a counselor named Mātali, who, seeing the asura Vemacitra addressing the Lord of Devas with harsh words and insults before the assembly, immediately addressed Śakra in verse:
"Is it out of shame or fear that the Heavenly King Śakra endures this, or is it because he lacks power?"
"Having heard such coarse and wicked abuse, he endured it all and remained silent.
At that time, Śakra replied to Mātali in verse:
"It is not out of shame or fear that I harbor patience, nor is it because I lack the power to overcome the asuras."
"Who can possess divine strategy and counsel like mine? How could I be the same as those who lack wisdom?
At that time, Mātali again addressed the Lord of Devas in verse, saying:
"If you do not strictly issue severe reprimands, The fire of folly will blaze even more intensely."
If one were to subdue those who lack wisdom, they would flee like oxen fearing the staff.
Now, by allowing them their pleasure, they become even more arrogant upon reaching their destination;
therefore, the wise display majesty to manifest their valor and sever their folly.
At that time, Śakra again answered Mātali in verse:
“I have long known such matters as these; it is for the sake of subduing the ignorance of men that they revile me with anger and hatred, yet upon hearing them, I am able to restrain my own mind.”
Then Mātali again addressed Śakra in verse, saying:
"O Śakra, King of Devas, pray consider this well: such forbearance has one drawback;
when that fool reviles me thus, he says, 'He is a coward, afraid and ashamed to speak.'"
At that time, Śakra again answered Mātali in verse:
“The foolish follow their own whims; thinking ‘I am afraid of them,’ they remain silent.
If one wishes to benefit oneself and seek profit and peace, one must practice patience toward such people.”
In my view, when faced with such abuse, one should not give rise to anger in response to anger;
to repay anger with anger toward an angry person—such a battle is difficult to win.
If one is tormented by others, it is difficult to possess the power to endure;
know that this patience is the most powerful, and such patience at such a time deserves praise.
Whether the mind is aroused by oneself or another, it seeks only rescue and deliverance from the place of great fear;
once one has been met with the anger and abuse of another, one should not give rise to resentment or hatred toward them.
If one should bring benefit to both oneself and others— these two parties—
and having recognized that another is angry, resentful, or abusive, one is able to cause one's own anger to be extinguished.
Thus, with a mind intent on benefiting these two parties— whether for oneself or for others—
if one considers another's thoughts to be deluded, it is because one does not understand the causes of phenomena.
If there are powerful men who can practice forbearance for the sake of those who are weak, such forbearing people are praised by others; they endure before the weak and do not give way to anger.
Because they lack the power of wisdom and possess only the power of delusion, they abandon the Dharma due to their folly; such people as these have no correct practice.

When the foolish mind gives rise to the thought "I am superior," and with anger one utters insults and coarse words, he who can endure those evils possesses constant victory; this excellence of patience is difficult to describe fully.
The Victorious One does not speak of fear regarding equal opponents, for he endures them lest enmity arise;
but as for those who can endure even when hearing the arguments of inferior opponents, this patience is praised by all the wise.
"O bhikṣus! You should know that at that time, Śakra was none other than myself.
At that time, I was the king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; I ruled with sovereign power, received superior karmic rewards, and enjoyed unrestrained happiness."
They constantly maintain patience and also praise patience; they delight in practicing gentleness and are free from anger, and they constantly praise those who are without anger. Monks!

However, you yourselves have now declared that in your practice there is a mind of faith and understanding; you have renounced worldly life to go forth as monastics, exerting yourselves with diligence and without slackening.

If you can, toward other sentient beings, practice patience, praise those who are patient, be disciplined, compassionate, and kind, always acting for their peace and happiness, eliminating anger, and praising those who are free from anger.
"O bhikṣus!
You, too, should train yourselves in this way.
O bhikṣus!"
I recall that in the past, when the hosts of devas and the asuras were each arraying their weapons, desiring to engage in battle,
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the assembly of devas,
saying: "O virtuous ones!..."
"If the Asuras engage in battle with the gods and the gods achieve victory, you must bind them with the fivefold fetters.
As previously described, the gods received these instructions and carried them out.
The Asura King likewise commanded his military hosts. Monks!
At that time, in the battle, the Asuras were victorious; Śakra, the Heavenly King, was terrified and fled back in retreat.
At that time, the charioteer turned the thousand-spoked, well-bred chariot, intending to head toward the celestial palace.
At that moment, there was a *kuṭaśālmali* tree upon which sat a king of the garuḍas; within its nest were many eggs.
Having seen this, Śakra addressed the charioteer Mātali, saying:
“Mātali, you know there are eggs upon the tree; Turn back the shafts of this chariot for my sake.
I would rather give up my life for the sake of the asuras than allow the nests of these birds to be destroyed.”

Then, having heard this command from the King of the Śakras, Mātali the skillful charioteer turned that thousand-spoked, noble, and well-tamed celestial chariot to the right, and set its course back toward the palace of the Asuras.
"O Bhikṣus!
At that time, when the Asuras saw Śakra’s chariot suddenly turn back, they said:
'Śakra has another tactical stratagem; he is coming again to fight.'"
The asuras retreated, each returning to their own palace.
Monks! At that time, through the causal conditions of Śakra’s compassion, the devas regained the victory and the asuras were defeated.
"O bhikṣus! If you wish to know who that Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was at that time, it is my very self now, O bhikṣus!"

At that time, I was the Lord of Devas, ruling over the Heaven of the Thirty-three with sovereign power and transforming it through my governance; yet, while receiving such superior karmic rewards, I was still able to feel compassion for all sentient beings, acting for their sake to benefit their lives and give rise to a heart of loving-kindness and pity.
"O bhikṣus, having left the household life out of faith, you should benefit all sentient beings.
Bhikṣus, I recall that in the past,
when the devas and asuras were about to engage in battle, Śakra then addressed the asura king Vimalacitra, saying:"
"O Benevolent One!
Let us first set aside our various weapons.
Among both the devas and the asuras, there are those who possess wisdom; they are all capable of knowing whether we are acting well or ill, and can explain the meaning of the various dharmas."
"However, the Elder shall prevail by means of virtuous words.
Thus the devas and the asuras vied with one another to speak first.
At that time, the asura king Vemacitra immediately stepped forward and spoke a verse to Śakra, the Lord of Devas:
"One whose delusion is fierce and intense must be severely rebuked;
one who lacks wisdom should be subdued, just as an ox flees in fear of the whip."
"Folly brings no happiness; it is difficult to subdue wherever one may be.
Therefore, using the staff of discipline, quickly sever that folly.
When the Asura King Vemacitrin had spoken this verse to Śakra, Lord of Devas, all the Asura retinues were filled with great joy, praising him with exultation.
Śakra and the various devas, along with their retinues, all remained silent.
At that time, King Vemacitrin addressed Śakra, saying:
"O Great Heavenly King!..."
"You may now speak a verse.
Then, the Lord of Devas addressed the asuras and spoke this verse:
"I clearly see this matter; I do not wish to be the same as the deluded."
"The fool gives rise to anger within himself; who would dispute with the wise?
When Śakra, King of the Devas, had spoken this verse, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three and their retinues all praised it greatly, leaping for joy and rejoicing.
The various asuras and their retinues remained silent.
At that time, Śakra addressed the asura king Vemacitrin, saying:
"O worthy one!"
"You may further explain these virtuous words.
Then, the asura addressed the Heavenly King, responding with a verse:
"With a mind of tranquil forbearance, O Śakra, I too am aware of this.
"When the fool is victorious, he says, 'I endured out of fear.
At that time, after the Asura King Vemacitra had spoken this verse, all the asuras and their retinues leaped for joy, praising him with great delight.
Śakra and the various devas, together with their retinues, remained silent.
At that time, the asura addressed Śakra, saying:
"O Benevolent Lord of Devas!
"You may further explain such righteous and virtuous words.
Then, the Great King Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the host of asuras, speaking in verse:
"The fool follows his own [impulses], Claiming that patience is fear of others."
Seeking one's own benefit by this means brings no profit to the other side.
When I perceive that another is committing evil, I should not respond to their anger with my own anger;
for he who can remain silent in the face of anger will always be the victor in the conflict.
If one is troubled by others, yet possesses the strength to endure,
know that such endurance is the supreme among all forms of patience.
Whether concerning oneself or others, all seek a place free from fear.
If one knows that another is angry, one should not give rise to hatred toward them.
This brings benefit to both parties—both oneself and the other.
When another is angry, resentful, or reviles you, it is by means of your own anger that their anger can be extinguished.
One brings benefit to two places: oneself and others.
When another’s mind is deluded, it arises from not knowing the Dharma.
If there is a person of great power who acts toward one who is weak, one should endure it for that person’s sake.
This patience is supreme; no other patience surpasses it.
They lack the sinews of wisdom and possess only the power of delusion;
because they abandon the Dharma through delusion, they naturally lose their right conduct.
The fool boasts of his own superiority and utters harsh words out of anger;
yet, when one endures such abuse, one is always the victor.
When hearing superior words, one endures them out of fear; when hearing words from an equal, one endures them for fear of enmity arising.
“Those who are able to endure the base and evil abuse directed at them—such patience is praised by the wise.
When Śakra, King of the Devas, had spoken this verse, the Trāyastriṃśa gods along with their retinues praised it with joy, leaping for boundless delight.
The assembly of asuras remained entirely silent.

At that time, among the devas there was a wise deity, and among the asuras there were those who were wise; they gathered together in one place and collectively deliberated upon these verses. Examining them with careful reflection, observing them with discerning patience, and having praised them in unison, they spoke thus:
"O worthy ones!..."
Today, Śakra, Lord of Devas, has spoken these excellent words.
In their governance and transformation of beings, there is no use of weapons, staves, or whips; nor is there any strife, insult, or enmity, nor any litigation or seeking of retribution.

Furthermore, within the midst of birth and death, there is that which may be found wearying and loathsome; one seeks to distance oneself from desire for the sake of cessation, for the sake of tranquility, for the attainment of supernormal powers, for the attainment of the state of a śramaṇa, and for the realization of perfect awakening and nirvāṇa.
O virtuous ones!
If those verses spoken by the asura king Vemacitra lacked such excellent and sublime words;

if they consisted entirely of swords, staves, whips, beatings, strife, insults, disputes, enmity, and the seeking of retribution; if they nurtured birth and death without weariness, were attached to various desires, sought neither the practice of tranquility nor nirvana, did not hope for supernormal powers or the fruits of the śramaṇa, and held no expectation for perfect enlightenment or nirvāṇa—[then they would be worthless].
"O virtuous ones!
The verses spoken by Śakra, King of the Devas, are well-spoken;
the verses spoken by Vemacitrin, King of the Asuras, are not well-spoken."
"O virtuous ones!
The verses spoken by Śakra, King of the Devas, are well-spoken, truly well-spoken;
the verses spoken by Vemacitra, King of the Asuras, are not well-spoken, indeed not well-spoken."
"O bhikṣus! You should know that at that time, Śakra was none other than myself.
O bhikṣus!"

At that time, I was the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, ruling with sovereign power and enjoying blessings and happiness; yet I used virtuous words as my weapons for battle, and because of those virtuous words, I was always victorious in combat.
Now, you bhikṣus, within my well-expounded teaching of the Dharma, have purified your minds, left the secular world, abandoned your homes to go forth into homelessness, and possess diligent practice.
If you, among those who seek the well-spoken and ill-spoken teachings, wish to grasp their meaning, you should understand it thus:
"O Bhikṣus! I recall that in the past, when the various celestial kings and others were engaged in battle with the asuras."
When Śakra, King of the Devas, had defeated the asuras in battle,
he constructed the Palace of Victory (Vaijayanta), measuring five hundred yojanas in length and breadth from east to west, and two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth from north to south.
"O bhikṣus!
Outside that Palace of Victory, there is another hundred Nīliyū rivers; within each interval between those rivers, there are again seven kūṭāgāras, all fashioned from the seven precious jewels."
Within each and every *kūṭāgāra*, seven chambers were placed; within each chamber, seven couches were arranged.
Upon each couch were seven jade maidens, and each jade maiden was further attended by seven separate handmaidens.

As for the King of the Śakras and his retinue of celestial maidens, they have no further need for food, drink, or other necessities; all their fragrant flowers, garments, ornaments, and every object of pleasure are experienced as the fruition of their past karma.
"O Bhikṣus!
Within this trichiliocosm, among all the celestial palaces, there is none that can compare to such a magnificent hall as the supreme palace of Śakra, King of the Devas."
At that time, the asura king Vemacitra had this thought:

"I possess such divine merit and power that although the sun, the moon, and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven move above me, by my strength I could seize them and fashion them into earrings and pendants to wear while wandering about."
Once, on a certain occasion, the asura king Rāhu, with intense anger blazing within his heart and a mind filled with poisonous vexation and lacking joy, thought of the asura king Vemacitra.
At that time, the asura king Vemacitrin had this thought:
"The asura king Rāhu is now thinking of me."
He further thought of the minor asura kings under his command and their various retinues of minor asuras.

At that time, those minor kings and asuras, knowing that the asura king Vemacitra had formed this thought, immediately each prepared various kinds of weapons and went toward him; having arrived, they stood before him, each in their respective place.

At that time, the asura king Vemacitra donned his armor, took up his weapons, and prepared his chariot; surrounded by his minor kings and various military hosts, he went to the presence of the asura Rāhu and halted there upon arrival.
At that time, Rāhu, the Asura King, again thought of the two Asura Kings, Saṃjaya and Māyāvin.
When those two kings knew of his thought, they returned to the very same thoughts as those of King Vemacitra.
The minor kings and their respective retinues, having learned this, each equipped themselves with weapons and proceeded toward their king.
Upon arrival, they all went before Rāhu, the Asura King.

At that time, Rāhu, the Asura King, arrayed himself in various ornaments and weapons, accompanied by the three Asura Kings Vemacitra, Vala, and Māyāvin, along with their subordinate kings and retinues, who surrounded him in front and behind.
Emerging from the city of the asuras with a retinue of followers, they intended to engage in battle with the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.

At that time, the two great nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda, emerged from their palace; each encircled Mount Sumeru seven times with his body, shaking it—shaking it again and again, shaking it greatly and shaking it everywhere; trembling it—trembling it again and again, trembling it greatly and trembling it everywhere; surging it up—surging it up again and again, surging it up greatly and surging it up everywhere—and struck the ocean with their tails.
That single drop of water rose up as far as the summit of Mount Sumeru.
Monks! At that time, having formed this thought, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the host of devas, saying:
"O virtuous ones, do you see this great earth shaking in such a manner?
The sky is overcast like gathering clouds and rain, yet also like a light mist; we know for certain that the asuras wish to battle with the devas."

At that time, all the nāgas dwelling within the ocean each departed from their own palaces, fully equipped with various adornments and bearing weapons, emerging to go before the asuras and engage them in battle together.
The victors pursued and drove back their foes, proceeding directly to their palace.
Those who were defeated fled in terror, going to the side of the earth-dwelling yakṣas and others; having arrived, they addressed them, saying:
"You should know that the asuras wish to fight with the devas; you must now come together with us toward them to assist us in breaking them."
Having heard this, the yakṣa donned his armor and weapons and went with the nāga to battle.
The victor pursued, while the vanquished retreated, fleeing in terror.
He went to where the yakṣa Pādaśīrṣa was and, having arrived, addressed him, saying:
"Yakṣa Pādaśīrṣa, do you know?
The asuras wish to fight with the devas; you all should come and assist me in going there to strike them down."
Upon hearing this, Patcūḍa adorned himself, took up his weapons, and followed them, even retreating as he went.

He went to inform the Mālyagandha yakṣas as before; however, they did not retreat but instead went to inform the Sadāmatta yakṣa. Having heard this, Sadāmatta likewise armed himself and joined forces with the Mālyagandhas and others to fight together.
Those who were victorious pursued them into the palace.
Those who were defeated, fleeing in terror, went to the side of the Four Great Heavenly Kings; having arrived, they addressed the Four Heavenly Kings, saying:
"O Great Heavenly Kings of the Four Quarters, you should know that the asuras now wish to come and fight with the devas. You ought to assist me and strike them down so that they are defeated."

When the Four Heavenly Kings heard the words of Changzui, they each immediately prepared various weapons and set out on their mounts; however, they were eventually forced to retreat in flight, unable to subdue him.
At that time, the Four Kings immediately ascended to the Hall of Good Dharma (*Sudharmā*), the place where the devas assemble for deliberation, and addressed Śakra, saying:
"O Heavenly King, you should know that the asuras have now gathered together, desiring to fight with the devas; it is fitting that you go there and engage them in battle."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having heard these words from the Four Heavenly Kings, approved them in his mind and immediately called a celestial *māṇava*, saying:

"Come, you celestial son! You should now go to the Suyāma Heaven, the Saṃtuṣita Heaven, as well as the Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heavens. Having arrived at those places, speak on my behalf: 'O you gods!'"
If you know this, when the asuras desire to fight with the devas, you virtuous ones should assist me;
come together and go toward them to engage in battle.
At that time, having heard the words of Śakra, the Māṇava immediately went toward the Suyāma Heaven and reported the matter in full.
Then, having heard these words from the messenger of Śakra, the Māṇava, the King of the Suyāma Heaven immediately called to mind the assembly of the gods of the Suyāma Heaven.

At that time, when those celestial hosts perceived that the celestial king was thinking of them, they immediately donned various kinds of armor and weapons, mounted all manner of celestial vehicles, and each approached the presence of their celestial king; having arrived, they stood before him, each in his respective place.

At that time, the King of the Suyāma Heaven himself donned various celestial armors and took up precious weapons; accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of devaputras, he descended surrounded by them toward the summit of Sumeru, the king of mountains, and stood upon its peak on the eastern side, hoisting a pure blue banner difficult to subdue.

At that time, the celestial messenger, the māṇava, again ascended to the presence of the Śakradevendra, the son of Tuṣita; having arrived, he returned and addressed the Śakradevendra with these words:
"Venerable sir, you should know that Śakra, King of the Devas, has this request:
'The asuras wish to fight with the devas; we pray that you will come to assist us and join our forces in battle there.'"
When the Tuṣita Heaven heard these words, it immediately thought of that host of devaputras; knowing they had all arrived, they gathered at the side of the Great Heavenly King of Tuṣita.

Having arrived, they each solemnly took up their weapons and mounted various steeds; leading one another in a surrounding circle, they descended to Mount Sumeru and stationed themselves on its southern face. An immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of myriads gathered like clouds, hoisting yellow banners difficult to subdue, and stood there leaning against the peaks.
"At that time, the celestial mānava messenger again ascended toward the Nirmāṇarati Heaven and addressed them, saying:
'O Noble Lord of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven!'"
"You should know that Śakra spoke these words:
'Those asuras wish to fight with the devas.

Just as previously requested, up until those devas arrived with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of sons of gods; each donned armor and mounted various vehicles, descending to the western side of Mount Sumeru, where they raised red banners difficult to vanquish and stood upon the peaks."
In this manner, they addressed the sons of the gods of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven, each as before.

At that time, that host of devas, arrayed with weapons and twice as numerous as those of the Nirmāṇarati heaven, surrounded by immeasurable hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of thousands of sons of gods, descended toward the northern face of Sumeru, the King of Mountains. There they planted white banners and streamers, difficult to subdue, and stood upon the peaks.
"At that time, Śakra, seeing that the gods above had all gathered like clouds, thought of the various yakṣas in the air.
Then, the hosts of yakṣas in the void each spoke these words:
'The Heavenly King Śakra has his thoughts upon us.'"

Having understood this, they immediately exhorted one another, donned their armor, took up their weapons, and equipped themselves with all necessary gear; each having dressed accordingly, they mounted various vehicles and went before Śakra, Lord of the Devas, where they stood to one side.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again called to mind the minor deva kings along with their retinues from the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
As he thought of them in this way, they each donned armor, took up their weapons, and mounted various vehicles to go before the Lord of Devas.

At that time, Śakra himself donned various types of armor and weaponry and mounted various vehicles; surrounded before and behind by the aerial yakṣas, the minor kings, and the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens, he departed from his celestial palace, desiring to engage in battle with the asuras.

“Monks! When the devas and asuras were engaged in battle at that time, they possessed such various weapons as these: namely, swords, arrows, spears, clubs, mallets, vajra-maces, scimitars, face-arrows, chisel-arrows, barb-arrows, calf-tooth arrows, kāliṅga-leaf-barbed arrows, and fine-pointed arrows. Such weapons as these were of variegated and lovely colors, fashioned from the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musāragalva, and emerald.”

They cast those various weapons from afar toward the bodies of those asuras; yet they do not strike or harm them, but pass straight through their bodies and hang suspended. Furthermore, no wounds or scars are visible, yet because of the mere contact, they experience the pain of injury.
"O Bhikṣus!

When those asuras take up their various weapons to fight with the devas, they resemble them in appearance; both are fashioned from the same kind of seven precious jewels. When they strike through one another, no scars remain, yet by the mere condition of contact, they experience the pain of injury."
"O bhikṣus!
When the gods of the desire realm engage in battle with the asuras, they possess such various weapons of diverse forms; how much more so, then, for the people of the world!"
The Sutra on the Causes and Origins of the World, Scroll Eight;
The Sutra on the Causes and Origins of the World, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Dharmagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter Ten: The Duration of the Kalpa "Monks!
There are three kinds of intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*) in the world."
What are these three?
First is the intermediate kalpa of swords and staves; second is the intermediate kalpa of famine; and third is the intermediate kalpa of pestilence.
What is meant by the intermediate aeon of swords and staves? O monks!

During the intermediate aeon of swords and staves, those people lack right conduct; they do not speak according to the Dharma, hold perverted and inverted views, and fully engage in all ten unwholesome courses of action.
At that time, sentient beings lived for only ten years. Monks!
When people’s lifespan was thus ten years, girls were married at five months of age, just as today girls of fifteen or sixteen are given in marriage to their husbands.
Now, all that the earth possesses—clarified butter, fresh butter, rock honey, granulated sugar, and non-glutinous rice—will at that time entirely vanish and no longer appear.

When the lifespan of those ten-year-olds is reached, they will wear garments made solely of coarse wool; these will be as supreme and exquisite as the kāśika-kośeya, kṣauma, dukūla, kaurava, kārpāsa, and kambala-ratna garments of today. Their woolen garments shall likewise be so.
At that time, they will eat only millet, just as people now eat non-glutinous rice.
Furthermore, they will be cherished and loved by their parents; they will wish for a lifespan of ten years as the pinnacle of longevity, just as people today pray for a hundred years of life.

"O monks! When they were ten years old, all those sentient beings who were unfilial toward their parents, disrespectful toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and disrespectful toward their elders, also received offerings, praise, and respect from others, just as people today who practice the Dharma and teach it receive a corresponding reputation."
Why is this? Because such is the nature of karma.
Furthermore, O bhikṣus!
When people were ten years of age, there was no reputation for goodness; people did not practice the ten paths of wholesome action, and almost all performed unwholesome deeds.
When sentient beings saw one another, each gave rise to thoughts of killing, harming, and slaughtering, devoid of any sense of compassion or pity.
Now, when hunters encounter various birds and beasts in the empty mountains and marshes, they give rise only to the intent to butcher, harm, and slaughter them.
Furthermore, O Bhikṣus!
At that time, the very ornaments and necklaces used by people for adorning their bodies will all become swords and staves.

It is just as with those who today wear flower garlands, earrings, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, rings, hairpins, and tweezers—all these various ornaments adorning the body are of one kind and no different.
Furthermore, O bhikṣus!

At that time, toward the end of the intermediate kalpa, within seven days, whatever they touch with their hands—whether grass, wood, clods of earth, tiles, or stones—all these will become swords and staves, their blades exceedingly sharp, surpassing anything crafted by human hands.

Within seven days, each vied with the others to seize them, slaughtering one another; they all killed each other, and at the end of their lives, they all fell into the various evil realms to undergo the sufferings of hell.

Why is this? Because as they face one another, each gives rise to thoughts of killing, turbid thoughts, and evil thoughts; they lack thoughts of benefit, lack thoughts of compassion, and lack thoughts of purity.
"Monks! This is called the intermediate kalpa of swords and clubs. Monks!"
What is called the intermediate kalpa of famine? O bhikṣus!
During the time of the kalpa of famine, those people do not practice the Dharma; they hold perverted and inverted views and fully engage in the ten unwholesome paths of action.

For this reason, the heavens do not send down rain; because there is no rain, the world suffers famine. There are no seeds, people subsist on white bones, and they sustain their lives by eating skins.
What is meant by "white bones as sustenance"? Monks!

During times of famine, those people will collect white bones from crossroads, streets, city walls, and everywhere along the roads; they will boil them with water, take the broth to drink, and thereby sustain their lives. For this reason, it is called "white bones as sustenance."
What is meant by "subsisting on various tree barks"? O Bhikṣus!

During the kalpa of famine, those people, driven by the urgency of hunger, take the bark of various trees, boil it with water, and drink the juice to sustain their lives; therefore, this is called "making various barks one's livelihood."
"O bhikṣus!
At that time, those sentient beings who die of hunger shall all be reborn in the various evil destinies, or else fall into the world of Yama."
As for what are called *preta* (hungry ghosts), it is because those beings, being stingy, greedy, and envious, fear that all things will be exhausted and thus scramble to seize and hoard them.
Monks! For this reason, it is called the intermediate kalpa of famine.
“Monks, what is called the intermediate kalpa of pestilence?
Monks, [it is as follows:]”

At that time, those people also desired to practice the Dharma and to speak in accordance with the Dharma; they also desired to practice non-perverted views and were fully intent on practicing the ten paths of wholesome action.

However, at that time, because those who followed the Dharma lacked the superior retribution of the ten wholesome karmas from the past, non-human beings released calamitous vapors and spread various epidemics, causing many people to die therein.
Furthermore, monks!
During that period of illness, moreover, non-human beings from other world-systems come to inflict pestilential diseases upon these people.
Why is this? Because of negligence, they engage in negligent conduct.
Furthermore, by coming into contact with those evil signs, their minds are disturbed and their power is stripped away.
Among them, many people of little merit fall ill and pass away.
It is like a king or a royal minister who, for the sake of protecting the populace, stations sentries at the borders of his realm.

At that time, bandits from another region arrived; because those guarding the frontier were neither diligent nor heedful, the bandits slaughtered them all at once, destroying entire households, exterminating villages, ravaging settlements, or demolishing cities and capitals.
In this way, in this manner, when that person is negligent, non-human beings from other regions come to spread pestilence, and they all perish at the end of their lives; it is likewise so again.
Furthermore, at that time, when non-human beings from other regions come to inflict diseases, sentient beings do not engage in negligent conduct.

Those ghosts possess great power and forcibly oppress them, inflicting harmful contact that causes their minds to become distressed and disordered; they rob them of their vital strength, and among them, many encounter illness and die.
For example, suppose a king or a royal minister, for the sake of protecting various settlements, establishes garrisons and defenses.
At that time, if bandits from other regions come to harass them, those garrisons and defenses remain vigilant and guard them with diligent care.

Those bandits, possessing great strength, exerted violent coercion and slaughtered these people all at once; or they destroyed entire villages, households, and settlements, as briefly described above.
"In this way, monks, it is so!
When people encounter the disease of the pestilence eon and their lives are brought to an end by its pressing urgency, it is just like this.
Once they have died, they all attain rebirth among the higher devas."
Why is this? It is because those beings harbor no intent to harm one another, no distracted minds, but possess minds of benefit, loving-kindness, and purity.
At the time of their death, they will each ask one another:
"Is your illness bearable? Have you experienced some slight improvement?
Is there anyone who has been liberated from it, anyone who has risen from it, or anyone whose various ailments have been cured?"
"O bhikṣus! For this reason, they are reborn in the heavens; for this reason, it is called the intermediate kalpa of pestilence.
O bhikṣus!"
These are called the three intermediate kalpas of the world.
Chapter Eleven: The Abiding World. *Lokadhātunirdeśa-sūtra*, Chapter Eleven, "The Abiding World. "O Bhikṣus!
Within the world, there are four immeasurables that cannot be measured, cannot be weighed, and are inconceivable."

Whether among gods or humans, if one were to attempt to calculate its measure within the reckoning of the world—counting so many years, so many hundreds of years, so many thousands of years, so many hundreds of thousands of years, so many koṭis of years, so many hundreds of koṭis of years, so many thousands of koṭis of years, or so many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of years—one would ultimately never be able to reach it.
What are the four? Monks!

If one were to attempt to calculate the duration of the world’s endurance, it could not be known as being so many years, so many hundreds of years, so many thousands of years, so many hundreds of thousands of years, so many *koṭi* years, so many hundreds of *koṭi* years, so many thousands of *koṭi* years, or so many hundreds of thousands of *koṭi* years.

“Monks! If the world, having remained, were to be destroyed, it would be impossible to calculate and know by how many years, how many hundreds of years, how many thousands of years, how many hundreds of thousands of years, how many koṭis of years, how many hundreds of koṭis of years, how many thousands of koṭis of years, or how many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of years [it would take].”

"O monks! Even the time it takes for the world, after having been destroyed, to remain in that state is beyond calculation—it cannot be known by counting so many years, so many hundreds of years, so many thousands of years, so many hundreds of thousands of years, so many koṭis of years, so many hundreds of koṭis of years, so many thousands of koṭis of years, or so many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of years."

“Monks! When the world has been formed and remains so, this duration cannot be calculated as being so many years, so many hundreds of years, so many thousands of years, so many hundreds of thousands of years, so many koṭis of years, so many hundreds of koṭis of years, so many thousands of koṭis of years, or so many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of years.”

“Monks! These are called the four immeasurables, which cannot be measured, cannot be weighed, are inconceivable, and cannot be calculated; whether among devas or humans, there is no one who can calculate and know them as being so many hundreds of thousands of myriads of years, or so many hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of years.”
"O bhikṣus!
To the east of here, there are worlds that undergo formation, subsistence, and destruction without interval; some undergo formation, subsistence, and destruction."
