"Monks! The southern, western, and northern directions undergo transformation, subsistence, and destruction in exactly the same way. Monks!"

For example, it is like a five-part wheel from which the axle has been removed; as it revolves, it does not pause for even a moment, nor is there any interval of rest. To speak briefly, it is just so.
Furthermore, it is like summer rain, where the drops are large and fall in continuous succession without ceasing.
In this same way, for the eastern, southern, western, and northern directions, the cycles of formation, subsistence, destruction, and transformation proceed without any period of rest;
it is likewise for all of them. "O bhikṣus!
Within these intervals, there are furthermore three calamities."
What are these three?
First, the disaster of fire; second, the disaster of water; third, the disaster of wind.
At the time of the disaster of fire, the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven are the first to escape its calamity.
At the time of the calamity of water, the Śubhakṛtsna devas are the first to escape that disaster;
at the time of the calamity of wind, the Bṛhatphala devas are the first to escape that disaster.
What is the calamity of fire? Monks!

At the time of the calamity of fire, there are certain beings who have performed wholesome deeds, whose speech is in accordance with the Dharma, who are endowed with right view and free from perversion, and who fully practice the ten paths of wholesome action; they attain the second dhyāna, which is without vitarka and vicāra, not through strenuous cultivation but spontaneously.

At that time, those beings, by means of their supernormal powers, dwelt in the void, dwelt upon the paths of the sages, dwelt upon the paths of the devas, and dwelt upon the Brahma-paths; having so dwelt, they experienced the bliss of the second dhyāna, free from applied and sustained thought. Having thus realized and fully accomplished this, at the dissolution of the body, they were reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.

Beings from the hells, beings from the animal realm, the world of Yama, the world of asuras, the world of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, and even the gods of Māra’s retinue, as well as all beings up to the Brahma-world, are born among humans; they all fully accomplish the state without directed thought or sustained evaluation, realize happiness through direct knowledge, and upon the dissolution of the body, are reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
When all six realms of existence are completely severed, this is called the exhaustion of the world.
"Monks, how does the world,
having come to abide, subsequently undergo destruction?
"O Bhikṣus!

If at that time, or during immeasurable times and throughout the long course of aeons, there should be a drought across the world with no further rain or moisture, all grasses and trees would completely wither and dry up until nothing remains."
Just as when reeds and rushes are cut green, if they do not receive rainwater, they will wither, dry up, and decay until nothing remains; even so, O bhikṣus!
When it has not rained for a long time in the heavens, all grasses and trees wither and dry up;
it is just so with these things. O monks!
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are likewise: impermanent, not abiding for long, not solid, lacking self-mastery, subject to destruction, loathsome, and from which one should seek liberation.
"Furthermore, monks!

At that time, there arises the great wind called Kālika, which blows across and scatters the waters of the great ocean for eighty-four thousand yojanas. Thereupon, it brings forth the palace of the sun from below and casts it onto the mid-slope of Sumeru, the king of mountains, at a height of forty-two thousand yojanas, establishing it within the path of the sun."
"O bhikṣus!
This is called the second sun rising in the world; all small ponds, rivers, and streams will completely dry up until nothing remains."
"O bhikṣus!
All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are entirely impermanent; as briefly explained before, one should seek liberation from them.
Furthermore, O bhikṣus!"

To speak briefly as before: when a great wind blows upon the ocean and brings forth the sun’s palace, placing it within the solar path, this is called the third sun rising in the world. All great marshes, large ponds, great rivers, and the Ganges and other such major rivers—all these great rivers are completely dried up with nothing remaining;
so too it is with all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).

In this world, when the fourth sun appears, all great waters and great lakes—namely the Great Lake Sāgara, the Great Lake Anavatapta, the Great Lake Mandākinī, the Great Lake Apalāla, and so forth—all completely dry up until nothing remains;
so too it is with all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra).

When the fifth sun thus appears in the world, the waters of the great ocean gradually dry up and vanish; first they decrease to the depth of an ankle, then further to the depth of a knee, then to half the body, or even to the height of one, two, three, four, five, six, or seven persons, until finally they are completely exhausted.
"O Bhikṣus!
When five suns appear, the waters of the great ocean decrease by half a tāla tree, down to one tāla tree; or they decrease by two, three, four, five, six, or seven tāla trees;
even down to half a krośa, or they decrease by one, two, three, four, five, six, or seven krośas."

It may decrease by half a yojana, or it may decrease by one, two, three, four, five, six, or seven yojanas; it may even decrease by a hundred yojanas, or by two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight hundred yojanas.
"O Bhikṣus!
When five suns appear, the waters of the great ocean decrease by a thousand yojanas, and continue to decrease by two, three, four, five, six, and seven thousand yojanas."

"O monks! When five suns appear in this world, that great ocean water—briefly stated, down to seven thousand yojanas—remains; it may remain until six, five, four, three, two, one, or a thousand yojanas; likewise, it remains down to seven hundred yojanas;
or it may remain until six, five, four, three, two, one, or a hundred yojanas; or seven yojanas of its water remain."
Alternatively, there may remain water six, five, four, three, two, or one yojana deep;
or it may diminish further until seven krośas of water remain,
or even until six, five, four, three, two, or one krośa of water remains.
"O Bhikṣus!

When five suns appear in this world, the waters of that great ocean will remain at a depth of seven tāla trees; or again, there will remain water at a depth of six, five, four, three, two, or one tāla tree;
or the remaining water may be as deep as seven men."
Or again, it may be six, five, four, three, two, or one [yojana];
or again, it may be half a person’s height, or from the knees downward, or reaching only to the ankle bones, such that only a residue of water remains.
Furthermore, at the time of the fifth day, only a small portion of water remains in the great ocean, while the rest has been consumed.
Just as there is but a small amount of water in a cow’s footprint during the autumn rains,
even so it is with that great ocean at the time of the five-day period.
Furthermore, monks!
On the fifth day, throughout that great ocean, in every place, even the oily water will have no remnant left behind.

"O Bhikṣus! All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are likewise thus: impermanent and not long-lasting, existing but for a brief moment. In short, they are to be reviled and abandoned; one should seek liberation from them."
Furthermore, monks, to speak briefly as before:

when the sixth sun appears in the world, the four great continents, along with the eighty-four thousand minor islands, the various great mountains, and Sumeru, the king of mountains, all begin to emit smoke, rising again and again, just as when a potter wishes to fire his vessels, the flames upon them all arise at once.
That fire blazed intensely, filling and pervading everywhere.

In this very manner, the smoke rising from the four great continents, the various mountains, and so forth, was likewise fierce and powerful; in brief, it continued until [the realization that] all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, and one should therefore seek liberation from them.
Furthermore, monks!

To speak briefly as before, when the seven suns arise, the four great continents along with the eighty-four thousand minor islands, all other great mountains, and Sumeru, the king of mountains, will all be completely incinerated.
The subterranean water levels completely dry up; once the aggregate of earth is exhausted, the aggregate of wind is also exhausted.
Thus, when the fire element blazes intensely, seven hundred yojanas of the upper portion of Sumeru, the king of mountains, have their peaks collapse.
The flames blazed fiercely; driven by the wind, they ascended and burned the palaces of the Brahmā heavens, reaching even as far as the Ābhāsvara Heaven.

Among them, those devaputras who were later born in the lower palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven did not know that the world was undergoing the cycles of destruction and formation, or the transition from formation to abiding. They all became terrified, filled with alarm and trembling, and said to one another:
"May these flames not come to burn our Ābhāsvara palaces!"
At that time, the sons of the gods among the Ābhāsvara devas, who well understood the destruction, formation, and abiding of the world-aeons, consoled the sons of the gods below, saying:
"O you virtuous ones, do not be startled, do not be afraid. (The first two lines of the Sanskrit original are repeated.)
For what reason?
O virtuous ones!
In the past, there was also a flame that reached that place.

At that time, having heard these words, the sons of the gods immediately recalled the past; because they remembered that light never leaving their minds, they were given this name, called the Light Devas (Ābhāsvara).
In this way, they are utterly ablaze, with fierce flames so intense and brilliant that no remaining ash, soot, or charred residue can be discerned. Monks!

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are thus; to speak briefly, this continues up until [the point where] one may seek liberation. From here on, the Sanskrit original repeats the discussion concerning the period from the emergence of one sun up to the seven suns, which is termed "abiding and then destruction. This is now entirely omitted.
“Monks, how does the world,
having been destroyed, come to be formed again? Monks, ...”
At that time, after an immeasurable and incalculable period of vast antiquity, great heavy clouds arose, spreading until they completely covered the Brahmā world.

Having thus covered it, they poured down a great torrential rain; the drops of that rain were coarse, like the axles of chariots or even like pestles. For many hundreds of thousands of millions of years, that mass of water gradually increased until the Brahmā world formed its boundary, and the waters filled it entirely.
However, that mass of water is sustained by four wind-circles. What are these four?
They are: first, abiding; second, securely abiding; third, non-falling; and fourth, firm mastery.
At that time, after the rain of that mass of water had ceased, it receded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of *yojanas*.

At that moment, great winds arose simultaneously from the four directions; these winds were named Anābhirā, which blew upon that mass of water, causing the waves to boil and surge, churning it restlessly, and from within it, foam spontaneously emerged.

However, those foam-bubbles were blown and cast by the great wind Anabhiṣyanda; from above they were established as various palaces, exquisite and lovely, composed of an intermingling of the seven treasures—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.
"Monks! For this reason, the Brahmakāyika devas possess these palaces, walls, and so forth, which have arisen in the world. Monks!"

Having done this, that mass of water immediately receded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of *yojanas*. To speak briefly as before, winds arose from the four directions called the great winds of Anābhiṇda; they blew and cast up the boiling foam, which immediately formed a palace named the Heaven of the Body of Māra.

The surrounding walls and dwellings are no different from those of the Brahmakāyika Heaven; they possess only jewel-like colors, with subtle gradations of exquisite refinement, differing slightly in their upper and lower levels.

In this manner, he fashioned the palaces and walls of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas and the Nirmāṇarati devas; next, he fashioned the palaces of the Tuṣita devas, and next those of the Yāma devas. Thus they were produced, complete in every detail, just like those of the Brahmakāyika devas, as described in sequence.
“Monks! At that time, that mass of water further receded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of yojanas, shrinking and diminishing until it remained stationary in that state.”
Within that mass of water, on all four sides, froth spontaneously arises and floats upon the surface, sixty-eight hundred thousand yojanas in thickness and immeasurable in its vast extent.

It is just as if, in a spring, a pond, or a lake, there were a mass of floating foam that had spread across all four directions, covering the surface of the water and remaining there, completely enveloping it. Even so, monks!
Within that mass of water, throughout the four directions, foam rests upon the surface, sixty-eight hundred thousand yojanas thick and immeasurably vast; it is likewise so.

“O Bhikṣus! At that time, the great wind Anābhiya blew upon those water-bubbles and immediately fashioned the body of Sumeru, the great king of mountains; next, it fashioned the city walls, lovely in their various colors and composed of the four jewels—namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, along with other such exquisite treasures.”
"Monks! By this cause and condition, there comes to be that King of Mountains, Sumeru, produced in such a manner. Monks!"

Furthermore, at that time, the great Vīra wind blew upon those water-foams and, upon the upper reaches of Sumeru, the king of mountains, manifested all the mountain peaks in the four directions. Each peak was seven hundred yojanas high, composed of various subtle and exquisite seven treasures, including even musaragalva and agate. By these causes and conditions, the various mountain peaks and ravines were produced in the world.

In this manner, that wind successively blew upon the froth on the water to construct palaces for the hosts of the Trāyastriṃśa devas; subsequently, at a distance of forty-two thousand yojanas from the middle of the eastern, southern, western, and northern slopes of Mount Sumeru, it constructed various palaces, cities, walls, and ramparts for the Four Great Kings, adorned with the seven precious jewels in diverse colors, lovely and magnificent.

When this was completed, that wind then took up water-foam and, within forty-two thousand yojanas at the midpoint of the king of mountains, Sumeru, constructed a great city and palace for the Moon Deva-son, adorned with the accomplishment of various colors and the seven precious jewels.

Having done this, the wind again took up the foam and fashioned for the Sun Deity seven celestial palaces, with city walls, watchtowers, and battlements, variegated with the seven treasures and adorned in every way.
By these causes and conditions, there exists in the world this palace of seven days, established and maintained.
Furthermore, O Bhikṣus!

That wind subsequently blows upon the mass of water and, at the location of the great king of mountains, Sumeru, fashions three-tiered city walls adorned with various colors of the seven treasures, including even *musāragalva* and *aśmagarbha*. In this way, such clusters of cities arise in the world.

"O Bhikṣus! At that time, the great wind Anābhirava next blew upon the water-foam, forming crystal palaces and city-walls in the sky at a height of ten thousand yojanas above the surface of the ocean for the sake of the various yakṣas."
"Monks! By this cause and condition, there come to be the palaces, city walls, and ramparts of the Ākāśa-yakṣas in the world;
thus they arise. Monks!"

Then, that great wind Anābhiḷa blew upon the water's foam; at the side of the Great Mountain King Sumeru, extending one thousand yojanas to the east, west, south, and north, it fashioned four-sided Asura cities beneath the great ocean, made of various colors and the seven precious gems, exquisite and lovely. Thus, these four-sided Asura cities came into existence in this world.

Furthermore, the great wind Anābhiḷa blows those water-foams outside the Great King of Mountains Sumeru and casts them there, forming a mountain named Khadiraka. This mountain is forty-two thousand yojanas in both height and breadth; it is perfectly adorned with the seven precious gems of various colors, exquisite and beautiful to behold.
"Monks! For this reason, the mountain Kāḷagiri comes into being in the world in such a manner.

Furthermore, the great wind Anabhiṇha blows those water-bubbles and casts them beyond Mount Kāḷagiri, depositing them in that place to form a mountain named Isadhara. This mountain is twenty-one thousand yojanas in both height and breadth; it is lovely with various colors and composed of the seven treasures, including even *musāragalva* and *aśmagarbha*."
"O Bhikṣus!
By this cause and condition, the mountain named Īṣādhāra comes into being in the world in this manner.

Furthermore, the great wind Anābhiḷa blows upon that mass of water-foam and hurls it outside the Īṣādhāra mountain, where it forms another mountain that stands there, called Yugandhara. This mountain is twelve thousand yojanas in height and breadth; it is of variegated and lovely colors, even being composed of the seven treasures such as musāragalva and aśmagarbha."
"O Bhikṣus!
For this reason, there arises in the world Mount Yugandhara, the king of mountains.
Following this sequence, there is Mount Sudarśana, equal in height and breadth, measuring six thousand yojanas."
Next, he further fashioned Mount Aśvakarṇa (formerly called Bāndhava), equal in height and breadth at three thousand yojanas;
next, he fashioned Mount Nimindhara, one thousand two hundred yojanas in height and breadth;
and next, he fashioned Mount Vinataka, equal in height and breadth at six hundred yojanas.

Next, he further fashioned that circular mountain, equal in height and breadth at three hundred *yojanas*, lovely with various colors—namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate—accomplished from all seven precious substances, as described in detail above, no different from the fashioning of Mount Khadiraka.
"O monks! For this reason, this world-system of circular mountains arises.

Furthermore, the great wind Anabhiḷā blows upon those water-foams, scattering and casting them outside the circular mountains so that they settle on each of the four sides, forming the four great continents, eighty thousand minor islands, and various other great mountains."
In this manner, through successive stages of formation and completion,
O monks, by these causes and conditions, there appeared in the world these four great continents, along with eighty thousand minor islands and various great mountains, emerging in their proper order.

"Furthermore, the great wind Anābhila blows upon those water-bubbles, casting them beyond the four great continents, the eighty thousand minor continents, Sumeru, the king of mountains, and all other great mountains; there they are established and remain, named the Great Circular Wheel Mountain (Mahācakra-pariṇāha). It is equal in height and breadth at six million eight hundred thousand yojanas; it is firm and solid, composed of vajra, and difficult to destroy."
"Monks! For this reason, the Great Circular Wheel Mountain (Mahācakravāḍa) was produced in the world.
Furthermore, the great wind Anabhiṭāpa blew upon the great earth, digging it deeper and deeper; then, right there, a great mass of water was established, remaining perfectly still."
"O bhikṣus!
For this reason, it is from these causes and conditions that the great ocean comes into being within the world.
Furthermore, for what reason and by what causes and conditions is the water of that great ocean so salty and bitter as to be unfit for drinking or eating?"
"Monks! There are these three conditions.
What are the three?"

First, after an immeasurable period of time following the destruction by fire, during the long course of the aeon, great heavy clouds arise and remain, covering everything up to the Brahma Heaven; thereafter it rains, the drops of which are large, as described in detail previously.

When that great rain has washed the palaces of the Brahmakāyika devas, it next washes the palaces of the Māras, the palaces of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, the palaces of the Nirmāṇarati devas, the palaces of the Tuṣita devas, and the palaces of the Yāma devas. Washing them again and again, thus washing them thoroughly, as they are being washed, all salty, brackish, bitter, and pungent flavors flow downward.

Next, it washes the body of the Great Mountain King Sumeru, the four great continents, the eighty thousand small islands, and all other great mountains, including the circular ones. As it soaks, pours over, and rinses them, all the salty, bitter, and pungent flavors within them descend all at once and fall into the great ocean.
"Monks! For this reason, the waters of the great ocean are salty and unfit for drinking.
Furthermore, the waters of the great ocean are the dwelling place of various great deities and beings with massive bodies."
What constitutes a "large body"?

It refers to fish, turtles, shrimp, frogs, otters, *kumbhīra* crocodiles, *timira*, *timi*, *timiṅgila*, *tuntura*, *tunturakīla*, and so forth; among them, some have bodies measuring one hundred *yojanas*, while others measure two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight hundred *yojanas*.
A body of such great size dwells therein; all the excrement and urine they discharge flow into the ocean, and for this reason, that sea is salty and bitter, unfit for drinking.
"O monks! This is called the second cause and condition for its saltiness and bitterness.
Furthermore, the waters of the great ocean were also cursed by various sages of old, who made this aspiration through their incantations: [text continues]"
“May you become salt; its flavor is not fit for drinking”—these two phrases are repeated twice in the Sanskrit original.
Monks! This is the third cause and condition for the saltiness of the waters of the great ocean, such that they are not fit for drinking.
Furthermore, what is the cause and condition by which the great heat that parches and dries up the world arises? O monks!

When this world first evolved at the beginning of the kalpa, at that time, the great wind called Anabhiḷa gathered those six sun-palaces and their city-walls, casting them down into the waters of the great ocean, where they remained fixed in that place.
That great mass of water is entirely consumed and exhausted, never overflowing again. Monks!
For this reason, there is this great heat and parching in the world, manifesting its arising; this is called the world’s period of dissolution and its subsequent abiding.
"Furthermore, what is meant by 'the world having been destroyed, it is formed and remains'?
Monks, it is like this:
just as the world currently exists after having been formed, so too does it remain standing when a fire disaster occurs."
In this regard, how does the calamity of water occur? Monks!

At the time of the kalpa-ending calamity of water, those people act in accordance with the Dharma, speak words in accordance with the Dharma, are endowed with right view free from perversion, and maintain the ten virtuous actions.
Those people shall attain the third dhyāna, which is free from joy; they will obtain it spontaneously, without exerting effort and without weariness.

At that time, those beings will dwell within the path of the sages, devas, and Brahmās who abide in space. Having attained this state, they will experience a bliss detached from joy, and will exclaim of themselves:
"O noble ones, how joyful! How joyful!"
"This third dhyāna is thus blissful.
At that time, the beings there all asked those beings who had attained the dhyāna, and they replied:
"Excellent, O worthy ones!"
"This is the third dhyāna path, free from joy; it should be understood in this way.
Having understood this, those beings accomplished such a third dhyāna path, free from joy.

Having perfected meditation, he realized it; having realized it, he reflected upon it; having reflected upon it, he remained therein. At the dissolution of the body, after death, he was reborn in the Heaven of Universal Purity (*Subhakṛtsna*).

In this way, from the beings in the hells below, through the world of Yama, the asuras, and the Four Great Kings, up to the Brahma-world and down to the Ābhāsvara heaven, all sentient beings—everywhere and in every state of existence—were completely extinguished.
"O bhikṣus! This is called the turning of the world.
Furthermore, in this regard, how does the world, having turned, undergo destruction?"
"O Bhikṣus!

There was a time, an immeasurable, long-distant, and vast period, when a great cloud spread everywhere, reaching even as far as the Ābhāsvara devas, and rained down boiling ash-water for immeasurable many years—in brief, for hundreds of thousands of billions of years."
"O Bhikṣus!
When that rain of boiling caustic water falls, it dissolves all the palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, so that not even a trace, a speck of dust, or an image remains to be perceived."
For example, if ghee or fresh butter were thrown into a fire, they would be consumed and utterly extinguished, leaving no form or characteristic by which they could be perceived.
In this very way, when that boiling lye-water rains down, it destroys the palaces and dwellings of the Ābhāsvara Heaven; likewise, nothing remains there that can be known as a sign.
"O monks! All conditioned phenomena are impermanent;

they break apart and disperse, they flow on and perish. Before long, in a mere moment, they are likewise so. They are to be loathed and regarded as a source of suffering; one should seek liberation from them."
"O Bhikṣus!

In this manner, the palaces of the Brahmakāyika devas, as well as those of Māra, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, Tuṣita, and Yāma—just as previously described in brief—they are drenched, washed away, and utterly destroyed by a rain of boiling ashes. Just as when ghee is placed in fire, it melts and vanishes until its original form is no more, so too do these palaces become devoid of any physical appearance."
"Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; one should seek to escape and be free from them. O monks!
When that rain of boiling lye falls,"

The rain falls upon the four great continents, the eighty thousand small islands, and all other mountains, including Mount Sumeru, until they are completely worn away and extinguished, such that no form or characteristic remains to be identified; this is explained in detail as previously stated.
One should feel weary and disgusted by such transformations; only those who have seen them can believe in them. This is called the world’s turning, its abiding, and its subsequent destruction.
Furthermore, how does the destruction of what has already been formed occur?
"O Bhikṣus!

At that time, clouds arise and pour down great torrents of rain for many years. Winds arise and blow the foam upward, forming celestial palaces. This is explained at length, even unto the matter of the fire calamity; this is called the water calamity."
"Furthermore, what is the calamity of wind?

Monks! At the time of the calamity of wind, those beings who have practiced according to the Dharma and accomplished right mindfulness are reborn in the Abhāsvara Heaven (the Heaven of Vast Fruit) of the Fourth Dhyāna."
The sentient beings within those hells, having cast off their bodies and returned to the human realm, cultivate pure conduct and achieve the four dhyānas;

it is also thus for those in the animal realm, the world of Yama, among the asuras, and in the heavens of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three Gods, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, as well as the Māra-heaven, the Brahma-world, Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, Parīttābha, and so forth—achieving the four dhyānas, as explained in detail above.
"Monks! This is called the formation of the world.
How does it undergo destruction?"
"O Bhikṣus!
Within that immeasurable and long-extended past, a great wind arose; that great wind was named Saṃghāta, which in the language of Sui means 'Harmony' (or 'Union')."
"O bhikṣus!

That harmonious wind blows upon the palaces of the Śubhakṛtsna devas, causing them to strike and rub against one another until they are destroyed and annihilated, such that no form or trace remains to be known."

It is like a strong man taking two copper vessels in his two hands, rubbing them together until they are broken, worn away, and completely consumed, such that no form or characteristic remains to be perceived.
In the same way, that harmonious wind blows and utterly destroys the palaces of the Śubhakṛtsna devas.
Monks! All conditioned phenomena are impermanent and subject to destruction; they do not endure for long, but are momentary and even loathsome. You should seek liberation from them.

In this manner, it successively blew through the palaces of the Ābhāsvara devas, the palaces of the Brahmakāyika devas, the Māra-kāyika devas, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, the Nirmāṇarati devas, and the Yāma devas; they struck one another, rubbed against one another, ground against one another, and were extinguished, until their forms and marks vanished, leaving no shadows or dust by which their characteristics could be known.

"O bhikṣus! All conditioned phenomena are likewise thus: they are subject to decay and lack solidity; they possess no reality. You should cultivate weary detachment toward them and seek liberation from them with all haste."

“Monks! That great wind of Saṃghāṭa blows across the four great continents, the eighty thousand small islands, and all other great mountains, including Sumeru, the king of mountains. It raises them to a height of one krośa, dispersing and destroying them;
or at two, three, four, five, six, or seven krośas, it splits, scatters, and destroys them.”
Or they blow and lift them up to a height of one yojana, two, three, four, five, six, or seven;
or they blow and lift them up to a height of a hundred yojanas, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or seven hundred yojanas, dispersing and destroying them;
or they blow and lift them up to a height of a thousand yojanas, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or seven thousand yojanas.
Furthermore, it may lift up [the earth] for hundreds of thousands of yojanas, dispersing and destroying it.
Such is that wind; it blows, shatters, and ruins [all things] until nothing remains—neither form nor appearance—and not even a residue as small as a minute particle can be known.
It is like a strong and powerful man who takes a handful of parched barley, crushes it with his hand, and hurls it into the air; it scatters and drifts away until it is formless and shadowless.
In this very way, just so, that wind blows apart the various continents and mountains; it is likewise thus.
Only those who have seen it can believe it.
This is called the destruction of the world’s revolving abode.
Furthermore, how does the world, having been destroyed, undergo transformation? Monks!
At that time, during the course of immeasurable years and eons, great black clouds arise and cover the entire world, extending even to the abodes of the Śubhakṛtsna devas.

Once it had been thus covered, a great rain immediately fell; the drops were as coarse as chariot axles or even like pestles, pouring down in continuous succession for many years, hundreds of thousands of millions of years. That mass of water became so deep, vast, and expansive that it reached as far as the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, filling it entirely with water.
The four kinds of wind-circles support it as previously described;
eventually, they blow upon the foam to create the palaces of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, which appear and arise with the variegated colors of the seven precious gems.
Each and every one is explained in succession, just as in the case of the fire and water calamities.
O monks! This is called the transformation that occurs after the world has been destroyed.
"How does the world, having been formed, abide? Monks,
it is just as the world of devas and humans abides, having been formed, at this present time."
"Monks! In this sequence, there is the blowing of winds; these are called the three calamities of the world.
Chapter Twelve: The Most Excellent. *Sūtra on the Origin of the World*, Chapter Twelve, Part One: 'Furthermore, monks!'"
When that *samaya* had evolved in the world and such a formation was complete, those beings for the most part were born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
When they were born in that heaven, their bodies and minds were joyful and at ease; they took delight as their food and possessed natural radiance.
Furthermore, there are those with supernormal powers who travel through the air, possessing most excellent forms and long lifespans, dwelling in peace and happiness.
Monks! At that time, when the world undergoes dissolution, during the period of its dissolution, space is devoid of all things.

Within the Brahma palace, there was a sentient being whose merit, karma, and lifespan had been exhausted in the Ābhāsvara Heaven; descending from the Ābhāsvara Heaven, he was born within that Brahma palace. He was not born from a womb, but appeared suddenly through transformation. This Brahmā is named Sahampati (the two first characters of this name are repeated in the Sanskrit original); for this reason, he received this name upon his birth.

“Monks! At that time, there were other beings whose merit, karma, and lifespan had come to an end; having cast off their bodies and lives from the Ābhāsvara Heaven, they were reborn here. Their physical forms were upright and handsome, and they took joy as their sustenance. They possessed natural radiance and supernormal powers, traveling by soaring through the air. Their bodily color was most excellent, and they dwelt in this place for a very long time.”
When they dwell in this manner, there are no men or women, no noble or base; there are only sentient beings, and it is by this name that they are designated.
"Furthermore, monks!
At such a time as this, a terrestrial essence (pṛthivī-parpaṭaka) arises upon this great earth and remains solid."
For example, bhikṣus, it is just as when someone has boiled milk until it is done, and a thin film forms upon its surface, or as when a thin film forms upon the surface of water;
even so, bhikṣus, is it with this.
Furthermore, at a certain time, on this great earth, there arose a thickened essence of the earth that remained solid.
It was like the fresh butter produced from churning curd; it possessed such a form and appearance, and its taste was like honey free of wax.
At that time, among the various sentient beings there, those whose nature was inclined toward greed had this thought:
"I too should now take some of the flavor with my finger and taste it, so that I may know what this thing is."

When those sentient beings had formed this thought, they took the essence of the earth with their fingers at the level of a single joint and tasted it toward their mouths. Having sipped it, their minds were filled with joy; thus they did so once, twice, and thrice, until they developed a craving for it. Next, they began to scoop it up with their hands, gradually using their cupped palms, and finally they began to grasp and heap it up, eating it to their heart’s content.

At that time, when those beings were eating by scooping up food with their hands in this manner, there were other people who, seeing those beings thus devouring it, immediately imitated them and vied with one another to take and eat it.
"O Bhikṣus!

When those sentient beings thus scooped up the essence of the earth with their hands and consumed it, their physical forms naturally became coarse and unpleasant; their skin grew thick and rough, their bodies became turbid and dark, their appearance changed so that they no longer possessed radiance, and they could no longer fly through the air; because of the earth-fertility, their supernormal powers vanished."
"Monks! As previously stated, it shall be so hereafter; at that time, the world will become shrouded in darkness. Monks!"
For this reason, great darkness first arose in the world.
Furthermore, how did the sun and moon naturally arise in that period?
At that *samaya*, the forms of the constellations appeared, and there arose day and night, months and half-months, years, seasons, and their names.

Monks, at that time, the great and victorious palace of the Sun God emerged from the east, circled the midpoint of Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, and set in the west; having set in the west, it would again emerge from the east.
At that time, when sentient beings had seen that great palace of the Sun Deity, they said to one another:
"O worthy ones! This is indeed the luminous palace of the Sun Deity;
having emerged once more from the east, it has circled the mid-slope of Mount Sumeru to the right and set in the west."
Having seen this again and again, they said to one another:
"O worthy ones! This is the radiance of that celestial realm spreading forth; it is the radiance of that celestial realm spreading through the world."
Therefore, it is called *śūliya*, *śūliya*, *śūliya*; "śūliya" in the Sui language means "this" or "that," and thus such a name arose.
*Sūtra on the Causes and Origins of the World*, Scroll Nine;
*Sūtra on the Causes and Origins of the World*, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Dharmagupta during the Sui Dynasty.
Chapter on the Most Excellent, Part Two:

"Furthermore, monks, that great palace of the Sun of Radiance is fifty-one yojanas in length and breadth; its four sides—above, below, and across—are perfectly equal. It is surrounded on all sides by seven layers of walls, seven layers of railings, and seven layers of *tāla* trees, all interlaced with various colors to form a magnificent adornment."
Those walls were all constructed from the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.
On all four sides, there are gates; at each of those gates, there are watchtowers, defensive parapets, and palatial pavilions, as well as groves of trees, ponds, and gardens.
Within it, there grew all manner of trees, leaves, flowers, and fruits, perfumed by various fragrances.
Furthermore, there were the warbling sounds of various kinds of birds.
"O Bhikṣus!
Within that great palace of the Sun Deity, there are two kinds of structural elements that support the palace; it is square like a residence, yet from a distance it appears circular."
"O bhikṣus!
That great celestial palace of the sun is composed of much divine gold and divine crystal, interspersed and perfectly formed, with two parts being divine gold.
It is pure and stainless, free from all impurities, and possesses brilliant, radiant light."
One of its sides is made of celestial crystal, pure, radiant, well-polished, and well-refined, free from stain and impurity.
Monks! Within that great palace of the Sun Deity, there are five kinds of winds that blow and circulate.
What are these five?
They are: first, upholding; second, abiding; third, turning in accordance; fourth, reproving; and fifth, about to act.
"Furthermore, monks!"
Before that great palace of the Sun Deity, there were immeasurable devas proceeding ahead.

As immeasurable hundreds of devas, immeasurable thousands of devas, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas marched along, each constantly experienced firm and secure progress; such was the name for this firm progress.
Furthermore, monks!
Within that great celestial palace of the Sun God, a wondrous carriage made of Jambūnada gold is produced; this carriage is sixteen yojanas in height and eight yojanas in width.
Within that palanquin, the Sun Deity and his inner retinue entered; there, endowed with and fully possessed of the five celestial sensual pleasures, they moved about experiencing joy and delight.
"O bhikṣus!
As for the Sun Deity (Sūryadeva), his lifespan is five hundred years; his descendants succeed one another, all ruling there, and they dwell in that palace for the duration of a full kalpa."
"Furthermore, monks!

From within the various parts of the Sun Deity’s body, light issues forth and illuminates the Jāmbūnada chariot; once light has issued from within that Jāmbūnada chariot, it illuminates that great celestial palace of the Sun."
From that great celestial palace of the sun, rays of light emerge in continuous succession, illuminating the four great continents and the world. Monks!
That Sun Deity is endowed with a thousand rays of light: five hundred rays shine sideways as he travels, while five hundred rays shine downward.
Furthermore, for what cause and condition does the great and most excellent palace of the Sun Deity illuminate the four great continents and the various worlds? O monks!

There is a kind of person who is able to practice giving; when they give, they bestow upon śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, the solitary, and those who have come from afar to beg—namely, food and drink, vehicles, clothing, flower garlands, necklaces, ointments and perfumes, bedding, dwellings, and oil for lamps.
Whatever things serve to sustain the body and maintain life, when giving them, one gives swiftly and without guile.

Or again, one may provide various services to those sages who uphold the precepts, who are endowed with merit, and who practice the wholesome Dharma; because of this, one experiences immeasurable and manifold physical and mental peace and happiness.
For example, suppose there were a vast marsh, a desolate mountain forest, or a wide desert where a pool of water existed—its water cool, pure, light, and sweet.
At that time, a strong man traveling from afar became utterly exhausted; tormented by heat and parched with thirst, he had not eaten or drunk for many days.

Upon reaching that pond, they drank and bathed, thereby eliminating all thirst, exhaustion, and the torment of fever; emerging from the pond, their bodies and minds were serene and joyful, experiencing immeasurable bliss and delight.

In this way, because his mind was pure at the time of that giving, when his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn in the palace of the Sun Deity (*Sūrya-devaputra*). Having been born there, he obtained as a karmic reward such a swift, delightful, and celestial palace for flying through the air.
For this reason, the great palace of the Sun illuminates the four great continents and other worlds. "O Bhikṣus!

Furthermore, there is another kind [of person] who abstains from taking life, does not steal the property of others, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsehoods, and does not drink intoxicants; whose body is not negligent, and who makes offerings to the sages and worthies who possess the merit of upholding the precepts; who associates with those who practice the pure and upright wholesome Dharma—as explained in detail previously—such a person, at the breaking up of the body after death, proceeds according to their vow to the palace of the Sun Deity. There they shall receive swift karmic fruition; therefore, these are called the paths of wholesome karma."
For this reason, that solar palace illuminates the four great continents as well as other worlds.

Furthermore, there is another kind of person who practices non-killing up to right view; they have previously made offerings to various sages who possessed the merit of observing the precepts and pure conduct. Having encountered those pure causes and conditions, such a person shall likewise be reborn within a solar palace to receive swift fruit.
For this reason, that solar palace illuminates the four great continents and other worlds, as explained in detail previously. "O Bhikṣus!
Sixty kṣaṇas are called one lava; thirty lavas are called one muhūrta."
O Bhikṣus!
Through various kṣaṇas, various lava-s, and muhūrtas, as the sun-palace travels north for six months, the sun moves six krośas each day, never for a moment departing from its solar path.
In the six months of the southern course, the sun also travels six *krośas* in a single day, without deviating from its path. Monks!
While the sun palace travels that distance during those six months, the moon palace travels the same distance within fifteen days.
"Furthermore, what are the causes and conditions by which various heats and afflictions arise? Monks!

During the six months when the solar palace travels toward the northern path, it moves at a speed of six *krośas* per day; it never deviates from its solar course, yet within that period, ten kinds of conditions give rise to heat and affliction.
What are the ten? O monks!

Outside of Sumeru, the king of mountains, there is another mountain named Khadiraka, equal in height and breadth at forty-two thousand yojanas. It is variegated and beautiful to behold, perfected with the seven treasures. Within it, the light from the great celestial palace of the sun shines upon that mountain and causes heat upon contact; at that time, this results in burning affliction. This is the first cause for the arising of burning affliction.
Furthermore, monks!

Outside of Mount Khadiraka, there is another mountain named Īṣādhara, equal in height and breadth at twenty-one thousand yojanas. When the light from the great celestial palace of the sun reaches and touches that mountain, this constitutes the second affliction of heat.
Next is Mount Gandhamādana, twelve thousand yojanas in height and breadth; this is the third condition.
Next is Mount Sudarśana, six thousand yojanas in height and breadth; this is the fourth condition.
Next is Aśvakarṇa Mountain, three thousand yojanas in height and breadth; this is the fifth range.
Next is Nimindhara Mountain, one thousand two hundred yojanas in height and breadth; this is the sixth range.
Next is Mount Vinataka, six hundred yojanas in height and breadth; this is the seventh range.
Next is Mount Nemindhara, three hundred yojanas in height and breadth; this is the eighth range.
Furthermore, ten thousand yojanas above this great earth, in the sky, there are various palaces belonging to yakṣas made of crystal; this is the ninth causal condition.
Next, the four great continents, along with the eighty thousand minor continents, and all other great mountains such as Sumeru, the king of mountains, constitute the tenth condition.

The details should be understood as fully explained in the *Khadiraka* [Sūtra]. These are the ten kinds of great palaces of the sun that, during the six months, travel along the northern path; these are the causes and conditions for its scorching heat.
"Furthermore, for what cause and by what condition do coldnesses arise therein? O Bhikṣus!
After six months have passed, the great palace of the sun travels toward the south; within this process, there are further twelve links of dependent origination, and thus coldness arises."
What are the twelve? Monks!

Between Mount Sumeru and Mount Khadiraka, there is the Sumeru Sea, eighty-four thousand yojanas in width. It is completely filled with immeasurable *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses, which possess an intense fragrance. Within it, the radiance of the great palace of the sun shines forth and strikes [the waters]; this is the first cause and condition for cold.
In this successive order, Mount Īṣādhara is the second condition;
Mount Yugandhara is the third condition;
and Mount Sudarśana is the fourth condition.
Mount Aśvakarṇa is the fifth basis;
Mount Nimindhara is the sixth basis;
Mount Vinataka is the seventh basis.
The mountain of circular peaks is the eighth causal condition.
Within it, the various flowers are fully arrayed in their proper order, as should be explained in detail regarding Mount Khadiraka.

"Furthermore, all the rivers flowing within Jambudvīpa and the radiance of the great sun palace’s celestial mansion strike one another, thereby producing cold; briefly stated, this is the ninth causal condition for cold.

"Furthermore, all the rivers flowing through Jambudvīpa and those flowing through Aparagoyānīdvīpa are twice as numerous as those; when the radiance of the great palace of the sun shines upon them, this is the tenth cause and condition for cold.
"Furthermore, whatever rivers flow within Jambudvīpa, those flowing within Aparagoyānī are twice as many; this is the eleventh condition.

"Furthermore, all the rivers that flow through the continent of Pūrvavideha, and all the rivers that flow through the continent of Uttarakuru, are twice as many as those [in Jambudvīpa]. When the light of the great palace of the sun strikes them, this is the first coldness; this is the twelfth condition."

“Monks! During the six months when the great palace of the sun travels southward, the sun moves six *krośas* each day without deviating from its path. Within this process, there are these twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), which is why it becomes cold.”
"Furthermore, for what reason is it that during the winter season the nights are long and the days are short? Monks!
After the sun-palace has passed six months, it proceeds southward; day by day, the sun travels six *krośas*, without any deviation."
"At that time, however, the sun was at the southernmost edge of Jambudvīpa; because the terrain there is narrow and small, the sun passes through it very quickly. O Bhikṣus!"
For this reason, during the winter season, the days are short and the nights are long.
Furthermore, what is the cause and condition by which, during the spring and summer, the days are long and the nights are brief?

“O bhikṣus! After six months have passed, the celestial palace of the Sun God proceeds toward the north, traveling six krośas each day; it neither deviates nor shifts, nor does it stray from its usual path.”
However, at that time, the sun is moving within Jambudvīpa; because the ground is wide and its course is long, the days are therefore long.
Monks! For this reason, during the spring and summer, the days are long and the nights are short.
"Furthermore, monks!
When it is midday in Jambudvīpa, it is sunset in Pūrvavideha, sunrise in Aparagoyānī, and exactly midnight in Uttarakuru.
When it is midday in Aparagoyānī, it is sunset in Jambudvīpa, sunrise in Uttarakuru, and midnight in Pūrvavideha."
If it is midday in Uttarakuru, then it is sunset in Aparagoyānī, sunrise in Pūrvavideha, and midnight in Jambudvīpa;
if it is midday in Pūrvavideha, then it is sunset in Uttarakuru, sunrise in Jambudvīpa, and midnight in Aparagoyānī.
"O Bhikṣus!
That which is the western direction for the people of Jambudvīpa is the eastern direction for the people of Aparagoyānī;
that which is the western direction for the people of Aparagoyānī is the eastern direction for the people of Uttarakuru."
That which is the western direction for the people of Uttarakuru is considered the eastern direction by the people of Pūrvavideha;
that which is the western direction for the people of Pūrvavideha is considered the eastern direction by the people of Jambudvīpa.
"It is likewise in the two directions of south and north.
Within this context, the Buddha spoke these udānas:
"The shifting and the destruction, The emergence of heaven and the thin covering."
Twelve successive winds blow as the various devas pass before them.
As the watchtowers and battlements are swept by the wind, their bodies shine with radiance;
through the karma of generosity and upholding the precepts, they pass through kṣaṇas and lava-s.
"It is said that there are ten conditions for heat, and twelve kinds for cold;
regarding day and night, as well as midday, the four directions are explained as east and west.
'O Bhikṣus!'"

The greatest palace of that Moon Deity is exactly forty-nine yojanas in length and breadth; it is surrounded above and below by sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold networks of bells, and further encircled by seven rows of *tāla* trees of various beautiful colors.

Those walls are all composed of the seven treasures, from gold and silver up to musāragalva; at each of the four gates there are watchtowers and battlements, adorned in various ways as extensively described previously regarding the palace of the Sun Deity, even unto the various birds, each of which calls out its own song.
"O Bhikṣus!

That lunar palace is composed entirely of celestial gold and silver, interspersed with celestial blue lapis lazuli. Two parts of it are made of silver, pure and stainless, free from all dross and impurities; its substance is brilliant and exceedingly luminous.
That one part, of celestial blue lapis lazuli, is likewise pure, transparent both within and without, and its radiance shines afar."
"O Bhikṣus!
The most excellent palace of the Moon Devaputra is sustained and moved by five kinds of winds.
What are these five?"
First, upholding; second, abiding; third, conforming; fourth, gathering; and fifth, moving. Because it is upheld by these five kinds of causes and conditions, the lunar palace moves through space.
"O Bhikṣus!
Furthermore, there are immeasurable celestial palaces belonging to various devas that proceed before the lunar palace, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of devas proceed before it;
as they travel, they experience immeasurable varieties of bliss."
Those various devas all have names. O bhikṣus!

Within the great palace of the Moon Deva-son, there is furthermore a separate carriage made of blue lapis lazuli; this carriage is sixteen yojanas high and eight yojanas wide. The Moon Deva-son and his various celestial maidens enter into the carriage and, through the various merits of the five celestial sensual pleasures, experience joy in union, delighting and rejoicing as they travel wherever they wish.

“Monks! As for the Moon Deva-son, according to the reckoning of the devas, his lifespan is five hundred years; his descendants succeed one another, all ruling there, yet his palace remains for an entire kalpa.”

"O monks! From within the various parts of the body of the Moon Deity, light issues forth and immediately illuminates that carriage of blue lapis lazuli; the light from that carriage illuminates the great palace of the moon, and the light from the lunar palace illuminates the four great continents."
"O Bhikṣus!

The Moon Deva has five hundred rays that shine downward as he moves, and five hundred rays that shine sideways as he moves; therefore, the Moon Deva is called 'the one with a thousand rays,' and is also named 'the one with cool and refreshing light.'"
“Monks! For what reason and by what cause does the great palace of the moon illuminate the four great continents?

In a past life, he gave to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, to the poor, the solitary, and those who came from afar seeking alms—namely, food and drink, vehicles, clothing, flower garlands, various perfumes, beds, seats, dwellings, and all necessities of life. When giving these, he gave them promptly at the proper time with a mind free from deceit or crookedness; or again, he made offerings to sages who maintained the precepts and were endowed with merit, being upright, pure, and virtuous. By virtue of those causes and conditions, he now experiences immeasurable and manifold physical and mental happiness.”
For example, suppose there were a pool of water in a desolate mountain forest, a wilderness, or a vast desert, its waters cool, refreshing, light, and delicious, free from any turbidity or impurity.

At that time, a person traveling from afar, exhausted, tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat, enters that pool to bathe and drink, thereby eliminating all suffering and experiencing immeasurable bliss.
"It is so, it is so. By reason of those causes and conditions, he was born within the palace of the Moon Deva King and experienced the retribution of pleasure. Monks!"

Furthermore, there is another class of beings who abstain from taking life, up to and including abstaining from alcohol and heedless conduct, and who offer service and honor to various rishis; they too are born within that lunar palace and illuminate the four continents.

Furthermore, because there is the abstention from killing up to right view, one swiftly attains celestial palaces that travel through the air; these are called the various paths of wholesome action (*kuśala-karmapatha*).
By what cause and condition does the lunar palace gradually appear?
There are three causes and conditions. What are the three?
First, emerging from the side.

Second, there are gods with blue bodies whose forms, garments, and ornaments are all entirely blue; they constantly conceal their palaces during the half-month, and because of this concealment, the form of the moon gradually appears at that time.
Third, from within the great palace of that Sun God, sixty distinct rays of light emerge and obstruct the lunar disc.
For this reason, it appears gradually.
Furthermore, for what cause and condition does the lunar palace appear thus, perfectly round, pure, and full?
"O bhikṣus! There are also three conditions for this to be so.
First, at that time, the great palace of the moon emerges from its proper side; for this reason, it appears full."

Furthermore, those gods of the Blue Heaven have clothing and ornaments that are entirely blue. During the half-month, they remain hidden within the lunar palace; yet, on the fifteenth day of the *puṣya* month, the lunar palace becomes perfectly full and its radiance shines forth with intense brilliance.
For example, when many kinds of oily substances are present and a great torch is lit among them, all other lamps and lights are completely eclipsed and obscured.
In this very way, the great palace of the moon is always thus on the fifteenth day.
Furthermore, when sixty rays of light have issued from the great palace of the sun, they obstruct the pure lunar disk.

However, during the fifteenth day of the *puṣya* month, the lunar palace becomes perfectly full; at that time, it sheds all obstructions in every respect, such that the sunlight is unable to cover or obscure it.
"Furthermore, for what reason and by what causal conditions does the great lunar palace not appear at all on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight?"
"O bhikṣus!
On the fifteenth day of that dark fortnight, the lunar palace moves near the solar palace.
Because it is eclipsed by the light of the sun, it does not appear at all."
Furthermore, for what reason is the great celestial palace of the moon named "Moon"? "O Bhikṣus!
From the first day of the dark fortnight onwards, the light, color, and majestic power of that lunar palace gradually diminish and decrease; by this cause and condition, it is named 'Moon'."
Furthermore, for what reason and by what cause does there appear a shadow within the great celestial palace of the moon? Monks!

There is a Jambu tree, and because of it, this land is called Jambudvīpa. When the light of the pure lunar disk shines upon it, a shadow is cast; it is by this cause and condition that the shadow appears.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions do the various rivers flow in this world?

O monks! Because there is the sun, there is heat; because there is heat, there is distress; because there is distress, there is parching; because there is parching, there is perspiration and moisture; and because of this perspiration and moisture, juices and flowing waters emerge from within the mountains.
"Monks! For this reason and by these conditions, the world of rivers arises.
Furthermore, for what reason and by what conditions does the world of the five kinds of seeds appear?"
"O bhikṣus!
Whether in the eastern direction there be worlds that have already been destroyed after evolving, or that have already evolved after being destroyed, or that abide having already evolved;
so too it is in the southern, western, and northern directions regarding their evolution, destruction, and abiding."

At that time, the great wind Anāvilā, having shifted from another realm to become a dwelling place, blew five kinds of seeds and scattered them within this realm; having scattered them once, it scattered them again, and so on until they were widely dispersed—namely, root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, joint-bud-seeds, and seed-seeds. These constitute the five types of seeds.
"O bhikṣus! The great jambu tree has such fruit.
For example, like a measure-vessel of maṇi-jewels from the kingdom of Magadha, when they are plucked, their juice flows out; its color is like milk and its taste is as sweet as honey."
“Monks! The fruit of the Jambu tree has five divisions that produce benefit, namely: the east, the south, the west, the zenith, and the nadir.”

The eastern portion is the food of the various gandharvas; the southern portion consists of seven great settlements inhabited by humans, namely: first, Aviddhakarna; second, Kṛtaka; third, Avṛha; fourth, Aśva; fifth, Bhadraśva; sixth, Mānasa; and seventh, Uttaramanasa.

Within those seven great clusters of villages, there are seven Black Mountains (*kṛṣṇaparvata*), namely: first, Ekakaraṇḍa; second, Ekapiṇḍa; third, Kharjūra; fourth, Keśika; fifth, Śatakaraṇḍa; sixth, Abhibhū; and seventh, Abhyudgata.

Within those seven mountains, there are seven caves inhabited by brahminical seers: first, Fine Eyes; second, Fine Virtue; third, Small; fourth, Four-Tufted Head; fifth, Pool of Putrid Things; sixth, Black Entry; and seventh, Time of Increase.
Its western portion is consumed by the garuḍas; its upper portion is consumed by the *khecarā yakṣas*; and its lower portion is consumed by the various creatures in the ocean.
Regarding this, there is an udāna verse:
"First, the amount of rain was described, And its manifestation within the palaces."
In these two matters there is much wind as he proceeds before the various devas:
his palanquin and his lifespan; the radiance of his body shines forth, resulting from the karma of generosity and upholding the precepts, which extends particularly to the fulfillment of the wheels.
"The moon's reflection and its non-appearance; the causes and conditions for the presence of a reflection;
the various rivers and seeds; and lastly, the Jambu tree. O monks!"
At the beginning of the kalpa, when sentient beings consumed the essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa),
they remained in the world for a long time as it sustained and benefited them. Among them, those who ate much had inferior complexions,
while those who ate little possessed exceptionally radiant appearances.
At that time, because physical forms appeared, people began to deceive one another, disputing over who was superior or inferior; those who were victorious gave rise to pride.
Due to this conceit of self, the flavor of the earth vanished.
Immediately, a ground-skin (terrestrial fruit) appeared, perfect in both color and flavor.
Its color was like that of a fully ripened *karṇikāra* flower, and its taste was like that of pure honey without wax.
Those beings, having gathered together, were filled with sorrow and distress; they beat their breasts and wailed, fainting and exhausted, crying out:
"Alas, our earth-essence!"
"Alas, my earth-flavor!
It is like how, when people today have tasted some superior flavor and recognized it, they cry out: "Alas!..."
"This is my flavor.
Clinging to their former names, they did not understand the true meaning; those sentient beings were likewise.
At that time, those sentient beings ate the earth's crust, dwelling in the world for a long duration; they ate much of the coarse color and little of the superior form.
Due to the distinction between superior and inferior, they began to treat one another with arrogance and contempt; consequently, the surface of the earth sank down again.
Thereupon, forest creepers grew forth, possessing complete form and color, as well as perfect fragrance and flavor.

For example, it is like the kalamba flower, which possesses such a color that when cut, its sap flows out like waxless honey; as previously described, they gather together in mutual grief and affliction.

Following this sequence, once the forest creepers had disappeared, non-hybrid rice appeared; it was produced without plowing or sowing, manifesting spontaneously, free of awns and husks, consisting of pure grains, and endowed with both fragrance and flavor.

At that time, after those sentient beings had eaten in this manner, their various bodily parts—namely fat, marrow, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, pus, blood, and the network of vessels—as well as the characteristics of male and female sexual organs, began to manifest.
Once the characteristics of the sense organs have arisen, a defiled mind immediately emerges.
Because of this defilement, they gaze at one another repeatedly; having gazed at each other repeatedly, lustful desire is born.
Driven by sensual desire, they engage in unchaste conduct and impure sexual practices in secluded places.
At that time, there are other sentient beings who have not yet done so; having seen this, they say:
"O sentient being, what you have done is exceedingly evil; how can you act in such a way?"

Those sentient beings, subsequently feeling shame and remorse for having fallen into various unwholesome and evil states, immediately received the name *pāti-pāti*—in the Sanskrit language *pāti*, which in the Sui language means "husband."

At that time, because those sentient beings had fallen into such evil dharmas, when they engaged in sexual desire, they would bring food and say, "There is a *paliya*," or "There is a *paliya*. Thus they established this name; *paliya* in the Sanskrit language means "wife" (*bhāryā*) in the Sui language.

"O monks! For this reason, when the superior beings of former times saw couples appearing in the world, those multitudes would take them by the left hand with their right hands and push them away from that place."
After those sentient beings had departed for two or three months, they returned once more.
When the crowd saw them returning, they immediately struck and pelted them with sticks, wooden clubs, clods of earth, tiles, and stones, saying:
"You have hidden yourself well!"
"You must conceal yourself well.

This is like the present day, when women are being married; they may cast flowers, gold, silver, or clothing, as well as *rāja*—the term *rāja* being the Sanskrit for what the Sui language calls "hot rice-grain flowers"—and further offer such words of benediction:
"May you, our new bride, be peaceful, secure, and happy."
"O Bhikṣus! In this sequence, the people of the past committed such evil deeds; seeing that the people of the present likewise act in the same way."
For this reason, various sentient beings engage in unwholesome conduct within the worldly dharmas.
Following such a sequence, they construct houses as a means to conceal those evil karmas.
Thus the verse says:
"In the beginning he built Campā, and later Vārāṇasī;
at the end of the final remnant of the kalpa, he planned and measured out Rājagṛha."

“Monks! For this reason, when those former most excellent ones constructed villages, towns, settlements, cities, royal palaces, and the various abodes for beings in the world, such groups further increased during times of unrighteous conduct.”
There were other beings whose merit, lifespan, and karma were exhausted; they descended from the Ābhāsvara Heaven, casting off their bodies, and entered the womb of a mother. Monks!

For this reason, the former Victors were first born into the world. By the power of the remaining merit of those beings, there was no need for cultivation, and wild *śāli* rice appeared spontaneously.
If one wishes to take from it during the first watch of the day, it will immediately regrow by the last watch of the day;
if taken during the last watch of the day, it will regrow by the first watch of the following day, remaining of one consistent kind.
If not taken at all, it remains as it was, ever-present.
At that time, because the merit of those beings gradually diminished, they became indolent and lazy, and a mind of greed and stinginess arose within them. They thought to themselves:
"Now, since this non-glutinous rice requires no plowing or sowing, why should we toil and labor by taking it at different times—morning and evening? It is merely to exhaust ourselves in vain."
"I would rather take them all at once.
Thereupon, he took them all together.
At that time, the other beings called out to that person, saying:
"The time for the meal has arrived; let us go together to gather the non-glutinous rice.
The man replied, "I have already taken it all at once, both from the beginning and the end of the day, and brought it here."
"If you wish to depart, you may know the time yourself.
He then thought: "These sentient beings have well provided for their pleasure; at the end of the day, they take it all at once."
"I should now collect enough for two or three days;
it may even be gathered all at once.
He then took them all. At that time, another being called out to that being, saying:
"We should gather some non-glutinous rice together," they said.
He replied, "I have already taken enough for three days' supply; you should know the time for yourself."
Upon hearing this, those beings again thought:
"This person is most excellent; I too should now take the portions for four or five days at once, for the sake of storage."
At that time, those non-glutinous rice grains immediately produced husks and chaff that enveloped the grain;
those that had been harvested no longer grew,
while those in places not yet harvested remained as they were.
Those rice grains immediately broke apart and grew in clusters.
At that time, sentient beings gathered together, sorrowful and weeping, each saying to one another:

"I recall that in the past, our bodies were born of mind; we took joy as food, possessed natural radiance, traveled freely through the air, had most excellent complexions, and enjoyed long lifespans."
Then, for our sake, the "earth-flavor" (pṛthivī-rasa) suddenly appeared, complete in color, fragrance, and taste;
by eating it, we remained [alive] for a long time. Those who ate much became coarse in appearance and form, while those who ate little retained superior complexions.
Because they vied with one another over superiority and inferiority, prideful minds arose, and thus distinctions were established;

it was due to this condition that the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) vanished, and subsequently the earth-crust (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*) appeared, followed by forest creepers, and then non-glutinous rice, including its husks and chaff. When harvested, it did not grow back, yet when left unharvested, it remained as it was before.
For this reason, we have come to dwell as a distinct community in this single grove.
We should now demarcate our boundaries and establish a system of penalties, declaring: "That belongs to you; this is my portion. Whoever encroaches shall be punished."
"O Bhikṣus! For this reason, there arose in the world the designation of boundaries and punishments.
At that time, there was another being who, out of self-attachment to his own rice, stole the rice-grains of others."
When others saw this, they immediately said to him:
"O sentient being, you have committed an evil deed! You have committed an evil deed!
How can you, of your own accord, steal another's rice!"
Having rebuked him, he released him, saying, "Do not do this again.
Yet that sentient being committed it once more; he was rebuked and released again, and though this was repeated a second and third time, he still did not repent or reform.
He rebuked him with harsh words, struck his head with his hand, and, seizing his arm, led him into the midst of the assembly, declaring to the multitude:
"This man has stolen from another!"
Then that sentient being, in the presence of the assembly, denied and contested the conflict, saying to the multitude:
"This sentient being spoke harsh and evil words, reviled me, and struck me with his hand."
Then that multitude gathered together in sorrow, wailing and crying out:
"We have now come together to this place of suffering and misery."

"We have already given rise to evil and unwholesome states; because these afflictions increase, they will bring about the bitter fruits of future birth and old age, leading us toward the evil destinies.
We see before us how we are now being pulled, pushed, driven away, and rebuked by one another with our own hands."
"We should now seek a true protector to act as our lord.
He who ought to reprove us shall truly reprove us; he who ought to punish us shall truly punish us; and he who ought to expel us shall truly expel us."
"Let us each bring our own shares of rice from the fields;
whatever that guardian-lord requires, we shall provide.
Having thus deliberated together, the multitude then sought out a proper guardian.

"At that time, within that great assembly, there was another person who was exceptionally tall and preeminent, lovely and handsome, with a marvelous and extraordinary appearance, subtle and beautiful to behold, and fully endowed with a radiant complexion and dignified bearing."
Then the multitude of people spoke thus to that person:
"Excellent, O worthy one!
May you act as our true protector."
"We each have our own field boundaries here; do not encroach upon or deceive one another. Where censure is appropriate, censure rightly;
where reprimand is appropriate, reprimand rightly; even unto punishment, punish as is fitting; and where dismissal is appropriate, dismiss as is fitting."
"The unhusked rice that we have harvested shall be divided and given to you, so that you shall not suffer from want.

Having heard this, the man consented; he acted as the rightful master, reprimanding and punishing when necessary, while driving away wrongdoers and ensuring justice, such that no one could commit aggression.
The multitude gathered the rice grain to provide for him, ensuring that he lacked nothing.
Acting thus according to the law, he served as the lord of the fields.
Because he took a portion of the land from those sentient beings within their fields, he was given the name Kṣatriya; "Kṣatriya" means "lord of the fields" in the Sui language.
At that time, all those sentient beings were filled with joy and, relying upon his admonitions, practiced accordingly.

Among all matters of state, that Kṣatriya was skillful and wise; dwelling within that assembly, his radiant appearance was most preeminent. Therefore, he was given the title *Rāja*—*rāja* being the Sui term for "king"—and the great assembly established him as the Great Equal King (*Mahā-samata-rāja*). *Mahā-samata* is the Sui term for "Great Equal King. Thus, he was named Mahāsamata.
"O Bhikṣus!
When Mahāsammata was reigning as king, those people first received their name; they were called *sattva*, *sattva*—which in the language of Sui means 'sentient beings' (*sattva*)."
"O bhikṣus!
King Mahāsammata had a son named Hu-lu-che (Hulu-che), which in the Sui language means 'Joyful Intent' (Yixi).
O bhikṣus!"
During the reign of King Hu-lu-che (Huluca), those people were called Hei-yi-mo-ke (Heimaka), which in the Sui language means "Gold.
Monks! King Hu-lu-che had a son named Ke-li-ye-na (Kalyāṇa), which in the Sui language means "True and Righteous."
"O Bhikṣus!
When Kāliyaṇa reigned as king, those people called him Tilaśa, which in the language of Sui means 'born of sesame.'"
"O monks! King Kṛkin had a son named Brahmadatta (translated in the Sui language as 'Most Righteous and True'). O monks!"
When that Brahmadatta was reigning as king, those people were called Aparāntaka, which in the language of Sui means "Cloud Shards.
O Bhikṣus!
That King Meghaṇḍu had a son named Upoṣadha (translated in the Sui language as "Fasting and Abstinence"). Monks!
During the reign of that King Upoṣadha, those people were called Tālajaṅgha (translated in the Sui language as "Wooden-Shank").
"O Bhikṣus!
From the crown of the head of that King Upoṣadha, a fleshy sac spontaneously emerged, from which a boy was born, handsome and complete with the thirty-two marks. As soon as he was born, he cried out:
'Mātāta, Mātāta! (which in the Sui language means 'upholding the precepts')."
"Monks! That King Māndhātṛ possessed great supernormal powers and immense majesty; he ruled over the four great continents, governing and transforming them with sovereign ease."
The lifespans of these six kings were immeasurable. Monks!

From the right thigh of King Mūrdhaja, a child emerged from a membrane; he was handsome and complete with the thirty-two marks, named Dakṣiṇa-ja (Born of the Right Thigh), and possessed great power, ruling over the four great continents.

From the right thigh of that King, a membrane emerged from his left thigh, giving birth to a boy who also possessed the thirty-two marks; named Left-Thigh-Born, he was endowed with majestic power and ruled over three great continents.
From the left thigh of that king, a membrane emerged from his right knee, giving birth to a boy whose majestic appearance was as described before; he ruled over two great continents.
From the right knee of that king, a boy was born from his left knee, whose majestic appearance was as before, and he governed one great continent.
“Monks! From this time forward, there shall be wheel-turning kings who each rule over a single continent;
you should know this, monks! Monks!”
In this successive order, first the assembly established King Mahāsamata; next, King Manorama; next, King Samyaktva;
next, King Paramasamyaktva; next, King Upavāsaka; next, King Māndhātṛ; next, King Dakṣiṇajaṅgha;
next, King Vāmajaṅgha; next, King Dakṣiṇajānu; and next, King Vāmajānu.
Next is King Vimukta; next is King Vimuktatara; next is King Śarīra; next is King Rasāgra;
next is King Phalāratha; next is King Samudra; next is King Mahāsamudra; next is King Śakuni;
next is King Mahāśakuni; next is King Kuśa; and next is King Vikuśa.
Next, King Subhadra; next, King Mahāsubhadra; next, King Priya; next, King Mahāpriya;
next, King Rāvaṇa; next, King Mahārāvaṇa; next, King Nīlaka;
next, King Nāgūṣa; next, King Vṛka; next, King Sāgarabhāga; next, King Vajrabhuja.
King Bed, followed by King Lion-Moon, followed by King Nayaḍhi, followed by King Distinct,
followed by King Auspicious-Water, followed by King Feverish-Affliction, followed by King Maker-of-Light, followed by King Wilderness,
followed by King Little-Mountain, followed by King Mountain-Bearer, followed by King Flaming, followed by King Blazing-Flame.
"O Bhikṣus! The descendants of King Jvalana succeeded one another for one hundred and one generations, all of whom ruled and governed the world from that city of Puṇḍravardhana."
The last of these kings was named Śatrujit, so called because he was able to subdue all enemies. "O Bhikṣus!
The descendants of King Śatrujit succeeded one another in ruling and transforming the city of Ayodhyā; there were fifty-four thousand kings, the last of whom was named Durjaya."
