"O bhikṣus! The descendants of Prince Duryodhana succeeded one another in ruling and transforming the city of Vārāṇasī; there were sixty-three thousand kings, the last of whom was named Durmanas."
"O Bhikṣus!
His lineage, which was difficult to surpass, inherited the throne and ruled over the city of Kāmpilya; there were eighty-four thousand kings, the last of whom was named Brahmadatta."
"O Bhikṣus!
The descendants of Prince Brahmadatta succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the city of Śvetahastināpura. There were thirty-two thousand kings, and the last of them was named Gajamukha."
"O Bhikṣus!
The descendants of Prince Hastikaśirṣa succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the city of Kuśinagara; there were thirty-two thousand kings, the last of whom was named Ghoṣaka."
"O Bhikṣus!
The descendants of Prince Kuśa succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the city of Uruvilvā; there were thirty-two thousand kings, the last of whom was named Nagnajit."
"O bhikṣus!
The descendants of Prince Nādi succeeded one another in ruling and transforming the city of Durdharṣa; there were thirty-two thousand kings, the last of whom was named Jita."
"O Bhikṣus!
The descendants of that Prince Kṣemaka succeeded one another and ruled over the city of Kanyakubja; there were twelve thousand kings, the last of whom was named Jayasena."
"O bhikṣus!
The descendants of Prince Jayasena succeeded one another, ruling over the world from the city of Pāpā; there were eighteen thousand kings, the last of whom was named Devadatta."
"O Bhikṣus!

The lineage of those devas and nāga princes was passed down through generations, ruling and transforming the city of Tāmalipta; there were twenty-five thousand kings, the last of whom was named Sāgaradeva."
"O Bhikṣus!
The descendants of Prince Sāgaradeva succeeded one another and ruled over the city of Tāmaliptī; there were ten thousand kings, and the last of them was also named Sāgaradeva."
"O Bhikṣus!

The descendants of that Prince Sāgaradeva succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the city of Tāndrapura; there were eighteen thousand kings, the last of whom was named Sumati. His descendants succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the great city of Rājagṛha; there were twenty-five thousand kings, the last of whom was named Suśāsana."
"O bhikṣus! The descendants of King Kṣemadharman will succeed one another;
they will rule in the city of Vārāṇasī, numbering one thousand and one hundred kings. The last of these kings shall be named Mahādeva."
"O Bhikṣus!

The descendants of the Great Imperial Lord (Mahārāja) succeeded one another, ruling and transforming from the great city of Māyāpura. There were eighty-four thousand kings, and the last of them was named Sāgaradeva."
"O Bhikṣus!
The descendants of Prince Sāgaradeva succeeded one another and ruled over the city of Puṇḍravardhana; there were fifteen hundred kings, the last of whom was named Tapasvin."
"O Bhikṣus!
The descendants of Prince Duṣkaracaryā succeeded one another and ruled over the great city of Kuśāvatī; there were eighty-four thousand kings, the last of whom was named Bhūmipati."
"O Bhikṣus!
The descendants of that King Mahīpāla succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the city of Ayodhyā; there were one thousand kings, the last of whom was named Mahīdhara."
"O Bhikṣus!
The descendants of Prince Dharaṇīdhara succeeded one another and ruled over the great city of Vārāṇasī; there were eighty thousand kings, the last of whom was named Bhūmipati."
"O bhikṣus!

The descendants of that king, the Lord of the Earth, succeeded one another in ruling and transforming the city of Mithilā for eighty-four thousand generations. The last of those kings was named Mahādeva."
"O monks! The descendants of Prince Mahādeva succeeded one another, ruling and transforming from that city of Mahitīla.
There were eighty-four thousand Kṣatriya kings, and all those kings [ruled] in that Mahitīla."
In the Āmra Grove within the city, he practiced the holy life. His final kings were named King Nimi,
followed by King Mṛta, then King Dṛḍhasandhi, then King Kharaskandha, then King Upoṣadha, then King Nābhāga,
then King Sudarśana, then King Candrasena, and then King Śrutāyus.
King; next, King Dharmasena; next, King Vinaya; next, King Mahāvinaya;
next, King Punarvinaya; next, King Aśoka; next, King Vigatāśoka; next, King Skandhaka; next, King Rājaskandha;
next, King Malla; next, King Lauṇa; next, King Diśāpati; next, King Reṇu.
King, followed by King Kāla, followed by King Nanda, followed by King Ādarśamukha, followed by King Janaka, followed by King Droṇa,
followed by King Bhakṣa, followed by King Subhikṣa, followed by King Durjaya, followed by King Durjaya-vijaya,
followed by King Sthita, followed by King Susthita, followed by King Mahābala.
King [Dṛḍhadatta], followed by King Balavardhana, and followed by King Dṛḍhacārin. O monks!
The descendants of that Prince Dṛḍhacārin succeeded one another in turn.
While ruling and transforming the city of Kāśyapa, there were seventy-five thousand kings; the last of these kings was named Ambaṣṭha.
O bhikṣus!
The prince of Liśa was named Suvyūha. O bhikṣus!
The descendants of Prince Suvyūha succeeded one another in ruling and transforming the city of Potalaka; there were one thousand one hundred kings, the last of whom was named Kṛkī.
“Monks! At that time, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa; the Bodhisattva practiced the holy life under him and was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.”
The son of King Cīrika was named Sujāta; his descendants succeeded one another and ruled and transformed the city of Puṇḍravardhana.
There were one hundred and one kings, and the last of them was named Karṇa.
That King Karṇa had two sons: one named Gautama and the other named Bharadvāja;
one son of that king was named Ikṣvāku. Monks!

The descendants of that Ikṣvāku lineage succeeded one another and continued to rule and transform the city of Puṇḍravardhana; there were one hundred and one kings of the Ikṣvāku clan, the last of whom was named King Aśokadatta Ikṣvāku.
"O bhikṣus!
King Dīrghāyu begot four sons: the first was named Umuka, the second Suvarṇa, the third Gajapratibimba, and the fourth Śaṅkhapāda."
His son was Sthitapāda, whose name was Devapura.
His son was Govinda; their descendants succeeded one another, ruling and transforming the city of Kapilavastu, where there were seventy-seven thousand kings.

That last king was named King Vistara-ratha; next, King Prthag-ratha; next, King Dṛḍha-ratha; next, King Sthira-ratha; next, King Daśa-ratha; next, King Śata-ratha; next, King Navati-ratha; next, King Citra-ratha; next, King Jñāna-ratha; next, King Vistara-dhanu; next, King Bahudhanu; next, King Ubhayadhanu; next, King Sthira-dhanu; next, King Daśadhanu; next, King Śatadhanu; next, King Navati-dhanu; next, King Citradhanu; and next, King Jñānadhanu.
“Monks! King Jñānabāhu fathered two sons: the first was named Siṃhahanu, and the second was named Siṃhacara.
Siṃhahanu succeeded to the throne and fathered four sons: the first was named Śuddhodana, the second Śuklodana, the third Droṇodana, and the fourth Amṛtodana.”
Furthermore, he gave birth to a daughter named Amṛtā. O Bhikṣus!
King Śuddhodana fathered two sons: the first was Siddhārtha, and the second was named Nanda.
King Śuklodana had two sons: the first was named Tiṣya, and the second was named Nandika;
King Droṇodana had two sons: the first was Aniruddha, and the second was Bhadrika;
King Amṛtodana also fathered two sons: the first was Ānanda, and the second was Devadatta.
That Immortal Woman had but one son, named Śepha;
the Bodhisattva’s only son was named Rāhula.
"O Bhikṣus! [he said].

In this successive order, from Mahāsammata the Universal Monarch down through his descendants in that most excellent lineage, until the youth Rāhula attained arhatship, severed all afflictions, reached the end of birth and death, and shall never again be reborn.
"O monks! For this reason, in times long past, there arose in the world a superior kṣatriya who acted in accordance with the Dharma and not contrary to the Dharma."
"O bhikṣus! There is such a phenomenon:
among the world's kṣatriyas, there is a most excellent birth.
At that time, the rest of the sentient beings thought to themselves:"
"Worldly conditioned phenomena are a disease, an abscess, and a poisoned arrow.
Having reflected deeply thus, he abandoned all conditioned things and, in a secluded mountain marsh, constructed a thatched hut to dwell in silent meditative concentration.
When they have some need or requirement, whether in the first part of the day or the latter part, they emerge from their grass huts and enter the village to beg for alms.
When people see them, those who require something give it to them and even build dwellings for them; some even exclaim:
"These beings are most excellent at performing wholesome deeds; because they have abandoned the worldly, the stream of existence, and all unwholesome, evil dharmas, they are called Brahmins."
For these reasons, the Brahmin caste arose in the world.

There were some sentient beings who could not achieve meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and, dwelling in villages, taught many incantations and arts; for this reason, they were called "Teachers" (*Ācārya*).
Because they descended and entered village houses, they were called "Those Who Head Toward the Settlements" (*Grāmaga*).
Furthermore, because he accomplishes all dharmas of desire, he is called "one who accomplishes desire.
For this reason, in times past, he was born into the world as a preeminent brahmin of noble lineage and high conduct, acting in accordance with the Dharma and not contrary to it.

Furthermore, there are other classes of sentient beings who engage in various occupations involving the pursuit of profit, such as technical skills, crafts, and arts; for this reason, they are called Vaiśyas.
For this reason, in the distant past, members of the Vaiśya caste appeared in the world; they, too, acted in accordance with the Dharma and not contrary to it.
"Monks! After these three types have arisen in the world, there subsequently arises a fourth caste in the world. Monks!"

Furthermore, there is another kind who, having each disparaged their own family dharma, shave off their hair and beards, don the saffron robes, renounce the world, and leave the household life to practice the Way, proclaiming with their own mouths:
"I am a śramaṇa."
"Having made this declaration, he immediately becomes a Brahmin of Righteous Vows (Samyak-praṇidhāna);
the same applies to a Vaiśya.
Furthermore, there is another kind who, having previously engaged in such disparagement, likewise abandons the world to go forth as a renunciant, declaring with his own mouth:"
"I shall become a śramaṇa.
For that purpose, he formed such a right aspiration. O bhikṣus!

Furthermore, there is a class of kṣatriyas who practice evil deeds through body, speech, and mind; because of these evil deeds, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they experience nothing but suffering.
The same applies to brahmins, vaiśyas, and others.

Furthermore, there is a class of kṣatriyas who, because they practice wholesome deeds through body, speech, and mind, experience exclusively happiness after the dissolution of the body at the end of life;
the same is true for brahmins and vaiśyas.

“Monks! Furthermore, there is a certain type of kṣatriya who, through body, speech, and mind, performs two kinds of actions; at the dissolution of the body after death, he shall experience both suffering and pleasure.
The same applies to brahmins and vaiśyas.”
"O Bhikṣus!

Furthermore, there is a certain Kṣatriya who, having left the household life out of right faith, practices and realizes the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; he is able to exhaust all taints, attaining liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. Having realized the Dharma in this very life, he acquires the various supernormal powers. Having attained these realizations, he proclaims with his own mouth:
'Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence.'"
"The same applies to the Brahmins and the Vaiśyas. O Bhikṣus!

These three castes, though born from those [other] margins, are able to accomplish the perfection of knowledge and conduct (vidyācaraṇasampanna), attain Arhatship, and are thus called the most excellent."
"O Bhikṣus!
That Brahmā King Sahampati formerly spoke these verses before me:
'One born as a superior Kṣatriya, Who has emerged from among all castes...'"
"Endowed with the perfection of knowledge and conduct, he is the most supreme among gods and humans. "O monks!
That Brahmā Sahampati’s verse was well-spoken and not ill-spoken; I have approved it."
"O monks! I, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, also teach this meaning. O monks!"
In this sequence, I have fully explained how the world undergoes its evolution, dissolution, and subsistence. Monks!
Whatever duties a Teacher should perform for his disciples—acting out of compassion and for their benefit and welfare—I have already fulfilled them; you must now rely upon them.

"O monks! In these secluded forest mountains, beneath trees, in empty rooms, quiet chambers, earthen caves, cliff niches, or among burial mounds, one dwells in a grass hut made of rice stalks and the like, staying in such places far removed from village houses and inhabited settlements."
"You, bhikṣus, should cultivate meditative concentration; do not fall into negligence, lest you come to regret it later.
This is my instruction to you, all you bhikṣus."
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.

This tenth fascicle of the *Qishi yinben jing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Origins of the World), based on three leaves of a Sanskrit manuscript excavated from Central Asia, corresponds to the *Aṭṭhaka-vagga* of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, specifically the *Aṭṭhaka-sutta* and the *Saṅgīti-sutta*.

The *Kaiyuan lu*, section on the śramaṇa Nadi, states that the *Aṭānacitra-sūtra* (one fascicle) was translated at Cien Monastery in the third year of the Longshuo era; it is recorded in the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*.

The *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Shanjian lü*), fascicle 11, states: "If a king or a great donor (*mahādānapati*) of a village falls ill, they shall send someone to the monastery to invite a bhikṣu to recite for them the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. [The *Vinaya-saṃgraha*] fascicle 24 also cites the *Dīrgha Āgama*, specifically the *Aṭṭhaka-nipāta*, totaling thirty-four sūtras. Among these, four sūtras are entirely missing from the Chinese translation, while two are included in the *Madhyama Āgama*; here, their complete titles are now set forth."
